articles.title: NATO Scrambles F-16s and F-18s in Failed Intercept of Russian War Drone Over Romania
articles.body:
NATO defense forces on Thursday failed to intercept a single Russian war drone penetrating the air frontier of the member state Romania, in the second day in a row of unimpeded violation by Kremlin military aircraft of Atlantic Alliance airspace.
A Russian Geran strike drone entered Romania from Ukrainian airspace near the northern Romanian region of Botoșani on Thursday morning, at or shortly before sunrise. A major Russian missile and drone attack against Ukraine with more than 200 weapons, including hypersonic missiles, ballistic missiles, strike drones and decoy drones, had been in progress at the time.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to a Romanian Defense Ministry statement, Romanian military air defense radars first tracked the drone above Ukraine and heading towards the Romanian city of Botoșan. Two Romanian F-16s scrambled from Borcea airfield, a major Romania/NATO air defense base in the southeast of the country. The Russian drone flew in Romanian airspace for about four minutes before crashing in a forest near the village of Solca, Suceava County, that official statement said.
Defense Minister Radu Miruță subsequently told Digi24 television that the drone “did not pass through Moldova” and entered Romanian airspace from Ukrainian airspace.
A Russian Geran-2 drone flying into Romania from Ukraine via Botoșani would probably transit between 30 and 80 kilometers (19 and 48 miles) of Romanian territory before reaching Solca, and would have been in Romanian airspace possibly longer than the four minutes claimed by the Romanian Defense Ministry, Kyiv Post review of probable flight paths and typical Geran-2 cruising speeds found.
Ukraine’s Draft 2027 State Budget Envisages UAH 1.67 Trillion Deficit, KSE Institute Says
The Romanian F-16 fighter jet air base Fetești, near Borcea, is some 350-380 kilometers (217 and 236 miles) from Botoșani and Solca. Depending on the speed chosen by the pilot, an F-16 on an intercept mission would typically cover that distance in 10-20 minutes – possibly not fast enough to have intercepted the single drone flying towards Solca.
Following the crash, the Romanian Air Force launched an IAR-330 SOCAT helicopter from Bacău Air Base 95 “to monitor the situation in the area,” the Defense Ministry statement said.
A report by the major Romanian television channel Digi24 said that Russian military violations of Romanian airspace had tripled since 2025. Acting Minister of Defense Radu Miruță, in an interview aired Thursday by the channel, said that “it was an intense night from the perspective of the Romanian Army’s missions…Eight fighter jets were scrambled last night, from midnight until this morning, which is not a usual thing and is not something that is normal to happen.”
In Romania’s north-eastern Bucovina region, local residents recorded and uploaded to the internet video of a single, slow-moving propeller drone with a bat-wing silhouette and lawn mower engine sound consistent with a Geran drone, flying unimpeded in gray skies. Local chat groups reported loud noise similar to an explosion before the drone crashed, News Bucovina reported.
Journalists from News Bucovina and other media outlets reached the crash site prior to officials to film drone debris and the crash scene before officials arrived. Debris images published by Romanian media showed inscriptions in Russian.
The major Romanian news and information site, news.ro, reported Defense Ministry officials launched an investigation “immediately after the drone crash” and had sent specialists to the scene where they found dozens of fragments, and that an investigation was ongoing.
The Romanian Air Force’s failure to intercept the drone was the result of “dynamic” circumstances and peacetime rather than wartime rules of engagement, Miruță said.
“The Romanian Army and Romania are in a time of peace. Those who carry out such activities in violation of airspace, in violation of international law, must realize that it is not allowed,” Miruță said in part. “We, at the military level, have a responsibility to do everything we can with what we have at our disposal to defend the Romanian population.
Across north-eastern Romania, following the night-time air raid alert, schools in the Solca, Arbore, Botoșana, Cacica areas decided to suspend classes temporarily, until a 10 a.m. all clear.
Across the border over Ukraine, on the night, Russia, per Ukrainian Air Force counts, launched a 300+ weapon strike against Ukraine using anti-ship missiles, ballistic missiles, and 282 drones, including the Geran-2 that flew into Romania.
Within their own national airspace, per those Kyiv official claims, Ukrainian air defenses shot down four “Zircon” anti-ship missiles; three Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles; one “Banderol”/“Dan-T” cruise missile and 219 out of 282 Geran-type unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). By the standards of the Russo-Ukraine war, it was a mid-sized air attack by Russia whose most massive missile+drone raids have saturated Ukrainian air defenses with more than 100 missiles and 1,000 drones in a single night.
The single Russian drone violation of Romanian airspace was paralleled during the night of Sept. 23-24, by a drone or drones detected by Romanian air defense networks flying north of the village of Chilia Veche, over Ukrainian territory in the Danube delta region, where that river is the international border with Romania. Two Spanish F-18 fighters launched from the 57th Mihail Kogălniceanu Air Base, near Constanza, but per news and official reports found no targets over Romania to intercept.
Ukrainian civilian air watch networks on the night reported tracking four Russian drones crossing Moldova from Ukrainian airspace, and that two of the aircraft appeared to have crashed in Moldova’s Sholdaneshtsky and Floreshtsky districts, in the central part of the country.
The other two drones flew on into Romania, those Ukrainian sources said, citing military air tracking data. Moldovan and Romanian official and media sources did not confirm the Ukrainian claim that two more Russian drones had passed into NATO airspace, in this case from Romania, without being stopped by NATO air defenses. Kyiv Post was unable to reconcile the conflicting reports.
Less than 24 hours before the Russian drone violations of Moldovan and Romanian airspace, on Wednesday, a Russian air force Mi-8 helicopter launched from an airfield in the Kaliningrad region flew into Polish airspace for about 42 seconds, penetrating about 300 meters (984 feet) into NATO nation territory, Polish air defense forces reported. The chopper returned to Russian airspace without hindrance.
“The flight of the machine was observed by the radio-location systems of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Poland. Fighter aircraft were scrambled, and ground-based forces and assets remained on standby. The nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defense. The crews of the Republic of Poland’s air defense systems conduct round-the-clock observation, remaining in constant readiness to ensure the safety of Polish airspace,” an official Warsaw statement said.
❗️ Informujemy, że 23 września br. o godz. 11.08, na północ od miejscowości Braniewo, doszło do krótkotrwałego naruszenia przestrzeni powietrznej Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej przez śmigłowiec Mi-8 Sił Zbrojnych Federacji Rosyjskiej.
Śmigłowiec wykonywał lot z Obwodu Królewieckiego.… pic.twitter.com/afULQdSeTc
Systematic Russian drone violations of NATO air defense began in September 2025 and have taken place regularly since then. NATO air defenses have struggled to intercept the low-flying Russian drones. Even in successful intercepts, NATO air commanders have been forced to deploy manned aircraft costing hundreds of tens of millions of dollars, firing missiles costing hundreds of thousands of dollars, to attack cheap Russian drones typically costing $50,000-75,000. NATO has appealed to the Kremlin both officially and unofficially to cease and desist, but with little visible effect.

articles.title: Press review: US, NATO hamper nuclear dialogue as US gains partial control of Greenland
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. The United States and the North Atlantic Alliance hinder efforts toward restoring the nuclear dialogue, while the US-Iran dialogue appears stalled, despite a recent meeting between the two countries. Meanwhile, US leader Donald Trump secures partial control over Greenland. These stories topped Thursday's newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: US, NATO hamper efforts to restore nuclear dialogue
Seven months into the expiration of the New START Treaty in February, the global security system is facing new threats. Russian Permanent Representative to the United Nations Office and other international organizations in Geneva Gennady Gatilov told Izvestia that France and Britain have begun an opaque buildup of their strategic arsenals, disregarding their own principles of transparency in the nuclear sphere. The destabilizing practice of holding joint NATO-led nuclear missions is being expanded further, and "some new schemes of deterrence" that heighten nuclear non-proliferation risks are being introduced, he said.
Earlier, US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said that the United States possesses orbital weapons for space control. The Western media said his remark could imply electronic warfare systems rather than kinetic weapons. Outer space is a sphere covered by the Golden Dome, a proposed US multilayered anti-missile defense initiative, Dmitry Stefanovich, research fellow at the Center for International Security at the Primakov Institute of World Economy and International Relations of the Russian Academy of Sciences (IMEMO), emphasized.
He views the likelihood of talks about a new agreement in the nuclear sphere as low, even as the number of challenging issues that require compromises has increased, the expert stressed.
Pavel Anisimov, deputy director of the International Relations and Political Science Institute at Russian State University for the Humanities, said the parties could soon attempt to agree on at least temporary limitations or channels to prevent a crisis. Now that the US has obtained orbital weapons, nuclear arms control can no longer be discussed separately from anti-missile issues, space and high-precision non-nuclear weapons, he argued.
Meanwhile, contacts at various levels between Russia and the United States are ongoing, and the two leaders regularly exchange phone calls. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio held a meeting in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly High-level Week in New York. However, no dialogue on strategic stability is currently underway, and whether it will be resumed depends on whether Washington acknowledges the need to improve relations with Russia, Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov said.
Izvestia: US-Iran dialogue stalled, despite contacts at UNGA
The meeting between Iranian and US officials at the UN General Assembly is unlikely to end the confrontation between the two countries, experts interviewed by Izvestia said as they warned about escalation risks instead, even as US President Donald Trump described the three-hour talks as "very good." The US leader himself was absent from the meeting as he refused to tone down harsh rhetoric toward Tehran, saying that a deal could be made and threatening to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic. However, Tehran is standing its ground: the Iranian side said it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz as soon as the US lifts its naval blockade, unblocks frozen assets, pays compensation, and ends the war "on all fronts."
The US-Iran meeting on the sidelines of the UNGA was the first after the June ceasefire completely collapsed. The US team of negotiators included special presidential envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, while Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi represented Iran. At that, the two countries’ diplomats did not communicate directly, and Qatari officials acted as mediators as they moved between the two delegations during the day.
Experts interviewed by Izvestia do not expect any breakthrough from the New York meetings. The contacts themselves were positive, as they could help ease tensions for a while, Yelena Suponina, an expert in Oriental studies, said. However, she continued, one should not expect any lasting settlement amid the deep mutual mistrust and fundamental differences between the two countries.
Each side pursues its own pragmatic goals in this round of talks, with Tehran, for one, seeking to demonstrate readiness for dialogue, Igor Pshenichnikov, a political analyst, said. The talks could also help Trump to demonstrate to the US electorate at least minimal progress on the foreign policy track before the congressional midterms.
There is no chance of an actual settlement right now, another political analyst, Alexander Kargin, said. According to him, the points of the Islamabad memorandum, signed last summer, were basically never implemented, except for the brief reopening of the Hormuz Strait for purely pragmatic purposes: Tehran needed to resume oil exports and Washington sought to bring fuel prices down. Transit is blocked again, and the two sides are waiting to see who will be first to make concessions.
According to Pshenichnikov, Trump cannot get out of the conflict, as this would mean capitulation for the White House. However, he cannot continue the protracted campaign either. Since Tehran's conditions remain unacceptable to the United States, the confrontation may flare up with renewed vigor and escalate to a large-scale regional crisis after the November election, the analyst warned.
Kommersant: US gets partial control of Greenland
At a ceremony on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly session in New York on September 22, the United States, Denmark and Greenland signed an agreement on defense cooperation that will allow the Americans to expand their military presence on this strategically important Danish island and make it almost inaccessible to non-Western countries. Even as Greenland remains an autonomous Danish territory, the document gives such broad powers to the US that a case could easily be made for its partial control of the island.
Among other things, the US will get the right to modernize and expand the Pituffik space base, formerly known as Thule, and build two new facilities in Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig. Besides, the agreement provides a legal opportunity to accelerate the deployment of additional military bases there.
Alexander Yermakov, researcher with the Center for International Security at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of World Economy and International Relations, explained in a column for Kommersant that the US decided to resume expanding its military activities on the island after their gradual reduction there peaked in the 1950s-early 1960s.
Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig will likely host patrol aircraft and drones for monitoring the northern Atlantic Ocean and the Arctic, even as other activities, including the deployment of offensive arms or anti-missile systems, cannot be ruled out either, the expert argued. It’s hard to predict for now but it is a matter of modernizing space surveillance systems as the US base there has primarily served this purpose over the past few decades.
As regards the Pittufik space base, a line in the new agreement reads that the sides agree to deploy elements of the new generation Golden Dome missile defense system currently being built on Trump’s orders there. "This could perhaps imply anti-missile deployments as a radar modernization would hardly require a separate article in the agreement," Yermakov argued.
"It would be useful for the US to set up a permanent base for patrol flights and long-range UAVS there to monitor the Northern Sea Route and the broader Arctic and deploy infrastructure for more frequent and longer deployment of fighter jets in order to provide air defense purposes on the island and approaches to the United States," the expert concluded.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: Trump seeks to pave way for new meeting with North Korea’s Kim
US President Donald Trump held a meeting with his South Korean counterpart, Lee Jae-myung, on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York. As the US leader wished, he and Lee mostly discussed $350 billion in proposed South Korean investment in the US economy in exchange for lower tariffs on South Korean exports. Among other issues, the two leaders discussed the potential resumption of Trump’s contacts with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un.
Besides, the Trump-Lee meeting discussed fuel supplies to nuclear-powered submarines and South Korea’s push to secure US agreement to transfer wartime operational control to Seoul. Even as no combat has been conducted on the Korean Peninsula since 1953, the US maintains an 18,000-strong military contingent in South Korea that would form the backbone of an allied group of forces should war break out again. This does not sit well with the government led by the Democratic party which came to power in 2025 as it seeks to appeal to nationalist sentiments in society.
Alexander Vorontsov, head of the Korea and Mongolia Department at the Oriental Studies Institute under the Russian Academy of Sciences, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta in an interview that this was a long-standing issue. "Under the US-South Korea agreement signed in the 1950s, the US should hold the core war-fighting command of a combined US-South Korean force. Under a South Korean government led by Democrats, as is the case now, they say that this infringes upon the country’s sovereignty. <…> Therefore, they seek the transfer of operational command over their forces to South Korea. The Americans were previously skeptical of this idea. On the contrary, Trump takes a different view as he believes that allies should pay the US more for their defense and, whenever possible, defend themselves independently. Given this stance, he is more constructive toward South Korea’s ambitions."
Lee also hinted that Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping scheduled for September 24 could contribute to improving South Korea’s relations with China.
Also, Lee told Trump that he expected the US leader to help him restore ties with North Korea. Trump agreed to help as he also said he had established a good relationship with North Korea’s Kim. There has been no confirmation that Trump-Kim relations have been established indeed. There was only a statement from the US president that he would agree to meet with the North Korean leader and that he looked forward to such a meeting. If work toward this goal is underway indeed, a partial transfer of control over the joint US-South Korean battlegroup to Seoul could be part of the effort to create positive conditions for a meeting with Kim.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Moscow might need new mega-tall skyscraper
There are 2,594 buildings over 200 meters tall globally, including 256 supertalls of 300 meters or more, Oleg Bogdan, the creative director of Genpro architects, said at a discussion hosted by the Moscow State University of Civil Engineering. As many as 222 cities across 52 countries have at least one skyscraper of more than 200 meters. Burj Khalifa in Dubai is the world’s tallest at 828 meters, but it will soon lose that status as Saudi Arabia should build Jeddah Tower at 1,008 meters in 2028.
Russia appears to be an outsider against this background. The 462-m tall Lakhta Center in St. Petersburg is Europe’s tallest, and the Federation East tower in Moscow City, which is 373.7 meters tall, is second-tallest. Moscow is among the top ten global cities for buildings over 300 meters.
Moscow is currently building more skyscrapers than all European capitals combined, Vasily Solomin, the creator of the Neboskryoby (Skyscrapers) channel on Telegram, said. Almost as many towers as there already are is currently being built in Moscow City, meaning the number of skyscrapers in the business center will double in the next two to three years. And even more skyscrapers are being erected outside that area in the Russian capital.
The growing number of skyscrapers in and around Moscow City even distorts the silhouette of the business quarter and may deprive it of its postcard appearance, Filipp Nikandrov, chief architect at Gorproekt, argued. To prevent this, the capital needs a new mega-tall building, or a taller flagship building rising to 800-900 meters.
Projects are no longer being developed solely for PR, the expert said, as economic viability is increasingly being considered. In 2025, 114 skyscraper projects, or a record high, were put on hold worldwide. Only projects with genuine demand for commercial space survive, Bogdan explained.
TASS is not responsible for the material quoted in these press reviews

articles.title: Exclusive: The Admiral Who Must Prevent War With China
articles.body:
In the summer of 1986, when he was a college student in Pennsylvania, Samuel Paparo took his future wife Maureen to watch Top Gun.
Many young Americans emerged from theaters across the country with a new hero: the brash, daring, risk-taking Maverick, played by Tom Cruise, who became an avatar of American power at the twilight of the Cold War. But Paparo took away a different lesson.
“The hero of the movie is supposed to be Maverick, but the hero of the movie is actually Iceman,” Paparo tells TIME, referring to the main character’s rival at the elite Navy pilot training school. “Maverick’s got all the personal charisma, but Iceman is fastidious, quiet. He’s the hard-working guy that does the right thing, that doesn’t do flashy, dangerous stuff for its own sake.”
Paparo had already passed the Navy’s entrance exams when he went into the theater that day, and joined the next year. His career would precisely mirror the fictional Iceman’s: He attended the Navy Fighter Weapons School, also known as TOPGUN; became a fighter pilot; then a four-star admiral; and eventually commanded the Pacific Fleet. But Paparo would go further, taking the helm of the U.S. Pacific Command, the nation’s oldest and largest geographic combatant command, which covers about half of the earth’s surface.
Few Americans will have heard of Admiral Paparo, and that suits him fine. “If I do my job right, history will never know my name,” he says in his office at the headquarters of the U.S. Pacific Command in Hawaii, on a hill overlooking Pearl Harbor, in late July. But his role places him at an inflection point, as American dominance in the Pacific faces its most serious challenge since World War II.
His command is designed to be the immovable object that blocks the unstoppable force of China’s expansionist ambitions in the region. And those ambitions have been stated clearly: Beijing has vowed to bring Taiwan, the self-ruling island that has been politically separate from the mainland since China’s civil war ended in 1949, under its control—by force if necessary. China’s President Xi Jinping has described unification as “a historical inevitability.”
Paparo’s job, in its simplest terms, is the projection of American power. His most important mission is to deter a Chinese invasion of Taiwan, an event that would challenge the very foundations of a global system underpinned by American hegemony. That the outlines of this mission stay the same regardless of which party or President is in the White House speaks to the importance of his role. The force Paparo builds and the plans he puts in place last for decades, and could determine to whom the next century belongs.
The public face of American military power is, of course, the Commander in Chief. The public voice emanates from the Oval Office and the podium in the White House press briefing room. But behind that power sits commanders like Paparo, overseeing the often hidden and awesome infrastructure that backs up that public face and voice—his command oversees some 400,000 military and civilian personnel, a Pacific Fleet of some 200 ships, including five aircraft carrier strike groups, and more than 1,000 aircraft. He marshals that power in distant oceans, islands, and military bases that most Americans will never see or even think about.
With President Donald Trump set to meet Thursday with China’s Xi for their third face-to-face summit since he returned to office, the cameras are trained on the White House; reporters will parse each utterance by the two leaders to divine whether the two powers are heading toward cooperation or conflict. It is Paparo’s job to ensure that whatever happens when the leaders talk, U.S. power remains pre-eminent—and that if somehow in the future conflict breaks out, it comes out on top. He must hold to that approach even as wars elsewhere consume the munitions and resources he may need, and upheaval at the Pentagon raises the stakes of pushing back.
“I’m almost quoting Sun Tzu when I say winning without fighting is the acme of skill,” he says, referencing the Chinese military strategist who wrote The Art of War. “Mission success for me is not to fight and win a war; it’s to provide a deterrent capability so that we never go to war in the first place.”
Paparo, 61, speaks deliberately and in a low voice, smiling often. But when conversation turns serious, so does his expression—his brows become furrowed, and he stares into the middle distance to summon his words. “We don’t seek to become great wartime leaders,” he says. “We seek to be great peacetime deterrers.”
What if deterrence doesn’t work? The U.S. emerged from World War II with its dominance of the Pacific unquestioned, but that may now be changing. Over the past few decades, as China has transformed into the world’s second largest economy, it has been engaged in a historic military buildup. China’s defense spending has increased 13-fold over the past three decades, and it now spends more on defense than the next 22 Indo-Pacific countries combined, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a bipartisan Washington, D.C.–based think tank. It has made rapid technological advances in artificial intelligence and fielded several generations of fighter jets. Its navy has grown from a coastal force into something capable of projecting global power, and by hull count it is now the largest in the world.
Brian Hart, deputy director of the China Power Project at CSIS, describes it as a “comprehensive, across-the-board modernization effort,” one that has changed the calculus for every power in the Pacific. The People’s Liberation Army, he tells TIME, has “significantly transformed the balance of power.”
Paparo need only look out his office window at the turquoise waters of Pearl Harbor to be reminded of the last time U.S. supremacy in the Pacific was truly tested. He describes China’s buildup as “historic” and “an exponential increase in military power, and more specifically, in power projection capability.”
“Twenty-five years ago the People’s Liberation Army Navy was about 37 warships, and today it’s 12 times that,” he says. “Just in the last 18 months they’ve delivered two cruisers, eight destroyers, eight frigates, an aircraft carrier, 11 submarines, four amphibious ships, and four long-range combat logistics ships.” He is particularly concerned by China’s advances in space and missile development and the rapid expansion of its nuclear arsenal. “They’re moving toward world reach,” he says.
For all of its global ambitions, much of China’s military development has been pursued with one target in mind. U.S. intelligence assesses that China’s Xi has ordered his military to be capable of seizing Taiwan by force by 2027, the centenary of the People’s Liberation Army. The intelligence community’s annual threat assessment, released in March, suggests no invasion is currently planned for next year, but by then, the pieces Xi needs to do so will likely be in place.
If there appears to be a path to capturing Taiwan without using force, Xi insists he would prefer to take it. Presidential elections in Taiwan in January 2028 may provide some clarity in that regard: China’s old rival, the Kuomintang, is increasingly amenable to negotiations with Beijing. If the political party wins in 2028, the likelihood of an invasion may decrease. If Taiwan’s President Lai Ching-te, a fierce opponent of China’s sovereignty claims, wins reelection, Hart says, “Beijing could significantly ramp up pressure on Taiwan.”
Paparo’s job is to convince Xi that the costs of military action will be too much to bear, regardless of what is happening politically on the island. By act of Congress, the U.S. is obliged to sell Taiwan the weapons it needs for its own defense; while it does not require the U.S. to defend the island directly, the commitment could go further to include direct conflict with China. He describes his mission as a delicate balancing act between ensuring that his counterparts know American capabilities well enough to understand the risks of engaging, and protecting its necessary secrets and strategy. “It’s demonstrating credible combat power, demonstrating capability and will, but keeping the crown jewels of the nation that are going to deliver combat success opaque to your counterparts, so that they can’t build a counter for it,” he says.
Paparo describes the strategy as deterrence by denial. “It’s a way of expressing that we’re not seeking the overthrow of the Communist Party,” he says. “It’s just that you should know that where America’s direct vital interests are involved, there’s a high probability of denying your aggression.”
This theory of deterrence operates on a grand, geopolitical scale, and in much smaller interactions. Paparo recounts a confrontation with a Chinese counterpart over what he describes as an “unsafe” encounter in June 2023 during a transit of the Taiwan Strait in which a Chinese Luyang destroyer cut across the bow of an American ship.
In the ensuing back-and-forth, Paparo told his counterpart that he had been in command at the watch center for the engagement and had video showing that their version of events was not true. He offered to share it, then let the matter rest.
“I’m not going to impugn his own character in it. He’s representing his country. He’s in uniform, and you know, if we do have a fight, him and I might have to shake hands at the end and agree to go to our separate sides,” he says.
In that moment, Paparo chose a diplomatic approach. He does, however, have a more direct plan to deter a Chinese attack on Taiwan. It is based on a term he uses to describe the environment Chinese forces would walk into if they took military action: “Hellscape.”
The strategy has been partly inspired by Ukraine’s defense against Russian invasion, and its ability to halt Moscow’s advances by turning the front lines of that conflict into a no-man’s-land patrolled by killer drones. Paparo would aim to saturate the Taiwan Strait with cheap, mass-produced precision drones, along with more conventional high-tech missile power, to deny China the ability to land an amphibious assault, or at least significantly delay it.
“We’ve seen that assault warfare, whether that is an amphibious assault, an airborne assault, has become a much more costly human endeavor,” he says. “In the ways that Ukraine is about a 600-mile-by-30-mile hellscape of drone warfare, I seek to put those principles at work to deter an armed invasion.”
He continues: “Putting 21st century technological change to work for the United States of America is what that’s about. We need not gain air or maritime superiority of a space; we need only deny its use to aggressors.”
Direct American involvement in a conflict over Taiwan is by no means assured. Paparo is tasked with building a force to confront China, but the President will decide how to respond. “The highest ideals of American civil-military relations are such that policy is king,” he says.
Who would win that conflict is something that is fiercely debated. A 2023 CSIS war game found that the U.S. and its allies defeated a Chinese amphibious invasion of Taiwan in most scenarios, but the costs to the U.S. were substantial: two aircraft carriers, dozens of ships, and hundreds of aircraft, the heaviest American losses since World War II. Those war games were run before the war in Iran depleted U.S. missile stocks.
“I am confident in our ability to prevail,” Paparo says. “What I am working toward is the margin by which we do, and that margin expresses itself in lives, capability, money, and time. I want to drive that bill down to zero.”
An enormous map of the Indo-Pacific theater lines the wall of Paparo’s office. His desk overlooks a large room adorned with historical Pacific artifacts and gifts given to the admiral and his predecessors: a five-star flag that belonged to General Douglas MacArthur; a barometer gifted to Admiral Harry Harris Jr., who led the command from 2015 to 2018, by China’s Ministry of National Defense. Closer to his desk is a large computer screen showing the positions of every vessel under his command. As he toggles through the ships on the screen to demonstrate the scale of his fleet, he pauses somewhere near the Indian Ocean to press home a point: His command is not merely preparing for war; it is fighting one. “The Iranian frigate was sunk by us,” he says. He is referring to an incident in March, when the U.S.S. Charlotte submarine torpedoed and sank the Iranian navy frigate IRIS Dena in the Indian Ocean as it was returning to Iran from India, where it had taken part in an international exercise. More than 100 Iranian sailors were killed. Paparo’s forces have also helped enforce a blockade of Iran’s coastline and support logistics for the war.
That the U.S. Pacific Command is fighting one war on one side of the world while preparing for another 6,000 miles away in the Taiwan Strait is a measure of its scale. As he stands in front of his map, Paparo sweeps his arm down the Western seaboard, along the coast to Southern California, and across the central Pacific, pointing out an array of U.S. territories and possessions. These places may seem like distant lands to many Americans. To Paparo, they are as much a part of the U.S. as New York or California. To see the Pacific in this way is to understand the meaning behind this projection of power: it’s not just for the protection of an important strategic partner in Taiwan; it is for the protection of the U.S. itself. “There’s no more Pacific a country in the world than the United States of America,” he says.
It’s not just about Taiwan and China, either. The North Koreans, he says, “are seeking a nuclear deterrent” and want to present the world with a “fait accompli.” The Russians “have increased their air, missile, and maritime capabilities.”
Much of the job is managing friends rather than enemies. The Pentagon has called on Paparo to mediate between allies at odds with one another, and he says there is nothing new in that. Those military-to-military relationships, he adds, “tend to be an anchor that attenuates the ups and downs of policy disagreements among political leaders ... but it always respects the national policy of our civilian leadership.”
Few conflicts in the world today do not brush up against the Indo-Pacific theater or impact it in some way. The Iran war and U.S. support for Ukraine have placed severe strain on the resources available to all commands, causing a depletion in the stockpiles for missile defense like the Patriot and THAAD systems, and in long-range ground attack missiles, according to the Pentagon and CSIS estimates.
In May, a planned $14 billion arms package for Taiwan was put under review in part to preserve munitions for the Iran war. Experts have warned it may take years to replenish those stocks, a timeline that could affect the calculus of China and Russia.
Those shortages are no secret, but it’s a perilous time to be out of step with the White House and the Pentagon. At least 20 top military leaders, including generals and admirals, have been fired or left their positions since Pete Hegseth became Secretary of Defense at the start of the second Trump Administration. The turmoil culminated in the late August resignation of Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who reportedly left his role after clashing with Hegseth over the firings of senior generals and the Secretary’s alleged stymieing of Army modernization efforts in the midst of a U.S. war against Iran.
Hegseth has characterized those departures as part of a campaign to undo what he saw as the promotion of “woke” leadership. In a speech in September 2025 in Quantico, Va., to the military’s generals and admirals, all of whom were required to attend, Hegseth criticized the promotion of leaders for what he described as “the wrong reasons, based on their race, based on gender quotas, based on historic so-called firsts.” Paparo was visible in the front row of that gathering, his expression giving nothing away.
He has been careful in his public remarks about the impact the war in Iran has had on the readiness of his command. When questioned in the Senate about how prolonged conflict could impinge on his mission, Paparo conceded only that “there are finite limits to the magazine, and I have all the faith in the world that they’re being employed judiciously.”
In private, he appears to have been more candid. Paparo’s name emerged recently in a Washington Post report on a classified assessment, along with other combatant commanders, in which he is said to have objected to the continued use of an aircraft carrier strike group and destroyers for the war in Iran. He was also named in a New York Times report as one of several “private interlocutors” who had been offering “unvarnished” views of the Iran war to Vice President JD Vance. Vance’s team declined to comment on the report.
Ward Carroll, a Navy veteran who flew in F-14s and a friend of Paparo’s for many years, says the admiral’s circumspection is part of his character. “He doesn’t want headlines,” he says. “He’s not out there like some other folks have been, saying Epic Fury was a huge mistake. He may say it in private ... but he’s certainly not going to say it to the media or allow it to be leaked.” Paparo excels, Carroll says, by choosing not to “wade into the food fight that is modern-day media and politics at all.” A spokesperson for Pacific Command declined to comment on Paparo’s private conversations about the Iran war.
When TIME asks Paparo about the potential impact of Ukraine and Iran, he is again cautious, pivoting to the lessons the U.S. is learning from both: namely the rapid deployment of drones in Ukraine and of AI-enabled operations in Iran, which were used to select and recommend targets for the U.S. military.
“The nature of an operation in the Pacific would be to counter an amphibious invasion. Well, we’ve just not used a lot of anti-ship weapons—we still maintain robust inventories of those,” he says. “And so, while I’m not going to whistle past the problem of the expenditure of munitions, it is our job to charge into the learning, and for us to get better.”
If there is a permanence to America’s projection of power in the Pacific, it can also be found in Paparo’s own family. His father Samuel Paparo Sr., who died in February, served four years in the Marine Corps before becoming a shipworker at the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard. There he helped refit the aircraft carrier U.S.S. Kitty Hawk and repair the U.S.S. John F. Kennedy. The younger Paparo would later fly from both. “He was really proud of that,” he says of his father. His grandfather was a Seabee, serving in one of the Navy’s construction battalions across the Pacific during World War II, in Bora Bora, Guam, and other islands. He died when Paparo was 13, but he left behind an old wooden scrapbook he had built with pictures from the war and all the places he had been. A young Paparo would pick it up from time to time and leaf through it. “I don’t think he imagined his grandson to be here in command,” he says.
His mother washed hair in a South Philadelphia barbershop and later worked a makeup counter in a department store. “Neither my father nor his father finished high school. In fact, nobody in my family before me had ever had a university education,” he says. He would later attend Villanova, the Catholic college also attended by the first American Pontiff, Pope Leo XIV. “We make Popes and admirals,” he says of his alma mater.
He joined TOPGUN, whose exacting culture left a lasting impression. “What the school confers is attention to detail, dedication to execution, dedication to getting better, and being introspective and running to your own problems, of seeking the perfect flight that you’ll never get,” he adds. He flew F-14, F-15, and F/A-18 jets, and clocked more than 6,000 flight hours and 1,100 carrier landings. He says he initially aimed to serve as long as his father. “Serving for four years was intentional, and serving for 40 was a blessing,” he adds.
Paparo’s time leading the Pacific Command is historic not just for the opponent he faces, but also because it coincides with a rapid and dramatic change in the nature of warfare. On one wall of his office hangs a reprint of a TIME cover from May 18, 1942, depicting Admiral Chester Nimitz, the naval commander who led the U.S. to victory over Japan at sea in the Pacific war. Nimitz took command of the Pacific Fleet in December 1941, also at a time of great technological change.
After Pearl Harbor, and under Nimitz’s watch, the battleship would be eclipsed by the aircraft carrier. Amphibious warfare would be revolutionized and directed under a single commander. And then there was the kamikaze—organized suicide attacks by aircraft flown by Japanese pilots—and their foreshadowing of the questions posed by the advancement of unmanned aerial drones in warfare today. “He adapted to change, including the unknown,” Paparo says of Nimitz. “That’s the greatest leadership model I can think of.”
Paparo hopes that he never has to fight the war he has spent so long preparing for, that his plans go untested and passed on to the next commander. In the meantime, he will continue with the quiet work. “Mine is not a heroic story,” he says. “Heroism is service that happens at the unforgiving hour. The best service prevents the unforgiving hour.”

articles.title: Russia Launches Deadly Attacks On Ukraine; Zelenskyy Calls For Pressure On Putin
articles.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine with missiles and drones, killing at least eight people in Kyiv and the Kharkiv region, Ukrainian officials said.
The attacks early on September 24 came hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, speaking at the annual UN General Assembly meeting in New York, called on the world to step up pressure on Russia.
"A war that was not prevented in time, was not stopped in time, and for which Russia was not punished in time, keeps spreading," Zelenskyy said of the full-scale invasion Russian President Vladimir Putin launched in February 2022, warning that Moscow's aggression is not limited to Ukraine.
"The more freedom Putin has to act, the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else," he said.
In Europe and elsewhere in the West, there has been increasing concern over drone incidents, acts of sabotage, and other evidence of "hybrid warfare" attacks carried out by or blamed on Russia, as well as over the possibility that Moscow could launch a military attack on a NATO nation.
Poland's digital affairs minister suggested Russia could have been behind a fire that broke out late on September 23 at a Starlink satellite communications station in central Poland that, among other things, transmits Internet traffic through Poland to Ukraine and other countries.
"This act of sabotage was deliberately designed to disable the station...disrupting Internet access for various institutions, including the Ukrainian Army," Krzysztof Gawkowski told Polish public broadcaster TVP Info. He said the station was still operational.
"There is much to suggest that we are dealing with an element of the next phase of hybrid warfare," Gawkowski said, adding that "many indications suggest that it fits into this new Russian doctrine of attack."
Meanwhile, in an updated assessment of the threat from Russia, the Danish Defense Intelligence Service (DDIS) said Moscow is likely to intensify hybrid attacks against targets in the West, possibly including cyberattacks intended to "cripple critical societal functions."
It said that while hybrid attacks had "mainly been aimed at creating fear and weakening public support for aid to Ukraine," they have begun to include efforts to prevent support from reaching Ukraine, such as sabotage against defense companies or trains carrying military equipment.
In addition, DDIS chief Thomas Ahrenkiel said there is "a low but growing risk that Russia will launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries bordering Russia."
The agency still believes it is "highly unlikely that Russia would see any interest in invading a NATO country, but we cannot rule it out," he told a press conference on September 24.
In New York for the UN General Assembly, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said on September 24 that "Russia is doing more and more" when it comes to cyberattacks and other forms of interference, but that "NATO is ready for this."
He urged countries to provide "more support for Ukraine" if they "really want to give a signal to the Russians on every hybrid incident, hybrid attack."
In Ukraine, six people were killed and 10 injured in an overnight Russian drone strike on a farm in the eastern Kharkiv region, Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskiy and senior regional official Oleh Synyehubov said. Koretskiy initially said seven were killed but later revised the death toll to six.
In Kyiv, two people were killed in ballistic missile strikes, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said, and emergency authorities said 10 others were injured.
One of those killed died in a parking lot near a maternity hospital in the Podil district that was damaged by missile fragments, Klitschko said.
The Ukrainian Air Force said Russia fired Zircon anti-ship missiles, Iskander ballistic missiles, and 282 drones in the overnight strikes, which it said mainly targeted Kyiv and the Odesa region in the south. Russia has been hammering Ukraine's capital with attacks on a nearly daily basis for weeks.
The September 24 strikes began not long after midnight, and Zelenskyy suggested they started while he was meeting with US lawmakers to discuss sanctions against Russia, including legislation that US President Donald Trump signed on September 18 and is aimed at increasing economic pressure.
"Russia will not end this war without pressure," Zelenskyy said in a Telegram post. He emphasized the need for more air defense systems.
Ukraine is suffering from a shortage of systems such as the US-made Patriot, in part due to the US focus on the war with Iran that began in February, and Zelenskyy emphasized that Kyiv needs more.
"Each such attack is due to the fact that the pressure on the aggressor has not become total and Russia believes that it can continue to rely on ballistic terror," he said. "Now the United States has the opportunity to react strongly. We need ballistic interceptors to protect lives."
Zeelsnkyy met with Trump on September 22 on the sidelines of the annual UN General Assembly.
Trump, who made ending Russia's war against Ukraine a priority when he took office for a second time in January 2025, said that peace could come "sooner than people think," while Zelenskyy said it would be preferable if the war could end before the onset of winter.
Putin has given no sign he is ready to end the invasion without capturing the entirety of the eastern Donetsk region at a minimum.
"For almost five years now, Russian generals have been trying to carry out Putin's crazy order to seize our eastern land, the Donetsk region," Zelenskyy told the General Assembly.
Noting Russia's massive losses, he said, "It's madness.... But they still keep going."
Russia has rejected calls for a cease-fire. At the UN Security Council after a meeting with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in New York on September 23, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Russia would not halt attacks while any peace talks were under way.
"We will not pause the special military operation for the duration of negotiations, regardless of the format," he said, using the Kremlin's term for Russia's war on Ukraine.
Rubio said that the United States has invited Putin to attend the Group of 20 summit in Miami in December. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on September 24 that Russia appreciates and values the "kind invitation" but that Putin had not yet decided whether to make the trip.
It would be Putin's first trip to the United States since he and Trump held a summit in Alaska in August 2025 and emerged with conflicting interpretations about what, if anything, was agreed upon about Russia's war on Ukraine. Putin has not attended a G20 summit in person since 2019.
Asked whether the EU would participate if Putin attends, European Commission spokesman Olof Gill said that "the G20 is a key forum for addressing existing and emerging global challenges, some of which have been created precisely by Russia's war against Ukraine," and that "Russia is escalating attacks on Ukrainian civilians as we speak."
"Since 2022, the EU has consistently and forcefully used G20 meetings to condemn Russia's full scale invasion and to call for it to end," Gill told reporters. "What I can say today is that this approach, from the European Union perspective, will continue, irrespective of the participants at any G20 meeting."
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that if "inviting Putin to the G20 could bring us closer to a just peace, I would be absolutely in favor of it."
"However -- and this is both my concern and what my experience tells me -- at this stage, Russia might well view it as an encouragement to continue its aggressive policies," Tusk told a news conference on September 24. "That is what I fear."

articles.title: ‘No one needs more fuel on the fire.’ Italy pushes back on report that CIA warned of possible Russian sea-launched drone attacks.
articles.body:
‘No one needs more fuel on the fire.’ Italy pushes back on report that CIA warned of possible Russian sea-launched drone attacks.
The CIA warned Spain, France, and Italy about a possible Russian operation to launch drones from civilian ships, the Spanish newspaper El Mundo said on September 24, citing sources.
A source close to Lithuania’s Defense Ministry said Russian forces could use Geran-5 drones hidden in shipping containers. The source cited Ukraine’s Operation Spiderweb, in which drones hidden in truck trailers attacked Russian military airfields.
Russian forces have launched drones from ships before, El Mundo said. The paper cited a drone Swedish forces shot down in February 2026 and a drone attack on Leipzig Airport that German authorities blamed on Russia.
British expert Keir Giles told the paper that Southern Europe might be chosen for such an operation because of its “political fragility.” All three countries are due to hold elections in 2027.
Spain also lacks air defenses capable of effectively countering drone attacks from the sea, El Mundo said. “The target will be wherever Europe’s weakest point lies,” Giles said.
The Russian news outlet Agentstvo noted that, before El Mundo’s report appeared, the pro-war Telegram channel Rybar had published a post titled “Russkoye ‘lekarstvo’ ot frantsuzskogo vysokomeriya” (“A Russian ‘Cure’ for French Arrogance”). The post considered a scenario in which Geran-5 drones would be supplied to Algeria, saying they “would put an array of strategic sites in southern France within range — key air bases, nuclear power plants, and strategically important factories such as the Airbus production complex in Toulouse.”
Several military analysts told El Mundo on condition of anonymity that they knew about the CIA warning. They said French authorities took it seriously and increased their readiness for possible drone strikes.
Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto responded to El Mundo’s report on X. “The alarm raised this morning by a Spanish newspaper about possible attacks on Italy, Spain and France by Russian ships and drones helps no one, and there’s no evidence to back it up. We’re already living through difficult and ‘tense’ times, and no one needs more fuel on the fire.” he said.
Over the past several weeks, Western media outlets have repeatedly said Russian authorities may escalate by intensifying hybrid warfare and sabotage targeting European countries allied with Ukraine.
Speaking in parliament in mid-September, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he had information that Russia was planning “hybrid” strikes using missiles and drones.
Vladimir Putin, for his part, said Russia does not threaten European countries and has no intention of doing so, despite what “European elites” say. At the same time, Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev threatened that Lithuania would “disappear from the map” if it decided to station nuclear weapons on its territory.
The war in photographs: Kyiv
Russia continues to strike Kyiv with drones and missiles. Two people were killed and a maternity hospital was damaged in a Russian attack on the Ukrainian capital overnight on September 24. The people inside the hospital were unharmed after reaching a basement shelter in time. A baby boy was born in the shelter during the attack, Ukrainska Pravda reported.

articles.title: UN General Assembly: Which Arab leaders are missing and why?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UN General Assembly: Which Arab leaders are missing and why?
The UN General Assembly (UNGA) kicked off on Tuesday, with around 130 heads of state and government gathering in New York for high-level debates and speeches.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres opened the session, held under the theme "Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all".
Other high-level meetings are being held on issues including climate action, rising sea levels, pandemic preparedness and the elimination of nuclear weapons.
While several speeches have already focused on the wars in the Middle East and the genocide in Gaza, some prominent Arab leaders have been notably absent from the stage.
The New Arab looks at who they are and what is known about the reasons behind their absence.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi was absent from the UNGA in New York for the fifth consecutive year, prompting speculation over why he has once again stayed away.
Sisi's decision not to attend is particularly noteworthy as he previously attended UNGA sessions, while delivering speeches virtually in 2020 and 2021 due to the Covid-19 pandemic.
Since then, Egypt has instead been represented by officials including Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly, former Foreign Minister Sameh Shoukry and current Foreign Minister Badr Abdel-Aty.
Some analysts have previously attributed Sisi's absence to strained relations with US administrations, while others have pointed to the possibility of protests over Egypt's human rights record.
Earlier this month, Sisi attended the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India, where he met Russian, Iranian and Indian leaders.
His continued absence from the UNGA has therefore attracted attention, with some commentators speculating that he may be seeking to avoid possible confrontations with US President Donald Trump, pressure over US demands concerning Gaza or involvement in the war on Iran.
Relations between Washington and Cairo have faced fresh tensions in recent weeks after the US Treasury Department imposed sanctions on branches of Banque Misr in the UAE over allegations that they helped finance Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
The US Congress has also refused to approve a deal for F-15 fighter jets for the Egyptian military since 2022 and has not supplied Egypt with AIM-120 missiles for its F-16 fighter jets, which the country's air force has relied on for years.
No official reason has been given for Sisi's absence. Speculation has ranged from Egypt's economic crisis and domestic pressures to regional tensions involving the Red Sea, Gaza, Yemen, Sudan and Iran, as well as potential threats to Egyptian security and the Suez Canal.
Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas
Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas is also absent from the gathering after the US barred the Palestinian delegation from attending the UNGA in New York in person.
Abbas was denied an entry visa for the second consecutive year.
The State Department did not give specific details on the decision but said the visa restrictions were imposed over actions by Palestinian officials to "internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian conflict", including pursuing cases against Israel at international tribunals.
At least 152 countries voted for a resolution last week calling on the US to reverse its decision. The US, Israel and Paraguay voted against the resolution, while Colombia, Honduras, Panama and Peru abstained.
The countries supporting the resolution argued that preventing the Palestinian delegation from attending constituted a violation of the UN Headquarters Agreement.
The agreement between the UN and the US requires Washington, as the host country, to facilitate the entry of diplomatic delegations, member states and observers attending General Assembly meetings.
Abbas is expected to use his address to press for international recognition of Palestinian statehood, highlight Israel's war on Gaza and push for renewed momentum towards a two-state solution.
He is also expected to address Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank and the continued expansion of illegal settlements on Palestinian land.
Sudanese Armed Forces chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan
Sudanese Armed Forces chief General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan is another prominent Arab figure absent from New York after the US refused to grant him a visa.
Burhan's army has been fighting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) since 2023 in a devastating conflict that has displaced millions.
The US State Department said neither the army nor the RSF, "nor their respective leaders, represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan".
UN chief Guterres was "deeply concerned" that Burhan had not been issued a visa, according to his spokesperson.
Sudan rejected the US decision and called on Washington to engage positively with Khartoum.
The foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Sudan "upholds its national sovereignty" and strongly rejected the State Department's position questioning the legitimacy of the Sudanese Armed Forces in relation to constitutional governance.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia threatened to withdraw from the Quad, a diplomatic grouping involving the US, Egypt, the UAE and Saudi Arabia, in protest at the visa decision, according to The Africa Report on Thursday.
Morocco’s King Mohammed VI
Morocco’s King Mohammed VI did not attend the UNGA, sending instead Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita to deliver the national address.
Bourita included the king’s strategic vision on global stability and international law in his speech.
King Mohammed has skipped the UNGA for several consecutive years, having last attended in September 2012 for the 67th session.
Since then, he has not attended in person and instead has sent other representatives, such as his brother Moulay Rachid or the foreign minister.
There have been various reports about why the king has long been absent from the UNGA, with some reports stating it is due to underlying medical conditions. In 2018, he underwent a heart operation in Paris for an irregular heartbeat.
He has also reduced his public appearances, with reports noting that he has appeared visibly frail since 2025.

articles.title: ‘Needed Every Day’: Zelensky, Rutte Talk Patriots
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky called for a NATO-backed winter air defense package after Russia launched three waves of ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv, saying Ukraine needs Patriot interceptors “practically every day.”
Zelensky made the appeal during a meeting with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte in New York, according to a statement published on Thursday, Sept. 24.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“When we met with Secretary General Mark Rutte, there had already been three waves of ballistic [missile] attacks on Kyiv,” Zelensky said.
He said he briefed Rutte on the destruction and casualties caused by the strikes, describing Russian attacks as the “constant reality” in which Ukrainians live.
“It is impossible to counter this terror against life alone,” he said.
Only Patriots can currently stop ballistic missiles
Zelensky said Ukrainian forces had learned to intercept Russian cruise missiles and drones and were developing ways to counter jet-powered Shahed attack drones.
“We are already seeing good results,” he said. “But against ballistic missiles, only Patriot interceptors work for now, and they are needed practically every day.”
The two officials discussed Ukraine’s current interceptor requirements and ways its partners could assemble a winter support package.
Zelensky thanked Rutte for his readiness to seek solutions, adding that stronger air defenses were also important for NATO members amid what he described as Russia’s continuing threats to expand its aggression.
Kremlin Says Too Early to Discuss Putin’s G20 Trip After Welcoming US Invitation
Ukraine intercepted approximately 60% of the ballistic missiles launched during the latest Russian attack, Zelensky said earlier on Thursday.
He acknowledged, however, that interception rates during previous attacks had fallen as low as 10%, while some barrages ended with no ballistic missiles intercepted.
“It’s not because someone lacks experience. Someone lacks missiles,” Zelensky said.
Three waves hit Kyiv
The Russian assault killed two people and injured at least six in Kyiv, according to city authorities.
Missile debris damaged a private house, a 16-story apartment building and an eight-story nonresidential building in the Dniprovskyi district.
In the Podilskyi district, debris damaged the facade and windows of a maternity hospital and set vehicles on fire in a nearby parking lot. A diagnostic center and several warehouses were also damaged.
No patients or medical workers inside the maternity hospital were reported injured.
The ballistic missile assault followed a major Russian drone attack on Kyiv on Wednesday that killed two people, injured dozens and damaged businesses, gas stations and transport infrastructure.
European allies of Ukraine were struggling to find enough Patriot missiles before winter because of limited stocks and competing defense requirements.
Most PAC-3 interceptors capable of engaging ballistic missiles are manufactured in the United States, making Washington central to efforts to replenish Ukraine’s air defenses.
