articles.title: Why Yemen's Houthis are so difficult to fight
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
From insurgents to regional force: Why Yemen's Houthis are so difficult to fight
On 10 September, Ansar Allah, also known as the Houthis, captured the Red Sea port city of Mocha during a major offensive against Yemeni government-aligned forces.
The group then advanced south, reportedly reaching the coastal town of Dhubab on 11 September, before moving against strategic islands near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, including Mayun, also known as Perim, and the Hanish Islands.
These gains have strengthened Houthi control along Yemen’s western coast and near the southern entrance to the Red Sea, threatening shipping on the wider Suez–Red Sea route, which carries about 12% of global trade and a significant share of global oil and LNG.
The offensive is part of a broader campaign that began in July, intensified in August, and peaked in September, including a Houthi naval blockade targeting Saudi-linked vessels and renewed attacks on Saudi oil facilities.
In September, Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline was also hit by drones launched from Iraq.
Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s internationally recognised government and allied factions have so far struggled to stop the Houthi advance.
Saudi forces have provided air support against Houthi positions and reinforcements, while Yemeni government forces and allied groups continue ground operations.
Meanwhile, the Houthis have pushed from the Red Sea coast toward strategic positions in the Kahboub Mountains in Taiz and Lahj, triggering heavy clashes over high ground overlooking the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
The Houthis have learned from years of war
The struggle to halt the Houthi offensive reveals how the Iran-aligned group has refined its military capabilities and tactics over years of conflict to expand its territorial and political leverage while advancing an agenda broadly aligned with Tehran. The offensive is also deepening Yemen’s role in wider regional tensions involving the US and Iran.
The Houthis, a Zaydi Shia Islamist movement, were formed in northern Yemen in the 1990s, emerging as a major political and military force in September 2014, when they captured Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, effectively splitting the country and triggering a civil war against the internationally recognised government and allied forces.
In 2015, a Saudi-led coalition of Gulf and other Arab states intervened militarily in support of the government. A UN-brokered truce in April 2022 temporarily reduced major combat operations.
The Houthis’ military strategy and tactics have evolved significantly over time. Their early insurgency relied on guerrilla tactics, mountain terrain, tribal networks, local alliances, and captured weapons.
With Iranian training and technical support, and assistance from Hezbollah, the Houthis developed increasingly sophisticated ballistic and cruise missiles, UAVs, and anti-ship capabilities, which gradually allowed them to strike targets in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and across the Red Sea.
This has led them to evolve into a regional force capable of targeting military, oil, and maritime interests beyond Yemen.
Their latest operations have also become more coordinated. The group, whose fighters are estimated to number up to 350,000, tends to attack using a combination of missiles, drones, artillery, and mobile ground forces.
The Houthi assault on Yemen’s western coast earlier this month, for example, suggests a shift toward smaller assault units that attack specific targets from multiple directions, according to Mohammed al-Basha, analyst and founder of risk advisory Basha Report.
“This approach makes them harder to target with airstrikes and allows them to maintain pressure on government forces,” he told The New Arab, adding that Houthi operations combining drone and missile strikes show growing firepower and ammunition capacity.
The latest escalation also highlighted the role of information warfare. The Houthis have allegedly used social media and digital platforms to put out propaganda and disinformation.
They were accused of using an AI-generated voice deepfake of Tareq Saleh, commander of the National Resistance Forces and nephew of former president Ali Abdullah Saleh, to send out a false withdrawal message, potentially causing confusion and lowering morale.
“The Houthis understand these forces really well and know that Tareq Saleh’s forces on the Red Sea coast are not trusted by the local people,” Michael Knights, head of research at New York-based strategic advisory Horizon Engage, told The New Arab. He explained that the Houthis effectively used SMS, email, and WhatsApp to flood Yemeni commanders with confusing messages.
“They also know that the Saudi forces are not particularly trusted by the Tariq forces, which makes it very easy for them to exploit the gap.”
A fragmented coalition struggles to respond
Internal divisions within the anti-Houthi coalition seem to have translated into poor coordination, making the Houthis more difficult to counter.
While the Houthis appear to have a more cohesive command structure, the anti-Houthi coalition remains divided, with Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) backing rival Yemeni factions.
In December 2025, tensions boiled over when Saudi-led forces struck a UAE-linked shipment at Mukalla, which Riyadh said was destined for UAE-backed separatists. Yemen’s Saudi-backed authorities then demanded the withdrawal of UAE forces.
“It’s impossible to bring them to work together because each of these groups has different political agendas,” Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen at the International Crisis Group, told The New Arab.
“There are also many issues related to military coordination, which have weakened the government and prevented it from mounting a strong resistance when the Houthis move toward any of their fronts.”
Internal divisions have, as a result, left Saudi Arabia without a unified, effective Yemeni ground partner.
RANE's Middle East and North Africa analyst Freddy Khoueiry told The New Arab that “airpower can destroy infrastructure and slow advances, but historically it has struggled to translate that into durable territorial gains without a capable ground force”.
This, coupled with weaknesses in the Saudi-led command structure and an intelligence failure to detect the Houthi buildup, has "likely contributed to the rapid collapse along the Red Sea coast".
Yemen’s geography is also a factor to take into account. The Houthis benefit from the country’s mountainous terrain, which means airstrikes have limited impact.
But at the same time, local forces have taken advantage of the same terrain to hold off Houthi attacks. This week, government and local forces in Taiz reportedly held strategic positions and slowed the Houthi advance.
Saudi Arabia is also struggling to secure external direct military support. The US said it won’t join the conflict for now, while Turkey and Pakistan, part of the Mecca agreement with the Kingdom, have yet to provide military assistance.
Riyadh has sought air-defence support from Egypt. The UK has agreed to provide defensive air-to-air refuelling.
Basha doesn’t rule out US intervention but said Washington’s reluctance reflects its existing commitments in the Iran war and concerns over diverting resources to Yemen.
“The Houthis appear to understand this risk,” he told The New Arab. “Their strategic communications have been carefully calibrated to avoid directly threatening American interests and to reduce the likelihood of US intervention.”
US President Donald Trump said earlier this month that the Houthis had contacted the US and “don’t want to fight us,” adding that they were “letting most ships go through,” while excluding Saudi-linked shipping.
Houthi control of Bab al-Mandeb adds a further layer to the US-Iran war. It potentially gives the Houthis leverage over a key strategic chokepoint while advancing their own agenda, and it could give Iran an additional pressure point alongside tensions over the Strait of Hormuz.
Fatima Abo Alasrar, a researcher and founder of The Ideology Machine, a publication on authoritarian information systems, said the Houthi campaign could serve a broader Iranian strategy of raising economic costs for Saudi Arabia and the US by disrupting oil and trade.
With Iran constrained by sanctions, its allies can disrupt rivals’ energy flows and create pressure for negotiations.
“The Houthi strategy is to drive a wedge between Washington and Saudi Arabia, leaving Saudi Arabia exposed while offering not to attack the US,” she said, noting that Tehran employed a similar coercive approach in 2018, when former President Hassan Rouhani warned that if Iran could not export oil, “no one else” in the region would be able to either.
“If that weakens Saudi Arabia and erodes trust in Washington, the Gulf security architecture begins to shake,” she told The New Arab.
The Houthis’ growing regional role has prompted Iran to become more vocal in its support. Nagi said the Iranians “are no longer supporting the Houthis from behind the scenes”.
Despite developing some military autonomy, the Houthis “remain heavily reliant on Iran for key components of their missile, air-defence and anti-ship systems,” Knight explained.
And despite being part of the ‘Axis of Resistance’, the Houthis still pursue their own priorities. Khoueiry argued they have incentives to calibrate escalation independently rather than automatically joining every stage of the US-Iran conflict.
“Houthis are more likely to complicate the wider war than fundamentally change its military balance,” he said.
Dario Sabaghi is a freelance journalist interested in human rights
Follow him on X: @DarioSabaghi
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russia takes aim at Ukraine's internet infrastructure
articles.body:
Key developments on Sept. 24:
- Russia puts Ukraine's internet in its sights as attacks on Kyiv infrastructure intensify
- Polish Deputy PM says Starlink station fire possibly Russian sabotage
- Denmark warns Russia could escalate hybrid attacks against NATO in coming months
- Ukrainian drones attack Russia's Rostov Oblast, Krasnodar Krai, allegedly targeting oil depots
Russian strikes have hit multiple data centers and internet providers in Kyiv over the past two days, disrupting service for around 100,000 households as Moscow expands its attacks on Ukraine's internet infrastructure.
Ukraine's Digital Transformation Ministry said around 100,000 households in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast experienced internet problems following the Sept. 23 drone attack, as specialists worked to assess the damage and restore stable service.
"This is the beginning of a phase where, since September, they have started taking it out systematically," Anatolii Frolenkov, a representative of the 1-IX internet exchange point, told the Kyiv Independent.
Frolenkov added that attacks on Ukraine's communications infrastructure are not new, pointing to earlier strikes on energy and telecommunications networks. But the recent escalation of attacks on data centers and communication nodes marks a shift in intensity, he said.
Several providers reported direct damage to their infrastructure. UTELS reported damage to a Kyiv data center housing its core equipment, leaving it without power, while Pavutyna said one of its data centers was hit, causing outages for some customers.
Crazy Network said a strike damaged a central internet traffic exchange in Kyiv, disrupting internet and telephone services in the capital and in Vinnytsia and Khmelnytskyi oblasts.
The disruption continued into Sept. 24. Kyiv-based provider Etherlink said an attack damaged its main network node, knocking some customers offline and forcing the company to relocate the core of its network.
Other companies reported more extensive losses. Hosting provider MiroHost said the data center in Ukraine that housed its infrastructure was destroyed in the attack, company founder Oleksandr Olshansky told dev.ua. Around 90-95% of MiroHost customers use infrastructure outside Ukraine and were unaffected, he added.
CityHost also said equipment it stored at a Kyiv data center had been destroyed, disrupting some of its services.
read also
Polish Deputy PM says Starlink station fire possibly Russian sabotage
A fire at a Starlink ground station in Poland may have been a deliberate attempt to disrupt internet access used by Ukrainian forces at the front, Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski told reporters on Sept. 24.
Gawkowski said there were indications that the fire at the station in Wola Krobowska, in Poland's Masovian Voivodeship, on the evening of Sept. 23, may have been an attempt to disrupt its operations.
The station is operated by the state-owned telecommunications company Exatel and serves as an internet hub that carries traffic through Poland, including to Ukraine, Gawkowski said.
He suggested Russia could be behind the incident, describing it as potentially part of Moscow's hybrid warfare. Polish authorities have not concluded their investigation into the incident.
He said a disruption could affect internet access for the Ukrainian military, potentially depriving Ukrainian forces of communications at the front.
On top of allowing flawless high-speed communications between combat positions and command posts, Starlink internet, when mounted on drones, allows for an almost unjammable connection not constrained by the limits of traditional radio antennas.
Over 2026, Ukrainian forces have found increasing success using Starlink-enabled drones over Russian-occupied territory, most notably in the "middle-strike" range (50-200 kilometers from the front line), where Russian logistics routes have been devastated by Ukrainian attacks.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk separately said on Sept. 24 that the circumstances of the fire "do not look good," while cautioning that it was too early to determine whether the incident was sabotage or an accident, Polish news agency PAP reported.
read also
Denmark warns Russia could escalate hybrid attacks against NATO in coming months
Russia is likely to intensify its hybrid campaign against NATO and Western countries in the coming months, carrying out more frequent attacks with potentially greater consequences, Denmark's military intelligence service warned on Sept. 24.
The Danish Defence Intelligence Service (DDIS) said Russia had become increasingly willing to take risks as the security situation in Europe deteriorates.
"Russia will intensify its hybrid war by carrying out more frequent attacks against the West and NATO, with greater consequences for the targeted countries than in the past," the agency said in its latest threat assessment.
The attacks could include destructive cyber operations targeting critical infrastructure as well as sabotage carrying a significant risk of casualties, according to the assessment.
DDIS also warned of a "low but growing risk" that Russia could carry out a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia, even while the war in Ukraine continues.
"A limited military attack would be a desperate move on Russia's part" and could take place "in the coming months," the agency said.
Such an attack could involve isolated drone or missile strikes against infrastructure supporting Ukraine, with Russia potentially claiming that the weapons crossed into NATO territory because of Ukrainian electronic warfare, according to the assessment.
DDIS also said Russia could stage a false-flag attack using Ukrainian-made drones or deploy a limited number of troops, potentially without national insignia, into a NATO country bordering Russia.
At the same time, DDIS assessed that Russian President Vladimir Putin remains unlikely to compromise on Moscow's core war aims and may see the next several years as a "window of opportunity" before European military capabilities grow significantly stronger.
Despite the increased risk of escalation, DDIS said it saw no indication that Russia was preparing a full-scale invasion of a NATO country. Such an invasion remains "highly unlikely," according to the assessment, although the agency said it could not be ruled out entirely.
The intelligence service estimated that Russia would need at least six months to prepare the forces required for an invasion.
read also
Ukrainian drones attack Russia's Rostov Oblast, Krasnodar Krai, allegedly targeting oil depots
Ukrainian drones allegedly targeted oil depots in Russia's Rostov Oblast and Krasnodar Krai overnight on Sept. 24, according to local authorities.
Russia's Defense Ministry claimed that Russian air defenses intercepted and destroyed 40 Ukrainian drones over several Russian regions, including Rostov Oblast, Krasnodar Krai, and occupied Crimea, overnight on Sept. 24.
Rostov Oblast Governor Yury Slyusar claimed Russian air defenses intercepted Ukrainian drones over Taganrog and the Kagalnitsky and Neklinovsky districts.
According to Slyusar, falling drone debris damaged administrative buildings at an oil depot in Kagalnitsky district, but there were no casualties or fire.
Additionally, Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ said on Sept. 24 that an oil depot in the settlement of Novotitarovskaya in neighboring Krasnodar Krai also caught fire following a drone attack.
Russian state-controlled media TASS claimed that a fire broke out on the premises of "a facility" after debris from a drone fell in the Dinsky district of Krasnodar Krai. No injuries were reported.
Ukraine has not commented on the strikes, and the Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claims.

articles.title: Russian ballistic missiles rock Kyiv as air defenses engaged
articles.body:
Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv kills 2, injures 8 after day of drone strikes
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Two people were killed and 8 others were injured as Russian ballistic missile explosions rocked Kyiv overnight on Sept. 24.
At the same time missiles were battering the capital, President Volodymyr Zelensky was meeting with members of the U.S. Congress, discussing the recently passed Lindsey Graham law while attending the U.N. General Assembly. 
"Right now, the United States has an opportunity to respond strongly," Zelensky wrote on X. "We need ballistic missile interceptors to protect lives. Sanctions against Russia and those helping it make money must be implemented."
Yaroslav Yurchyshyn, a lawmaker from the opposition Holos party, told the Kyiv Independent he believed the timing of the attack was deliberate.
"Russia is clearly trying to influence the positions of the U.S. and Ukraine and push us to accept its terms, which would effectively amount to capitulation. It is also trying to pressure the U.S. ahead of the elections so that Washington puts even more pressure on us," Yurchyshyn said.
He argued that the appropriate response would be for the U.S. and its partners to provide greater support to Ukraine and tighten sanctions against Russia.
Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the Ukrainian parliament's Foreign Policy and Interparliamentary Cooperation Committee, told the Kyiv Independent that Russia routinely uses provocations and strikes to test how the U.S. and its allies will respond.
Merezhko said Moscow may see Trump as increasingly focused on Iran and the upcoming U.S. midterm elections, creating what he described as an opportunity for Putin to escalate without facing a strong response from Washington.
"Russia acts in a very primitive way. They carry out a provocation, for example, and watch the reaction. If there is no reaction, they intensify their attacks," Merezhko said.
"They see that there is no reaction from Trump. Putin believes that Trump is busy now and has no time for Ukraine... Putin is using this," he added.
Russia launched 282 attack drones of various types overnight, including jet-powered drones, as well as Zircon anti-ship missiles and Iskander-M, S-400, and KN-23 ballistic missiles, according to the Air Force.
Ukrainian air defenses shot down 227 aerial targets, including 219 drones, four Zircon missiles, three ballistic missiles, and one Banderol munition. Strikes were recorded at 13 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at 10 locations.
"We had three waves of ballistic attacks. Today in Kyiv, 60% of the ballistic missiles were shot down," Zelensky told reporters at a press conference in New York on Sept. 24. "It is important. We would like more to be shot down, but today it was 60%, not 10% and not zero."
Zelensky added that there had been attacks earlier this year in which Ukraine intercepted none of the incoming ballistic missiles, attributing this to shortages of interceptor missiles.
"Russia has shifted to effectively round-the-clock attacks on Kyiv, Kharkiv, Dnipro, Odesa and other major Ukrainian cities," Ukraine's ambassador to the U.K. and former commander-in-chief Valerii Zaluzhnyi said.
"They are using everything they can. Old and new Shaheds are effectively going straight from the production line to Ukraine, while ballistic missiles are being stockpiled for nights like tonight," he said.
"For years, Russia has continued to receive imported components that allow it not only to continue, but also to increase its weapons production," Zaluzhnyi added. "The world must finally stop this. Otherwise, tomorrow it may fly not only at Ukraine."
Loud explosions were first heard in the city center of Ukraine's capital at around 1:00 a.m. local time, Editor-in-Chief Olga Rudenko said.
Ukraine's Air Force also warned that a ballistic missile was headed toward Kyiv after an air raid alert had been declared in Kyiv at 12:59 a.m.
"I got woken up by the sound of an explosion, slept through the air raid alert. When I checked my phone, I saw alerts for incoming missiles and went to my hallway as a series of explosions blasted out, one of them set off car alarms near my flat," War Editor Chris York said.
Then another ballistic missile was headed toward Ukraine's capital at 1:27 a.m., the Air Force said.
"It was quiet for about 30 minutes until another wave of ballistic missiles came in, I counted eight explosions," York said.
A third wave of ballistic missile explosions rocked the city again at around 1:52 a.m. local time, he added.
Updates from authorities
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that paramedics were headed to sites in the city's Solomyanskyi, Svyatoshynskyi, and Podilskyi districts as Russian missiles continued to target the city.
In the Dniprovskyi district, debris fell into a residential building courtyard, where there could be people trapped under rubble, he said. Debris also fell onto an administrative building in the district.
"In the Podilskyi district, debris fell on a parking lot near a medical facility. Several cars caught fire. Emergency services are en route," Klitschko said.
Kyiv City Maternity Hospital No. 2 was partially damaged in the attack, with windows and doors on the first through fifth floors damaged, as well as windows in the laundry and boiler room, Kyiv's Health Department said. No patients or medical staff were injured, as they were sheltering during the attack.
At 2:05 a.m., during the height of the attack, a baby boy was born in the hospital's shelter, where medical staff continued providing care.
"Even on such a terrible night, life goes on," Tetiana Mostepan, head of Kyiv's Health Department, said. "Our medical staff remain with patients under any circumstances and do everything possible to ensure that care is provided on time."
Although there were no casualties in the maternity hospital, one person was killed in a nearby parking lot, Klitschko said, adding that a medical diagnostic center was also damaged.
The attack also destroyed the production facility of Ukrainian jewellery business Dukachi, the company told the Kyiv Independent.
"When we arrived, we saw two groups of firefighters and realized that our premises were burning," co-founders Ana and Liza Knyzhenko said. "When we ran up, we saw a wall of fire. We understood that this was the end, that it was hell, and that nothing had survived."
The company said the building was effectively destroyed, with only some walls and partitions remaining. Equipment, furniture, and stock inside were burned, leaving the facility unusable and forcing the business to rebuild its production from scratch.
Dukachi said the loss was particularly difficult for a small business that had spent eight years building up the production facility. "We don't have programs or resources that would allow us to recover quickly. Everything will have to be rebuilt at our own expense, and that is very expensive and will take a long time," the co-founders said.
Russia regularly strikes civilian infrastructure and cities across Ukraine in fatal missile and drone attacks.
The prior day, on Sept. 23, a series of deadly Russian drone strikes on Kyiv killed two people and injured at least 43 others during the morning.
Railway infrastructure, residential buildings, and a historic market were damaged in the Russian attack.
On Sept. 22, Russian jet-powered drones struck Kyiv, injuring at least eight people and hitting sites across several districts of the capital, authorities said.

articles.title: Zelenskyy asks Japan for air-defense technology and offers Ukraine’s drones in return, while courting Chile to expand Ukraine’s reach in Latin America
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has used the UN General Assembly in New York to court partners outside Ukraine's NATO core, pitching air-defense cooperation with Japan and drone cooperation with Chile, Ukrainska Pravda reported. In a single day of bilateral talks, he met Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Chile's President José Antonio Kast, and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
The meetings turned on shielding civilian infrastructure before winter and trading Ukraine's battlefield-tested technology for capabilities it still needs. More than four years into Russia's war, a nation that entered the war reliant on donated arms now iterates drones faster than many of its Western backers, and that expertise has become leverage in its own diplomacy.
Zelenskyy pitches Ukraine's know-how for Japan's air-defense tech
In their first summit meeting, Zelenskyy cast the relationship as a two-way exchange.
"Ukraine is ready to share its experience and technologies on a mutually beneficial basis," he said.
While Japan has advanced technologies for protecting lives, particularly in air defense, that could carry Ukraine through the winter if Russia again rejects talks, the President's Office reported.
Ukraine walks into winter with two air-defense problems. It is still testing home-built interceptors to catch Russia's jet-powered drones. And it does not have enough Patriot interceptors to stop ballistic missiles over its cities. Japan holds the key to the second one.
North Korea has fired around 150 ballistic missiles at Ukraine, learning from each one. Same missiles threaten Japan, and Kyiv just shows its speaker what is inside them
Mitsubishi Heavy Industries runs the only plant outside the US licensed to assemble the PAC-3, the advanced Patriot interceptor. Japan is also the sole maker of the guidance gyroscopes inside older PAC-2 missiles. It has already shipped Japanese-made PAC-3s to the US to refill stocks drained by transfers to Ukraine, and Zelenskyy has floated Mitsubishi as the model for Ukraine's own Patriot line.
The exchange runs both ways. Russia keeps pressing Japan over the Kuril Islands the Soviet Union seized in 1945. Against that backdrop, Ukraine's combat-tested drones could appeal to Tokyo. Kyiv offers the drone know-how it now leads in, and asks for the air-defense edge Japan already has.
Zelenskyy also thanked Tokyo for its sanctions on Russia, energy packages, and humanitarian projects, and Takaichi assured him of continued support. Zelenskyy invited her to Ukraine, including the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, which Japan helped restore after a Russian drone strike in June.
Chile opens a door to Latin America
With Kast, Zelenskyy discussed deepening security and drone-technology ties and thanked Chile for backing Ukraine at international forums and for helping return Ukrainian children abducted by Russia. He welcomed Santiago's willingness to help expand Ukraine's presence across Latin America, calling it an opening for "even more promising opportunities," and invited Kast to visit.
Building on ties already in place
Both partnerships rest on existing ground. Japan, barred by its own laws from sending lethal weapons, has delivered generators, transformers, and non-lethal gear, pledged a $6 billion package for 2026, and agreed to help rebuild the Lavra through UNESCO. Talks in Tokyo in July recast Ukraine as a security partner rather than an aid recipient.
Chile joined the coalition to bring abducted Ukrainian children home and, in an April call, heard Zelenskyy float a security arrangement modeled on Ukraine's Gulf-state pacts. The outreach tracks Kyiv's drive to turn its wartime industry into an export business under its "Drone Deals" framework.

articles.title: From Zelensky to Pezeshkian, five speeches that stood out at this year’s U.N. General Assembly debate
articles.body:
From Zelensky to Pezeshkian, five speeches that stood out at this year’s U.N. General Assembly debate
United Nations meetings on September 23 generated an unusually large number of headlines. Heads of state addressed the annual General Assembly debate at U.N. headquarters in New York, and the Security Council met there as well. Below are excerpts from some of the remarks that drew the most press attention: speeches by the presidents of Ukraine, Iran, and Argentina, plus an indirect exchange between the Russian and Polish foreign ministers over Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Volodymyr Zelensky, president of Ukraine
To add another thousand square kilometers, Putin is paying with 248 people for every kilometer… […] And we know that Putin recently once again promised representatives from the American President that he would seize our Donetsk region. And he said he needs just a few more months…
This is probably the 17th or 18th time in 5 years that he has made this promise. It is always the same: “Just a few, a few more months”…
And then he moves the deadline again. […] Something always seems to stop Putin from simply saying: “That’s it. Enough. Peace.”
Something always stops him from admitting that 17 million square kilometers of his own territory — internationally recognized by all of you — should be enough for this man. […] He is “patient zero” — the one from whom this idea of war keeps spreading further. […] The more freedom Putin has to act – the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else.
That is why “patient zero” must be stopped.
Sergey Lavrov, Russia’s foreign minister
Russia — and President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly confirmed this — is prepared to negotiate to achieve precisely such a lasting and just peace. […] But having learned from bitter experience, we will not pause the special military operation during negotiations, regardless of their format. Europe wants exactly that, however, with the same simple goal of gaining a respite and replenishing the depleted military arsenals of the Kyiv regime, which, out of desperation, long ago resorted to openly terrorist methods.
[…]
When President Donald Trump said that Greenland could very well become part of the United States, a U.N. spokesperson was asked at a press conference what he thought about it. He replied: “The issue must be resolved on the basis of international law, the U.N. Charter, the principle of Denmark’s territorial integrity, and the right of Greenland’s population to self-determination.”
At a press conference on January 29 of this year, António Guterres was asked: “Does the right to self-determination also apply to Crimea and Donbas?” The secretary-general replied (I am compelled to quote him in full): “We have had some very interesting discussions on this subject. There are two principles. One is the territorial integrity of states. The other is the self-determination of peoples. But the self-determination of peoples entails a whole series of requirements, given the way this principle was formulated. And after a very careful study by our Office of Legal Affairs, our position is that the principle of self-determination does not apply to the situations in Crimea and Donbas. Therefore, in this situation, the principle of territorial integrity prevails.” If anyone understood any of that, I envy you.
As we can see, Greenland is neither Crimea nor Donbas, and “never the twain shall meet.” We eagerly await the next episode in this “series.” It will be interesting to hear the Secretariat’s response to possible questions from journalists about the plans of Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland.
Radosław Sikorski, Poland’s foreign minister
After more than four years of a senseless colonial war, Vladimir Putin has achieved nothing. He is running out of troops and resources and needs a pretext to mobilize. […] At any moment, Putin might try to provoke a NATO country and spread the war further, as we have heard from others.
To the representatives of the Russian Federation, I have this to say: […] You have been stopped by heroic Ukraine, a country with one tenth of Russia’s GDP. But Poland has almost half of your GDP, Europe has ten times your GDP, and NATO has 25 times your GDP.
You can still kill a lot more people, but you cannot win. […] Sergey, I know you’re listening. Tell your boss: Enough is enough.
Masoud Pezeshkian, president of Iran
The United States President described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism. I come from an Iran in which our esteemed Supreme Leader was assassinated without any legal framework or reason. I come from an Iran where, in truth, they bombed a school. You see these children? These children perished under bombs, with weapons used by the United States and Israel. They were innocent, had committed no crimes.
[…]
Those who are terrorists and train and protect terrorists describe us as such. We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists. Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country, and we defended ourselves with utmost strength. America and Israel attacked us, equipped with the latest technology and weapons systems, and our people stood steadfast. Yes, they did hit us, but we did not bend the knee. We did not bow our head.
[…]
Two hundred years—for the past two centuries— Iran has not attacked any country or any territory, but we’ve always defended ourselves steadfastly. But now we’re being accused of being [a] source of instability in the region? We’re labeled terrorists?
[…]
I will repeat: the nuclear weapon is in Israel, but the inspectors [are] in Iran. Israel kills, but Iran is subject to sanctions. […] Iran does not seek special treatment. We seek equal rights. […] Iran must be understood by Mr. Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force.
The U.S. representative left the room during the Iranian president’s speech.
Javier Milei, president of Argentina
That is, it became a useless organization whose only purpose is to feed a caste of parasites — hopelessly arrogant people disguised as well-intentioned bureaucrats. […] And as if that were not enough, an organization created to defend the territorial sovereignty of its members decided to look the other way when it came to the Malvinas Islands, South Georgia, the South Sandwich Islands, and the surrounding maritime areas.
[…]
Mr. President, just as I have shown you how the U.N. failed to do what it was supposed to do, I now want to tell you how it excelled at doing what no one asked it to do and what it never should have done. Alongside this failure, they have built a bureaucratic leviathan devoted to deciding how the peoples of the world and their citizens should live.
[…]
During the pandemic, agencies under this organization placed themselves above scientific evidence and the sovereignty of nations, promoting forced lockdown policies around the world that destroyed jobs, ruined the education of an entire generation of children, and cost millions of people their lives as they died alone, without basic medical care. Where some see a public-health policy mistake, we see a global experiment in social control disguised as science. And when a state, blinded by public-health considerations, strips its population of the right to work, to receive an education, and to say goodbye to their dead, and this results in millions of preventable deaths, there is a word for it: genocide.
[…]
That is why I tell you: when it comes to artificial intelligence, Argentina will put itself at the forefront of freedom. We have the critical minerals, the energy, the talent, and the capacity to compete at every link in that value chain, and we want to be the most competitive place in the world to develop it, with a cutting-edge legal framework, a commitment not to regulate preemptively, a commitment not to regulate preemptively, limited liability for companies that operate with AI agents, and tax benefits.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: 8 more die in Russian strikes on Ukraine while UN mull war's end
articles.body:
At least eight people were killed in Russian drone and missile strikes across Ukraine overnight into Thursday, officials said, as Moscow’s 4 1/2-year invasion grinds on despite renewed calls for a settlement at this week’s U.N. General Assembly.
A strike on Ukraine’s northeastern Kharkiv region killed six agricultural workers and wounded 12 others, Interior Minister Ihor Vyhivskyi said.
An attack on the capital Kyiv killed a man and a woman, he said, while officials in the southern port of Odesa also reported a major bombardment.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy appealed in a speech at the United Nations late Wednesday for countries to starve Russia of revenue through sanctions and trade bans, denying Moscow the money it needs to prolong the war.
He and other leaders at previous U.N. general assemblies have sought to pressure Moscow into giving up its ambitions in Ukraine.
But despite years of diplomatic efforts there is no sign of a breakthrough in ending a war that has had repercussions for the global food and energy supply, as well as severely straining relations between Russia and Western countries.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov repeated Moscow’s demand for a comprehensive peace deal, not a temporary break in hostilities, following Ukraine’s call for a complete and unconditional cease-fire.
"We believe it’s necessary to seek peace, not a temporary truce,” Peskov told reporters Thursday. Russia's demands for Ukraine to surrender its territory, among other things, are unacceptable for Kyiv.
The aerial war has intensified in recent months. Russia keeps hammering Ukraine with cruise and ballistic missiles, powerful glide bombs and jet-powered drones, while Ukraine’s long-range drones target oil refineries and businesses that are a vital part of the Russian economy.
There have been few significant changes since last year along the roughly 1,250-kilometer (800-mile) front line in eastern and southern Ukraine, where a huge number of drones on both sides limit movement.
The attack on Kyiv damaged more than 50 civilian sites, including apartment blocks, post offices, a maternity hospital and a textile plant, Vyhivskyi, the interior minister, said.
Russia has repeatedly hit Ukrainian trains, shopping malls, supermarkets and gas stations, among other sites, keeping civilians on edge.
Valentyna Kolosenko, a 49-year-old Kyiv resident, said a solid oak door she was standing behind saved her when three blasts occurred around her home. She said she would endure the hardship, even though she was scared.
"Everything is paralyzed. Nothing works,” she told The Associated Press. "Getting to work is incredibly difficult and frightening.”
Liubov Paziuk, a 74-year-old pensioner in the capital whose house windows were shattered, said she remained determined to resist the Russian onslaught.
"We don’t get used to it, we adapt, because we have only one choice: to stay here, on our land, despite everything,” she said.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said the military overnight struck arms factories, telecommunications and logistical facilities in Kyiv and the Odesa region.
The United Nations said last week that more Ukrainian civilians were killed and wounded in the first eight months of 2026 than in the whole of last year.
Russian attacks in August killed at least 368 civilians and wounded 2,314 others, according to the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine.
"Russia’s escalation of terror demonstrates that active diplomacy must come hand in hand with devastating pressure on Putin’s regime and unwavering support for the defense of Ukraine,” Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X.
As another Ukrainian subzero winter approaches, Zelenskyy said things are likely to get worse. But he promised to keep fighting.
"Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us. But in response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia, too,” the Ukrainian leader said on social media. "And that’s exactly why we say that de-escalation steps are important are needed before winter.”
Officials in western Russia on Thursday reported Ukrainian long-range attacks but provided few details.
Ukrainian drone fragments damaged an administrative building of an oil refinery in the Rostov region but there was no fire, Gov. Yuri Slyusar said.
In the Krasnodar region, Ukrainian drone fragments sparked a brief fire on the premises of an industrial facility, regional emergency officials said.
Ukrainian officials made no immediate comment.
Romania’s Ministry of National Defense said Thursday that a drone violated its airspace for four minutes before crashing near a town in the north of the country, near the border with Ukraine.
The ministry had earlier scrambled two Romanian F-16s and two Spanish F-18s to monitor its airspace in two separate locations after a spate of drones were detected in Ukraine near the border.
Authorities did not specify who the drone belonged to.
Also, Moldova’s Defense Ministry said Thursday that it recorded a spate of airspace incursions during Russia’s attacks on neighboring Ukraine. The incidents prompted authorities to close part of Moldova’s northern airspace, the ministry said.

articles.title: Zelensky: Ukraine Intercepted 60% of Ballistic Missiles in Overnight Russian Attack
articles.body:
Ukraine intercepted 60% of the ballistic missiles launched by Russia during its latest massive overnight attack, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday, while speaking to journalists in New York.
Russia launched three separate waves of ballistic missile attacks early morning on Sept. 24, Zelensky said, adding that he discussed the assault with Armed Forces Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapaty and Air Force Commander Anatolii Kryvonozhko.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The ballistic strikes were part of a broader overnight assault that also targeted Kyiv with drones.
A Russian missile attack on the capital killed two and injured at least six people, according to Kyiv authorities. Missile debris damaged a private house, a 16-story apartment building and an eight-story nonresidential building in Dniprovskyi District.
In Podilskyi District, debris damaged windows and part of the facade of a maternity hospital and set cars on fire in a nearby parking lot. A diagnostic center was also damaged. Warehouses were damaged or set ablaze in Solomianskyi and Sviatoshynskyi districts.
The missile attack followed a major Russian drone assault on Kyiv on Sept. 23. That attack killed two people and injured dozens, while damaging warehouses, gas stations, transport infrastructure and other sites across the capital.
Despite the reported 60% interception rate in the latest ballistic attack, Zelensky said Ukraine needs to shoot down more incoming missiles.
‘No Other Choice’: Zelensky Warns Russia of Winter Strikes
He also acknowledged that Ukraine’s success rate has at times been far lower this year, with some attacks seeing only 10% of ballistic missiles intercepted – and others with none intercepted.
“It’s not because someone lacks experience. Someone lacks missiles,” Zelensky said.
Ukraine scrambles for air defense missiles
Zelensky said Ukraine’s interception rate for ballistic missiles has varied sharply this year. In some attacks, Ukrainian forces intercepted only 10% of incoming ballistic missiles, while in others they were unable to intercept any.
“And it’s not because someone lacks experience. Someone lacks missiles,” Zelensky said.
He said he had asked US President Donald Trump to help provide additional air defense missiles, despite shortages in US and allied stocks.
Ukraine is also seeking additional interceptors from European and other countries, Zelensky said.
He described the effort to replenish Ukraine’s air defense stocks as a painstaking process, with Kyiv sometimes obtaining missiles “two at a time” or “one at a time.”
“We are collecting hundreds one or two missiles at a time,” Zelensky said, adding that some of the requests have to be handled at the highest political level because routine discussions between officials do not always produce results when stocks are limited.
Zelensky said the United States has the greatest capacity to provide Ukraine with air defense missiles on a large scale.

articles.title: CIA Warns of Potential Russian Drone Strikes From Shadow Fleet Vessels
articles.body:
Spain’s El Mundo publication on Wednesday said that Russia may be preparing to launch drone strikes against Southern European countries from shadow fleet vessels passing through the Mediterranean.
Citing a source close to Lithuania’s defense ministry, the report said the warning originated from the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), which has reportedly alerted European governments to the potential threat.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to El Mundo, such a move would fit into Russia’s broader campaign of “hybrid” operations against NATO members supporting Ukraine. Experts quoted by the outlet said Moscow has so far stopped short of actions that could trigger a direct military response from the alliance. They argue, however, that recent escalations suggest the Kremlin is pushing those boundaries.
This has included increased numbers of drone incursions into Poland, Romania, and the Baltic nations, as well as the attempted use of armed drones at Leipzig Airport and the Wuntsorf airbase, both attributed to Russia.
Russia’s weapon of choice
According to the Lithuanian source cited by El Mundo, any such operation would likely target Spain, France, or Italy using Russia’s Gerbera drones.
“Launched from the sea, hidden in shipping containers; it’s not difficult at all,” the source said.
The report noted that the Gerbera’s compact size gives it an advantage over the larger and more complex Iranian-designed Shahed or Geran attack drones that are widely used by Russia against Ukraine.
Zelensky Says He Would Visit Moscow ‘On a Rocket’
The Gerbera is around 2 meters (6.6 feet) long, has a 2.5-meter (8-feet) wingspan, weighs 18 kilograms (40 pounds), and holds a 5-kilogram (11-pound) warhead.
It has a range between 300 kilometers (186 miles) and 600 kilometers (370 miles), depending on the fuel load and weather conditions, and can travel at speeds of up to 160 kph (100 mph).
A Gerbera-2 drone carrying a 4-kilogram (8.8 pound) fragmentation warhead was recovered off Poland’s coast on Sept. 14. According to the report, the drone was most likely launched from Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave rather than from a vessel at sea.
El Mundo also cited British military analyst Keir Giles, who said such attacks could be aimed at disrupting airport operations, starting fires in factories, threatening military installations, or simply a demonstration of Russia’s ability to strike “anywhere in Europe.”
A separate Lithuanian source told the newspaper that Russia wants to show that it can replicate Ukraine’s June 2025 “Spider’s Web” operation, during which small autonomous drones were launched from trucks attacking and damaging 41 Russian strategic military aircraft across multiple air bases deep inside Russia.
Russia’s been practicing the technique
In September 2025, the Ukrainian media outlet Defense Express reported that Russian drones, possibly Gerberas launched from a shadow fleet vessel, had forced the closure of Copenhagen and Oslo airports.
It also said that the Russian manufacturer Zala Aero had practiced launching its reconnaissance and Lancet attack drones from the BK-16E high-speed assault boat in 2020 and again in October 2024.
In February 2026, there were also reports that a Swedish naval unit detected and jammed a drone originating from a Russian signals intelligence vessel near the port city of Malmo where the French aircraft Charles De Gaulle was docked.

articles.title: Russia could launch limited attacks on NATO in coming months, escalating hybrid warfare without being ready for full-scale conflict, Denmark warns
articles.body:
Russia is likely to intensify its hybrid war against the West, including more frequent sabotage and cyberattacks that could cause greater damage and casualties, Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service (DDIS) said in a new assessment published on 24 September.
The assessment says Russia has become increasingly willing to take risks against European and NATO countries, even while its full-scale war against Ukraine continues. DDIS also assesses a low but growing risk of Russia carrying out a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia in the coming months.
Russia preparing to escalate hybrid attacks
DDIS said Russia’s hybrid attacks have increasingly shifted from attempts to create fear and weaken support for Ukraine toward efforts to directly disrupt Western assistance to Kyiv.
This includes sabotage targeting defense companies and railway transport carrying military equipment to Ukraine. The Danish intelligence service expects Russia to carry out such attacks more frequently and with greater consequences.
Future operations could include destructive cyberattacks capable of disrupting critical societal functions and sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties, according to the assessment.
DDIS also cited the foiled drone attack against Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany as an example of Russia’s growing willingness to conduct operations against targets in Europe. German authorities said the attack had been planned by Russia over several months.
Germany suspects Russian intelligence behind arson attack as hybrid warfare threat grows across Europe
Growing risk of a limited attack on NATO
The Danish intelligence service assesses that there is a low but growing risk Russia could launch a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia.
Such an attack could take the form of isolated long-range strikes against infrastructure supporting Ukraine. Russia could also use Ukrainian-made drones in a false-flag operation or deploy a limited number of troops, potentially without national insignia.
DDIS says Russia could attempt such an operation even while continuing its war against Ukraine and without having the forces needed for a regional war against NATO.
The purpose, according to the assessment, could be to divert European resources away from Ukraine and create divisions within NATO if Moscow believes the alliance would struggle to agree on a collective response.
Russia would likely try to ensure that any military attack remained below the threshold that would trigger a full NATO response. DDIS warns, however, that Russia may be uncertain about what would trigger such a response.
After CIA head’s visit to Moscow, Poland’s PM warns Russia is preparing to escalate war. He puts critical window at seven or eight months
No signs of an imminent Russian invasion
Despite the increased risk of limited attacks, DDIS says it sees no indications that Russia is preparing to invade one or more NATO countries.
The agency considers a full-scale Russian invasion of NATO “highly unlikely,” but says it cannot be ruled out. If Russia decided to launch such an invasion, DDIS estimates it would need at least six months to build up the necessary forces.
The intelligence service also says Russia would need several months to build up forces near a NATO border before a limited military deployment, making such preparations difficult to conceal.
Russian warship fires flares at Danish military helicopter as Moscow’s provocations escalate
Russia under pressure from Ukraine’s attacks
The assessment says Russia is currently under more pressure than at any other point in its war against Ukraine.
Ukraine’s sustained long-range strikes are causing increasing damage deep inside Russia, while Russian forces are suffering heavy losses for marginal territorial gains. Moscow is also facing economic pressure from military spending, international sanctions and Ukrainian strikes against Russian energy infrastructure.
DDIS assesses that there is no prospect of Russia achieving a major breakthrough in Ukraine over the next six months. At the same time, it says Putin is highly unlikely to compromise on his fundamental objectives in the war.
The agency says Russia believes Europe will develop a stronger independent military capability by 2030, which Moscow could view as an increasing threat. This could create what DDIS describes as a window of opportunity for Putin to attempt to change Europe’s security order.

articles.title: Rutte says Putin is in a 'bad place' as he reassures NATO allies amid threat reports
articles.body:
NATO chief Mark Rutte said the alliance was prepared to respond to Russian hybrid attacks against European countries following fresh warnings from Danish intelligence. Meanwhile, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth urged European allies to take greater responsibility for their own defence.
NATO is prepared to respond to sabotage and drone incidents across Europe and has plans in place to address such threats, Secretary General Mark Rutte said on Thursday.
"Russia is doing more and more when it comes to the cyber etc. domain, but... NATO is ready for this," Rutte said at an event in New York commemorating the September 11, 2001 attacks on the United States.
"We have all these response options in place... when it comes to hybrids to make sure that we stay strong," he added.
Rutte argued that the growing number of hybrid incidents in NATO countries indicated that Russian President Vladimir Putin was losing the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year.
"Putin is in a bad place," Rutte said, adding that Russia is not winning the war in Ukraine and that citizens of the 32 NATO countries can remain calm.
He urged NATO members to provide "more support for Ukraine" if they "really want to give a signal to the Russians on every hybrid incident, hybrid attack."
"All the response options are there, and we will use whatever we need," Rutte added.
His remarks came after Danish intelligence on Thursday warned of a growing risk of Russian military action against NATO countries, including further hybrid attacks.
At the same time, Spanish media reported that US intelligence had alerted European countries to a possible Russian drone operation targeting Spain, France or Italy.
U.S. Defense Secretary urges Europe to take the lead on its defense
Meanwhile, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Thursday that European allies must take the lead in defending their continent, calling for NATO to become a "real hard-line military alliance."
Speaking at a meeting of NATO defence ministers, Hegseth proposed a "NATO 3.0" focused on strengthening military capabilities and deterring threats in Europe.
His comments came weeks after Washington informed its allies that it would no longer provide certain warships and aircraft in the event of an attack on a NATO member. European allies and Canada are now assessing how to address the resulting capability gaps.
"NATO 3.0 is post-Cold War recognition that (NATO) needs to go back to a real hard-line military alliance that has real military capabilities capable of deterring right here on the continent and taking the lead for the conventional defense of Europe," Hegseth said.
Under Article 5 of NATO's founding treaty, an attack on one member is considered an attack on all. However, the provision does not automatically require allies to provide military assistance.
The US, which has NATO's largest armed forces, is seeking to reduce its role in Europe's conventional defence. It does not plan to withdraw its nuclear weapons stationed in Europe, which remain a central element of NATO's deterrence strategy.

articles.title: U.S. intelligence warns Spain, France and Italy of possible Russian Gerbera drone attack from commercial ships, El Mundo reports
articles.body:
U.S. intelligence has warned several European governments that Russia is preparing a drone attack against Spain, France, or Italy, according to a report by Spanish newspaper El Mundo. According to the outlet, the drones could be launched from a commercial vessel after being concealed inside a shipping container.
A source close to Lithuania’s Defense Ministry said:
“They will use drones launched from the sea, hidden in the container of a ship; it's not difficult at all.”
Lithuanian authorities even know the type of drone involved, according to the newspaper: the Gerbera, a Russian unmanned aircraft often used as a decoy or strike drone. The UAV weighs up to 18 kilograms, can reach speeds of about 160 kilometers per hour, and has a reported range of up to 600 kilometers. Its 4- to 5-kilogram warhead would not be powerful enough to destroy a major facility, but it could still start a fire or temporarily shut down a port or airport.
Lithuania received the information shortly after CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow on Aug. 25. According to El Mundo’s sources, authorities in Spain, France, and Italy were also warned about the possibility of such an operation, while a CIA report describing the potential attack in detail was circulated among European foreign ministries. The warning coincided with a response by French President Emmanuel Macron, who convened the country’s Defense Council on Sept. 16 and, two days later, invited leaders of all political parties to the Élysée Palace. After the meeting, the French president said protection of critical infrastructure against cyberattacks and drones would be strengthened due to “hybrid threats” from Russia.
El Mundo noted that elections are scheduled in all three countries in 2027 and that radical political forces could seek to capitalize on public fear about Russian attacks and general fatigue over the war in Ukraine. On Sept. 19, the pro-Russian Telegram channel Rybar published a map of possible targets in southern France, including aircraft plants, military bases, nuclear power stations, and petrochemical complexes that it said could be within range of Geran-5 drones launched from the northern coast of Algeria.
Last week, debris from a drone and a substance that investigators believe to be explosives were found in Lower Saxony near the German military’s Wunstorf Air Base. German federal prosecutors are examining whether the discovery is connected to an attempted act of sabotage at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August that Berlin has blamed on Russia. In that incident, a drone fitted with a detonator was found there near a Ukrainian transport aircraft.

articles.title: Russia will intensify hybrid attacks against West, NATO, says Danish intelligence
articles.body:
Russia is likely to intensify its hybrid war against the West in the coming months, Denmark's defense intelligence service said in a new threat assessment on Thursday.
Hybrid warfare and sabotage on European soil gained renewed attention after Germany recently blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at the Leipzig/Halle Airport, prompting European Union members to call for new sanctions against Russia.
Moscow has repeatedly denied any involvement in hybrid warfare, sabotage operations in NATO countries, or plotting any confrontation.
The Russian embassy to Denmark did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
More frequent attacks expected from Russia
The defense intelligence service said Russia will carry out more frequent attacks against the West and NATO "with greater consequences for the countries targeted than in the past."
It added that there was "a low but growing risk" that Russia would launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries that border Russia.
"A limited military attack would be a desperate move on Russia’s part and, like the intensified hybrid attacks, could potentially take place in the coming months," it said.
Such attacks could include isolated strikes with long-range weapons like drones or missiles on infrastructure supporting Ukraine, or false-flag operations using Ukrainian-made drones, intelligence service chief Thomas Ahrenkiel said at a press conference.
He said Russia could also deploy a limited number of troops into a NATO border area, potentially under the pretext of protecting Russian minorities.
"The aim is not to take over the country, but to divide NATO," he said.
A Russian frigate last week fired two flares towards a Danish military helicopter sent to photograph it in international waters off Denmark, with one narrowly missing the aircraft, according to the Danish military.
In a separate statement on Thursday, the Danish Resilience Agency said it was likely that Russia would attempt to carry out destructive cyberattacks against Denmark, and it raised its threat level.

articles.title: Russian attack puts three countries on alert as drones enter Moldova and Romania
articles.body:
Moldova’s Defense Ministry reported four drone incursions, Romania’s Defense Ministry confirmed a drone crash, and Poland’s Operational Command scrambled fighters twice during Russia’s 24 September attack on Ukraine.
The strike wave forced Moldova to close part of its airspace, Romania to warn residents and launch F-16 fighter jets, and Poland to activate aircraft, air defenses, and radar. No casualties were reported in the two confirmed crashes, and Poland detected no incursion during its first deployment. Moldova has recorded dozens of Russian drone incursions this year.
The drones approached from Ukraine’s Vinnytsia, Odesa, and Chernivtsi oblasts, according to Moldova’s Defense Ministry. Authorities temporarily closed part of the country’s northern airspace.
Near Cernița in northern Moldova, one drone struck a tree, fell into a field beside a farm, and exploded, police said. No casualties were reported.
Investigators preliminarily identified the camera-equipped wreckage as a Gerbera, a low-cost Russian drone often used during attacks on Ukraine. Police said it was the first device of that type found in Moldova.
Police also reported a resident’s account of another explosion near Vadul Rașcov, but said they were still investigating the location.
Romanian radar first tracked an aerial target over Ukraine near the border before it entered northern Romania, the Defense Ministry said. Romania launched two F-16s and sent emergency alerts to residents’ phones in the area. The drone remained in Romanian airspace for about four minutes before crashing near Solca, the ministry said. Officials reported no casualties or damage and had not identified the drone’s origin.
Poland’s Operational Command launched fighters twice in response to Russian strikes on western Ukraine. The first Polish deployment ended around 08:00 with no airspace violation detected; the command announced a second at 09:07. It also activated ground-based air defenses and radar.
The incursions came amid a wider assault. Ukraine’s Air Force said Russia launched 282 drones of various types, along with ballistic and other missiles, overnight into 24 September. Ukrainian officials reported detecting four drones over Chernivtsi Oblast, the Ukrainian region bordering Moldova and Romania, and shooting down three.
Moldova’s repeated airspace breaches
The latest incident followed several breaches in August. An unidentified drone exploded near Crocmaz on 9 August. Another object exploded near Talmaza on 17 August after Moldova briefly closed part of its airspace.
President Maia Sandu said Russian drones had entered Moldovan airspace 39 times in 2026, compared with 17 times throughout 2025. Moldova has portable air-defense weapons and electronic warfare equipment, but Sandu said these chiefly protect individual sites. Her government is working with partners to expand air-defense coverage and speed up threat warnings.
