articles.title: Russia could attack a Nato country within months, Danish intelligence says
articles.body:
Russia could launch a limited military attack against a Nato country in the coming months, Danish intelligence said, in one of the starkest warnings yet by western security services.
In a report published on Thursday, the Danish defence intelligence service warned of a “low but growing risk” that Russia could launch long-range strikes on Nato infrastructure supporting Ukraine, or carry out a limited incursion into a neighbouring country with a small number of troops, potentially operating without insignia.
The report came hours after a fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland that local authorities described as an “act of sabotage”.
Krzysztof Gawkowski, the deputy prime minister of Poland, said the blaze, which broke out overnight in the Masovian voivodeship, had been “deliberately designed to disable the station”, disrupting internet access for a number of institutions, including the Ukrainian military.
Gawkowski said it had not been established who was responsible for the fire, but that “many signs suggest this aligns with Russia’s new doctrine of attack.
“While everything is operational today, we must recognise, as prime minister [Donald] Tusk recently noted, that this is an element of hybrid warfare,” he said.
Starlink has become a key part of Ukraine’s military communications, and the incident comes amid a spate of suspected Russian sabotage operations across European infrastructure supporting Ukraine.
Earlier this month, Germany publicly blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle airport, while a series of other incidents – including fires at drone factories and sabotage targeting rail infrastructure – have also been investigated for possible links to Moscow. Russia has denied involvement in such attacks.
In recent weeks, several European intelligence chiefs have warned that Russia may be preparing more assertive actions to test Nato countries’ commitment to supporting Ukraine, though officials differ over how imminent such a move may be.
Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid attacks against European countries with “greater consequences” for those targeted in the coming months, the Danes warned, including “destructive cyber-attacks that cripple societal functions as well as sabotage attacks that carry a high risk of casualties”.
A source familiar with Moscow’s thinking agreed that Russia was likely to step up its hybrid attacks.
“Russian military top command is convinced some Nato countries are directly involved in the war against Russia – not just by supplying Ukraine with weapons and intelligence, but by helping to guide missiles and drones,” the source said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
“They therefore believe Nato is already waging a hybrid war against Russia, and that Russia has the right to respond in kind,” the source added.
“Hybrid attacks” are broad terms generally used to describe non-military tactics aimed at pressuring or destabilising an adversary, including cyber-attacks, sabotage and disinformation.
The aim of Russia’s actions would be to divert European resources away from supporting Ukraine, and deepen divisions within Nato if the alliance failed to agree on a collective response, the report added.
The service believes it remained “highly unlikely” that Russia would launch an outright invasion of a Nato country, but notably said it “cannot be ruled out”.
The Danish services said Russia could seek to test Nato’s article 5, which commits members to collective defence. They warned there was “a risk that Russia assesses that the Nato countries will not respond collectively”, particularly if Moscow believes the US is unable or unwilling to support its European allies in a potential war with Russia.
There have been ongoing jitters among Nato members over whether the alliance’s most powerful member, the US, would come to Europe’s defence under Donald Trump in the event of a Russian attack.
Questions over unity within Europe are also growing. Last week, Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico, who has maintained close ties with the Kremlin, cast doubt on his country’s commitment to Nato’s collective defence principle, saying he did not want Slovakia drawn into a military conflict “because of some article 5”.
Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russia continued to threaten countries beyond Ukraine, including Moldova, Poland and the Baltic states, while showing “no respect” for the sovereignty of countries in the south Caucasus and central Asia.
“The more freedom Putin has to act, the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else,” he said.

articles.title: Wired for War: The empire’s propaganda wing honors Palantir
articles.body:
Wired for War: German media giant Axel Springer awards Palantir’s Thiel
Germany’s Axel Springer media monolith has awarded its highest honor to Palantir founder Peter Thiel, in a ceremony illustrating the incestuous relationship between the mainstream media, the defense tech industry, and the US-Israeli order.
Thiel received the ‘2026 Axel Springer Award’ at a ceremony in Berlin on Thursday. According to Axel Springer CEO Mathias Dopfner, Thiel “is one of the rare entrepreneurs who does not merely found or finance companies but helps determine the direction of technological development...he reminds us that progress requires courage and nonconformism.”
The ceremony began at 7pm Berlin time, and anyone curious what Thiel had to say can watch a replay of the livestream below.
Previous recipients of the Axel Springer Award include Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, and Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky. None of these laureates have proven as controversial as Thiel, however.
According to Status News, employees at Politico and Business Insider – both of which are owned by Axel Springer – pushed back against the decision. In a letter to management on Tuesday, 120 staffers argued that Thiel, who funded the lawsuit that destroyed Gawker, should not be honored by a company which, in the words of Dopfner, “stands for freedom of speech and a culture of open discussions.”
They’re missing the point. Palantir and Axel Springer are cogs in the same machine. They share an almost identical world view, marked by a devotion to US-Israeli hegemony, a belief that private companies must serve the interests of this hegemony, and a common parent: the CIA.
The CIA connection
During the Cold War, the US saw strategic control of media outlets as key to preventing the rise of socialism and communism in Western Europe. Axel Springer, the anti-communist press baron who gave his name to the company, was a natural ally in this fight. Springer received $7 million in funding from the CIA in 1957, two former agents told The Nation in 1982. Adjusted for inflation, the donation would be equivalent to more than $80 million today.
Although the agents claimed that Springer ended his relationship with the agency in the mid-1970s, declassified documents show that he was still in contact with the United States Information Agency (USIA) – which funded pro-American news outlets – in the early 1980s. In 1982, Springer was introduced to CIA Director William Casey as “a strong supporter of the United States” who “is doing all he can to strengthen the ties between the United States and Europe.”
Thiel, who co-founded PayPal, launched Palantir in 2003 with the stated goal of taking “the approaches that PayPal had used to fight fraud…into other contexts, like fighting terrorism.” The CIA took notice, and invested $2 million in the company in 2005 via its in-house venture capital firm, In-Q-Tel.
“I wish I had Palantir when I was director,” former CIA chief George Tenet – who set up In-Q-Tel – told Forbes magazine in 2013. “I wish we had the tool of its power.”
The Axel Springer investment pays off
In both cases, the CIA’s investments paid off. Axel Springer is now Europe’s largest publisher, and owns Politico, Business Insider, Bild, Die Welt, The Telegraph, and nearly a dozen other outlets. The American deep state continues to finance its operations, with the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and the State Department’s National Endowment for Democracy (NED) pumping just under $34 million into Politico between 2016 and 2025.
In return, Axel Springer has openly pledged fealty to American neoliberalism. Whereas Springer himself described his first newspaper, the Hamburger Abendblatt, as “geared to the underdog and the little man,” staff at Axel Springer publications are today required to adhere to the following code of conduct:
- “We stand up for freedom, free speech, the rule of law, and democracy”
- “We support the right of existence of the State of Israel and oppose all forms of anti-Semitism”
- “We advocate the alliance between the United States of America and Europe”
- “We uphold the principles of a free market economy”
- “We reject political and religious extremism and all forms of discrimination”
In practice, this means that Axel Springer publications will feature lively debate over ‘red versus blue’ politics in the US and Europe, but will never question key tenets of US foreign policy, including America’s alliance with Israel, its dominance over Europe through NATO, and the legitimacy of its proxy war with Russia in Ukraine.
The world according to Palantir
More than two decades after taking CIA money, Palantir is now the largest of the Silicon Valley defense kingpins, and a synonym for the burgeoning surveillance- and military-tech sector as a whole. Palantir is valued at around $427 billion, a figure bolstered by lucrative contracts with the US’ defense and intelligence agencies, including all six branches of the US military, the CIA, FBI, NSA, and DIA.
Palantir’s flagship product is an operating system called ‘Gotham’, which is essentially a data analytics platform for military, intelligence, and law enforcement agencies. Gotham pulls together and analyses existing data that may otherwise take days to sift through. For example, if US Central Command is planning a missile strike in a foreign country, Gotham can combine maps and satellite footage from that country, data from other agencies, including human intelligence from the CIA and signals intelligence from the NSA, and local surveillance data to present CENTCOM with potential targets for military strikes.
Palantir’s international customers include the British, Israeli and Ukrainian militaries, NATO, domestic intelligence agencies in France and Germany, and police departments in Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, and the UK, among others.
However, Palantir is not a mercenary company selling its products to anyone with money. According to CEO Alex Karp, Palantir is inseparable from the US deep state, and “was founded to strengthen US national security, to protect Americans and their freedom.”
Because we get asked a lot.
The Technological Republic, in brief.
1. Silicon Valley owes a moral debt to the country that made its rise possible. The engineering elite of Silicon Valley has an affirmative obligation to participate in the defense of the nation.
2. We must rebel…
Earlier this year, Karp set out Palantir’s world view in a manifesto, which RT already covered in depth in our ‘Wired for War’ series. In the 22-point bulletin, Karp argued that “the engineering elite of Silicon Valley has an affirmative obligation to participate in the defense of the nation,” that “free and democratic societies” must pursue AI superweapons to preserve the hegemony of the US, which “has advanced progressive values” more than “any other nation on the planet.”
In separate comments, Karp has described pro-Palestinian protesters as a “cancerous” influence on American politics, while Palantir describes its work with the Israeli state as “in line with our global support of US allies and liberal democracies.”
Critics called Karp’s manifesto “technofascist,” but it differs little in substance from Axel Springer’s code of conduct. Karp’s remaining points wade into US-centric culture war territory, but the core argument of both documents is the same: the US and Israel are a benevolent force and the private sector has a duty to aid their foreign policy goals; by argument, in the case of Axel Springer, and by force, in the case of Palantir.
The incestuous security state
Back in Berlin, the guest speakers at Thursday’s ceremony further illustrate the incestuous relationship between Axel Springer, Palantir, and the US-Israeli order. Before Dopfner handed him his award, Thiel was lauded by CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss, a self-described “Zionist fanatic” who was appointed head of the network following its acquisition last year by billionaire and pro-Israel megadonor David Ellison, whose family has donated more than $26 million to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) since 2014.
Before the acquisition, Weiss repeatedly complained about CBS’ supposedly “anti-Israel bias.” Once in control of the network, she set about hiring pro-Israel editors and reportedly intervening personally in stories concerning the Jewish state.
Thursday’s ceremony also featured a questions-and-answers session with PayPal co-founder Max Levchin, a vocal defender of the NSA amid Edward Snowden’s revelations of warrantless wiretapping.
The award is equivalent to an ‘Employee of the Month’ prize from one department of the same company to another. It’s like USAID and CIA agents meeting for after-work drinks, or Weiss congratulating the IDF for its service.
Dopfner, Thiel, Weiss and Levchin understand they’re all on the same team. Anyone who’s followed RT’s ‘Wired for War’ series will grasp this. The only people yet to figure it out, apparently, are the Politico and Business Insider staffers complaining about the threat posed by Thiel to “Axel Springer’s own commitment to freedom.”
Thursday’s ceremony might help them understand the true nature of the power they serve a little clearer.

articles.title: Russia slams Kyiv with ballistic missiles as Ukrainians brace for harsh winter

Russia slams Kyiv with ballistic missiles as Ukrainians brace for harsh winter
Russia on Thursday hit Kyiv with ballistic missiles and drones, killing two people, while a strike on a farm in the Kharkiv region killed six, according to Ukrainian officials. As autumn approaches, Ukrainians are bracing for a tough winter following Moscow's intensifying attacks on the country's energy infrastructure.

Russian missile and drone attacks killed at least two people in Kyiv, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday, with the Ukrainian capital rocked by multiple powerful explosions after authorities issued a missile alert.
More than 20 blasts were heard on Thursday, according to AFP journalists, after the Ukrainian Air Force warned that Russian ballistic missiles were headed for the city.
"Once again, the main targets of (the Russian) attack were Kyiv and civilian infrastructure – residential buildings, a maternity hospital, energy facilities and logistics. Two people are already known to have been killed," Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
In a message on X, Zelensky noted that "Russia will not end this war without pressure. As people were sleeping, flashes from explosions lit up the sky. Once again, the main targets of their strike were Kyiv and civilian infrastructure, residential buildings, a maternity hospital, energy infrastructure, and logistics."

"Explosions in Kyiv. The capital is under ballistic missile attack. Remain in shelters!" Kyiv Mayor Vitaly Klitschko wrote in a Telegram message.
The strikes came as Zelensky was meeting members of the US Congress as part of his trip to the United States to request stronger sanctions against Moscow.
In Ukraine's eastern Kharkiv region, a Russian strike on a farm killed six people, said Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky.
The regional prosecutor's office said the farm in the Chuguiv district, southeast of Kharkiv, was hit as employees were sorting vegetables at a storage facility.
It published images showing the inside of a destroyed warehouse, where what appear to be piles of apples were scattered across the floor, with a gaping hole in the roof.

Kyiv residents brace for harsh winter
The barrage was the latest in an intensifying exchange of long-range attacks, with both Kyiv and Moscow signalling at the UN that they will escalate strikes and dimming prospects for diplomacy.
The first days of autumn chill have only barely set in over Kyiv, but winter is already dominating conversations among residents, who are making plans in case Russian strikes once again knock out the energy system.
The shadow of last winter hangs over Kyiv, which was plunged into darkness and bitter cold for weeks when Russian forces struck the country's power and heating infrastructure while temperatures dropped as low as -20C.
As Russia stepped up assaults on Kyiv, the question of what to do this winter is particularly pressing for families with children, said Oleksandra Matveieva, founder of a Facebook group for mothers.
"Now it seems Russians have started bombing Kyiv heavily," she said.
"Immediately, people, mostly mothers, started writing: 'we're ready to leave anywhere, as long as it's not too far and expensive'."
Travel Mama Club, originally founded for travelling mothers before evolving into an advice forum during the war, has recently seen a surge in publications concerning accommodation in relatively safer western Ukraine, or abroad.
"People are looking for a Plan B, even booking refundable apartments," she said. "They still don't know yet whether they will actually leave."
Russia has over the past month stepped up its attacks on the capital and air raid alerts urging locals to seek shelter due to incoming drones and missiles are now a nightly and, increasingly, daily occurrence.
If it used to target Kyiv mainly during the hours of darkness, Moscow now attacks more in broad daylight. The alerts paralyse life across the city – especially in schools and hospitals, which follow strict safety protocols.
'Critically cold'
The strikes are part of escalating infrastructure attacks by both Russia and Ukraine, which UN investigators warn are leaving civilians increasingly vulnerable as winter approaches.
US President Donald Trump said last week that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other's energy facilities, but the proposal failed to materialise.
Zelensky told the UN General Assembly in New York on Wednesday that, "Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us, but in response we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too."
Ukrainian authorities have rushed to reinforce the battered energy system. The energy ministry said the country has already repaired 4.8 gigawatts of generating capacity and plans to restore or build over 10 gigawatts this year.
The International Energy Agency said in September last year that Ukraine had about 38 gigawatts of despatchable power generation capacity before Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Last winter, demand peaked at 18GW, while the capacity had dropped to 11GW after years of attacks, the agency said.
Kyiv mayor Vitaly Klitschko, who has been criticised by the government for failing to present a clear strategy, has said the city completed 80 percent of its preparations ahead of winter.
The CEO of Ukraine's main gas provider Naftogaz, Sergiy Fedorenko, acknowledged Russia's strikes were "stronger, broader, more dangerous".
"But we prepared for this the whole time between heating seasons and we will withstand these blows over this difficult winter," he told AFP.
Besides heating and energy, there are fears Russia may seek to destroy water supplies, Ukraine's Energy Minister Denys Shmygal said in August.
Residents are making their own preparations, dusting off the generators, portable batteries and hot water bottles they relied on last year, while making adjustments.
Some hold on to the hope the weather will be milder this year.
"If it's cold again, as critically cold as it was last year, I will leave," said Matveieva, who has a daughter.
"I'll take her and get her out of here."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Le Pen Rules Out Ukraine Funding as Russia Targets French Election
articles.body:
French far-right presidential front-runner Marine Le Pen said France can no longer provide Ukraine with financial assistance.
She also rejected claims that France is at war with Russia, while European goverments brace for a possible increase in Russian hybrid attacks on NATO territory. Speaking to Politico at its Playbook Paris Live summit on Thursday, the National Rally leader repeated her pledge to stop financial help to Kyiv if she wins next spring’s election.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
However, “we can train their [Ukraine’s] soldiers and their military leadership, and provide them with military aid,” she said.
Le Pen says France not at war with Russia while EU braces for a possible attack
Le Pen dismissed the claims that France is already in a conflict with Moscow.
“Those who say that we are already at war give us the impression that they would like us to be at war,” she said, despite warnings from EU officials and analysts that the line between Russia’s frequent hybrid attacks and direct conflict is becoming increasingly blurred.
In the past several months, Russia’s campaign of drone incursions, sabotage and cyberattacks against EU infrastructure has nearly doubled, to the point that several EU members, including Poland, now describe it as direct attacks instead of isolated incidents.
On Sept. 19, Le Pen and her party’s President Jordan Bardella themselves acknowledged, in a joint statement, that hostile acts committed in Europe by agents working for Russia had intensified.
Ukraine Opens Second EU Negotiating Cluster as Reform Delivery Shapes Further Accession Progress, KSE Institute Says
In the statement, government measures to protect strategic infrastructure are also included. Politico described it as an effort to fend off opponents who portray the party as an ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Speaking to Politico, Le Pen also said she wants France to leave NATO’s integrated command, but not while the war continues.
“As long as there is a war on Europe’s doorstep, that is not the time to take action in that regard, but, of course, my will to do so remains,” she said.
Russian networks target Le Pen’s rivals
Her remarks come as Russian disinformation campaigns target possible contenders in the April 2027 elections, according to an analysis by Ukraine’s Center for Strategic Communications.
The targets include former Prime Ministers Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal and EU Parliament member Raphaël Glucksmann. The campaign used deepfakes, fabricated media reports and false claims about politicians’ alleged corruption and health problems.
According to the Ukrainian analysis, pro-Kremlin narratives also suggest a future French president should leave NATO and restore relations with Russia.
The European External Action Service’s fourth threat report, published in March 2026, found that France has become the second-most targeted country of Russian foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI) – behind only Ukraine.
Europe braces for escalation
Meanwhile, EU leaders increasingly prepare for Moscow’s possible turn on NATO.
Late August, CIA Director John Ratcliffe made an unannounced trip to Moscow, reportedly to warn Putin against attacking a NATO member and ending the war in Ukraine.
Speaking during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York on Wednesday, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Putin could target another EU country with drones, missiles or even a ground operation as Moscow seeks to fracture Western unity and weaken support for Ukraine.
He echoed previous concerns of Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk who said there was a “real risk” that drones or other missiles could enter the territory of one or several NATO countries on the alliance’s eastern flank, warning Moscow could portray such attacks as accidental.
Separately on Wednesday, 51 countries backed Ukraine in a joint statement, urging Russia to accept a full ceasefire and enter meaningful negotiations.
On Thursday, a Russian drone entered Romanian airspace and crashed in a forest in Suceava County after NATO jets failed to intercept it, while Moldovan President Maia Sandu said four Russian drones had violated Moldova’s airspace, with at least one exploding in the north of the country.
During Zelensky’s visit to Chișinău for Moldova’s Independence Day on Aug. 27, Sandu said five drones entered Moldovan airspace hours before the celebrations, framing them as “intimidation.”
Based on the pattern of their flight paths, Russia might be deliberately sending drones into the country’s airspace, she said on Aug. 17.

Russian Drone and Missile Barrage Damages Kyiv Maternity Hospital and Odesa Medical Facility
Russian forces launched a massive missile and drone strike across Ukraine on September 24, killing at least two people in Kyiv and damaging medical facilities in the capital and Odesa, despite Ukrainian air defenses intercepting over 200 drones and seven advanced missiles.
Russian forces launched a large-scale overnight assault on Ukraine, deploying a mix of anti-ship and ballistic missiles alongside a swarm of 282 strike drones, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on September 24.
Ukrainian air defense systems successfully intercepted a significant portion of the complex barrage, neutralizing four Zircon cruise missiles, three ballistic missiles, one S8000 “Banderol” jet-powered loitering munition, and 219 unmanned aerial vehicles.

Despite the high interception rate, the Air Force reported direct enemy hits in 13 locations and falling debris in 10 others, noting that the primary attack directions were the Kyiv and Odesa regions.

The Ukrainian capital also sustained widespread damage. The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (SESU) reported that the aftermath of the attack was recorded across four distinct districts of Kyiv, with two civilians reported dead and at least eight more injured.

articles.title: US Needs Ukrainian Expertise to Integrate Drones With Air Defense Radars
articles.body:

- World
US Needs Ukrainian Expertise to Integrate Drones With Air Defense Radars
Ukraine is ready to sign a landmark drone-defense deal with the United States, CBS News reported on September 23, citing three sources familiar with the matter.
According to the outlet, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is prepared to sign the agreement on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York City this week.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The deal has not yet been signed, however. The outlet's sources indicated it could instead be finalized at a later date, with the timing dependent on when the US is ready to sign.
Over the past year, the US Department of Defense and its Ukrainian counterpart have developed a framework to expand testing and production of Ukrainian defense technology in the US, CBS News reported.
Sources with direct knowledge of the deal described it as going beyond contracts for a handful of Ukrainian companies. It would instead let leading Ukrainian defense firms work directly with American counterparts and the US military.
Deborah Fairlamb, founding partner of Green Flag Ventures, an American venture capital firm investing in Ukrainian defense technology, emphasized that the deal's value will hinge on transferring Ukraine's operational know-how alongside its hardware.
"It's not just about having the tech. It's about how the tech is used," she told CBS News.
The war with Iran has underscored the value of Ukraine's defense industry to the US and its allies, CBS News noted.
In its first days, Iran began targeting American military installations across the Middle East with Shahed one-way attack drones, the same type Russia has used against Ukrainian cities. Because the US and Gulf states initially lacked cost-effective means of interception, Kyiv sent drone interceptors and pilots to help.
Ukraine has since signed defense agreements with Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, among other countries, matching foreign financing with its growing defense industry.
Zelenskyy has stated that Ukraine aims to produce 10 million drones this year. By comparison, the US Army acquired roughly 50,000 in 2025, according to former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll.
CBS News also detailed previously unreported episodes from the war's opening days.
In March, then-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll asked Eric Schmidt, the former Google CEO who founded the US drone company Perennial Autonomy, to supply 13,000 Merops interceptor drones and 10,000 Bumblebee reconnaissance and strike drones to the Middle East.
The drones reached the US military within days but took weeks to become operational because Ukrainian components arrived late, according to multiple sources familiar with the shipments.
According to CBS News, Merops drones use AI beacons manufactured by Ukraine’s Sine Engineering as well as Ukrainian warheads.
Washington's efforts to absorb the lessons of Ukraine's drone warfare have been uneven, the outlet added.
CBS News reported that Ukrainian expertise was also required to integrate the Merops drones into US air-defense radars before they could be used in combat.
In August, the US Army phased out a drone battalion tasked with studying those lessons, while the Pentagon's Drone Dominance Program invited American and select foreign companies, primarily Ukrainian ones, to compete for contracts.
The program aims to buy more than 200,000 drones by 2027, and Ukrainian manufacturer Skyfall won its first round earlier this year.
CBS News stated that it had reached out to the White House and the Pentagon for comment on the status of the drone deal and on the use of Ukrainian technology to defend bases in the Middle East.
The prospective agreement builds on a run of steps that have already brought Ukrainian systems into the American military ecosystem.
On July 22, Ukraine and the US signed a bilateral statement of intent establishing a framework for the temporary export of Ukrainian unmanned systems to the US for testing by the Pentagon.
By July 31, F-Drones had delivered the first 2,000 F10 FPV drones under the $1 billion Drone Dominance Program, making the F10 the first Ukrainian drone authorized for export to the US under the initiative.
Ukrainian personnel have also trained US service members at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia on the Sky Map software, a command-and-control platform used to identify Shahed-type threats and coordinate interceptor drones.

articles.title: Zelensky: Air Defense Intercepted 60% of Ballistic Missiles in Russian Attack on Kyiv
articles.body:
Ukraine’s air defense intercepted 60% of the ballistic missiles launched during three waves of Russian attacks on Kyiv overnight on September 24.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reported the figures. A video of his remarks was published by Novyny.LIVE.
According to Ukraine’s Air Force, Russia attacked using Zircon and Iskander missiles, along with various types of strike drones. The main targets were areas in the Kyiv and Odesa regions.
“It is important. We would like to see more missiles intercepted, of course… But it was not 10% or zero – it was 60%. And this year, there have been moments when the figure was zero,” Zelensky said.
The military reported that four Zircon missiles and three Iskander missiles were intercepted. The State Emergency Service of Ukraine said that two people were killed and at least eight others were injured as a result of the massive attack on Kyiv.
During his current visit to New York to attend the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky discussed strengthening Ukraine’s defenses against Russian ballistic missiles with Donald Trump.
Ukraine and the United States are also continuing work on launching the production of Patriot interceptor missiles in Ukraine and developing a winter air defense package.
In New York, Zelensky also discussed Ukraine’s ballistic missile defense with U.S. senators and members of the House of Representatives.
Intercepting ballistic missiles is one of the most difficult tasks for air defense systems because of their high speed, steep flight trajectory, and the very short time between detecting the target and intercepting it.
To counter such missiles, Ukraine primarily uses Patriot air defense systems. However, their effectiveness directly depends on the availability of interceptor missiles.
Ukraine has already received Patriot missiles from its partners this year. In particular, Poland and the Netherlands delivered air defense missiles for these systems in April, while Poland later officially confirmed the transfer of PAC-3 missiles. Spain has also said it will continue supplying missiles.
Meanwhile, Ukraine is contracting around 1,000 Patriot missiles using EU funds, although most of them are expected to be delivered over the coming years.
Ukraine also has an agreement with the United States for monthly deliveries of Patriot missiles. However, Volodymyr Zelensky has emphasized that the current supply levels are not sufficient.

articles.title: Moscow invites Kim Jong Un for official visit as Russia deepens diplomatic ties with Pyongyang
articles.body:
Russia has extended an official invitation to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un to visit the country, a deputy foreign minister said Thursday, according to the TASS state news agency.
Moscow and Pyongyang have drawn markedly closer in recent years, with North Korea sending troops to fight alongside Russian forces in Ukraine in 2024 and deepening military cooperation under a mutual defense pact.
Pyongyang refuses to halt nuclear tests
North Korea's foreign ministry on Thursday rejected an international statement urging it to halt nuclear tests, with a spokesperson calling it "a grave political provocation against our state" by "hostile forces."
A meeting of ministers from the Friends of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty — a grouping of Australia, Canada, Finland, Germany, Japan and the Netherlands — said any new nuclear test by North Korea would be irresponsible and unacceptable.
The meeting in New York on Tuesday urged Pyongyang to fully comply with all relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions.
The spokesperson for North Korea's foreign ministry described the country as a responsible nuclear-armed state, in a statement carried by state media KCNA.
In another statement carried by KCNA earlier in the day, North Korea's foreign minister Choe Son Hui said Pyongyang's nuclear weapons status is irreversible.
Choe was responding to a separate meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly this week between the United States, South Korea and Japan at which they reaffirmed their commitment to the complete denuclearisation of North Korea.
The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty, agreed in 1996, bans "any nuclear weapon test explosion or any other nuclear explosion" anywhere in the world, with the goal of reducing and ultimately eliminating nuclear weapons.

The president criticised North Korea for using citizens like ‘currency’ to aid Russia in its war against Ukraine.

He strongly criticised Pyongyang’s involvement in the conflict, questioning why North Korean soldiers were giving their lives in a war against Ukraine.

Ukrainian and South Korean estimates indicate North Korea has deployed approximately 15,000 soldiers to support Russia’s war effort since 2024, primarily in the Kursk border region.

Human rights groups, however, urged him to repatriate them to South Korea, citing the risks of punishments the soldiers faced. South Korean media reported that the two captured soldiers had expressed their desire to defect to South Korea.

articles.title: 4 takeaways from POLITICO’s interviews with French presidential candidates Le Pen, Mélenchon, Attal
articles.body:
PARIS — Top contenders for the 2027 presidential election in France laid out their vision for Europe, Ukraine and relationships with fellow capitals at POLITICO’s first Playbook Paris Live summit on Thursday.
The event gathered far-right leader Marine Le Pen — who is topping the polls and appears all but certain to make it to the contest’s second-round runoff — far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon and Gabriel Attal, a centrist former prime minister.
Here are the key takeaways from the event.
Advertisement
No alignment on Ukraine
Attal came out as a strong advocate for increased support for Ukraine. The 37-year-old said backing Ukraine was an “investment for us” rather than a humanitarian expense. He supported seizing Russian assets to help pay for Kyiv’s defense and did not “exclude” sending European planes to police Ukrainian skies.
Le Pen, on the other hand, made it clear that she believes France can no longer afford to assist Ukraine financially given the country’s budgetary constraints.
“We can train their soldiers and their military leadership and provide them with military aid. We can no longer provide financial assistance to Ukraine, and we regret that,” she said.
Le Pen was adamant that she believed French President Emmanuel Macron had not done enough to bring Moscow and Kyiv to the negotiating table. She said she supported U.S. President Donald Trump’s decision to invite Russian President Vladimir Putin to the G20 summit in Miami in December.
“Any initiatives aimed at putting an end to this slaughter are welcome,” she said.
Both Le Pen and Mélenchon argued that supplying any type of military equipment to Ukraine would likely put France in harm’s way.
Advertisement
“I would like to remind you that Russia is a nuclear power,” Le Pen added. “I do not want France to go to war with any nuclear power.”
Mélenchon said he wanted a ban on Ukrainian deep strikes into Russian territory.
“Do you really think the Russians will just stand by and let Moscow be fired upon without doing anything?” he said. “Do you realize that we’re firing with French and Ukrainian weapons? We’re becoming belligerents.”
In eyebrow-raising comments, Mélenchon doubled down on his opposition to Germany’s plans to beef up its armed forces, pointing to the “history” of German attacks against France.
“[The Germans want to build Europe’s] largest conventional army, to do what? … We need to talk about this,” Mélenchon said.
Advertisement
“There is history. It matters to me. I never believed that the Germans crossed the border several times just for the sake of crossing borders,” Mélenchon said — though he insisted he is not “anti-German.”
Berlin aims to become Europe’s predominant military power in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and American retrenchment from Europe — a move Mélenchon argued was motivated by economic interests, with Germany hoping that a stronger defense industry can make up for losses from its struggling auto industry.
Le Pen is up in arms against the EU budget (and von der Leyen)
Standing by her pledge to drastically cut France’s contribution to the EU budget, Le Pen went all out against European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, accusing her of wanting to “bypass democracy” by fast-tracking negotiations on the EU’s multi-year budget.
Von der Leyen’s “love of democracy is not evident in all of these decisions,” Le Pen said, saying the Commission chief was trying to avoid “accepting the will of the people” by speeding up negotiations before elections next year in France, Poland, Spain and Italy.
Attal marches in Macron’s footsteps on Europe
Attal, who leads President Emmanuel Macron’s centrist political party Renaissance (though the relationship between the two is notoriously frosty), pitched a strongly pro-European agenda, advocating for further economic integration as well as cooperation on environmental and tech regulation.
He once again pushed the idea of a United States of Europe, arguing that the bloc should become a “power continent” that could stand up to China and the U.S. But Attal suggested that could only be done by moving forward with a multi-speed Europe, in which a “small number” of countries, rather than all 27 EU member states, work on ambitious projects like a capital markets union.

articles.title: CIA reportedly warns of Russian plans to attack Spain, France or Italy with sea-launched drones

CIA reportedly warns of Russian plans to attack Spain, France or Italy with sea-launched drones
Spanish newspaper El Mundo has learned from its sources that the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) has warned of Russian plans to attack Spain, France or Italy using drones launched from ships at sea.
Source: European Pravda, citing an El Mundo report
Details: The newspaper reports that European foreign ministries have received a detailed report prepared following CIA Director John Ratcliffe's visit to Moscow.
According to information from the Lithuanian government, Russia plans to launch Gerbera drones with a range of 600 km from ships. Russia is thus reportedly preparing new drone attacks in Europe, this time targeting Mediterranean countries.
"They will use drones launched from the sea, concealed in a container on a ship. It is not difficult at all," a source told the newspaper.
El Mundo's sources say the governments of Spain, France and Italy have also been informed that Russia was preparing a possible drone operation against one of these countries. The warning coincides with an unusual move by Emmanuel Macron: after convening a meeting of the Defence Council on 16 September, two days later he invited the leaders of all parties and candidates in the 2027 presidential election to the Élysée Palace.
Several defence analysts interviewed by the newspaper confirmed that they were aware of the existence of a CIA report that had been circulated among European foreign ministries.
The attacks are reportedly being prepared specifically against France, Italy and Spain because elections will be held there in 2027 and right-wing political forces are already gaining support.
El Mundo says the main purpose of the Russian operation would not be to cause significant destruction. With an explosive payload of around four to five kilograms, a Gerbera drone would more likely be used to shut down an airport, start a fire, fly over a military facility or demonstrate that Russia is capable of reaching Europe's rear areas.
Background:
- Moscow has repeatedly stated that supplying Ukraine with weapons, intelligence and military advisers makes Western countries participants in the war and legitimate targets.
- However, Russia has so far sought to avoid crossing the "threshold of war" by refraining from actions that could provoke a coordinated NATO response, while testing the Alliance's reaction through individual incidents in Poland and the Baltic states. In particular, on 15 September, Italian fighter jets on a NATO patrol mission shot down a drone that had entered Lithuanian airspace. On 23 September, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter violated Polish airspace.

articles.title: US Democrat senator urges Trump to press Xi over China-Iran ties
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US Democratic senator urges Trump to press Xi over China-Iran ties
US Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen urged President Donald Trump on Wednesday to press Chinese President Xi Jinping over Beijing's support for Iran, accusing Chinese companies of providing Tehran with economic and military assistance.
The senior Democrat said Trump should use an upcoming summit with Xi to demand action against Chinese firms accused of supplying Iran with satellite imagery and components used in its missile and drone programmes, as well as helping Tehran circumvent sanctions on its oil exports.
Speaking in the Senate, Shaheen cited reports that Iran obtained high-resolution satellite imagery of a US base in Jordan from Chinese entities before carrying out a missile attack that killed three American soldiers and wounded four others.
She also pointed to China's role as the leading buyer of Iranian oil, saying around 90% of Iran's oil exports go to the country, providing Tehran with billions of dollars in revenue and a "critical economic lifeline".
Chinese and Hong Kong-based companies have also supplied components used in Iranian ballistic missiles and drones, Shaheen said.
"If we want to bring this war to an end, we need to cut off the outside support that allows Iran to keep fighting, and that starts with China," she told the Senate.
Shaheen called on Trump to "use his leverage" with Xi to stop Chinese companies from providing satellite imagery, missile and drone components and access to markets for sanctioned Iranian oil.
She also urged the Trump administration to step up enforcement of existing sanctions against Chinese entities accused of helping Iran.
"And if China doesn't stop, Congress should impose additional consequences," she said.
Shaheen linked China's relationship with Iran to its continued purchases of Russian energy, arguing that Beijing was helping finance conflicts involving both Tehran and Moscow, despite the US, alongside Israel, starting the war on Iran.
She said Trump should consider using powers contained in recently enacted legislation targeting Russia to impose penalties on Chinese buyers of Russian energy.
China was "the top funder of the war in Ukraine, as well as being one of the top funders of the war in Iran", Shaheen said.
Shaheen's call for tougher pressure on China comes despite broad public opposition to the US war with Iran, particularly among Democrats.
A Pew Research Center poll conducted in March found 59% of Americans believed the US had made the wrong decision in using military force against Iran, while 61% disapproved of Trump's handling of the conflict.
Opposition was especially strong among Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents, 88% of whom said the decision to use force was wrong and 90% of whom disapproved of Trump's handling of the war.
More recent Reuters/Ipsos polling has also found support for Trump's handling of the conflict remains weak, with only 34% approving of his strikes on Iran.

On Thursday morning, Zelensky told journalists in New York that Ukraine shot down 60 percent of incoming Russian ballistic missiles during the most recent attack – a modest boost compared to July, when the Patriot shortage let roughly three out of four ballistic missiles slip through, with an abysmal 29 percent intercept rate.
On Aug. 25, Zelensky said Ukraine received additional Patriot missiles, though again without specifying the quantity. Around two weeks earlier, he said only 5 percent of the US stockpile could protect Ukraine through the upcoming winter, and just weeks before that, he had requested 300 missiles from Washington for the winter.
The total number of Patriot missiles in Ukraine remains classified, though most publicized deliveries come in limited numbers, including a 5-missile batch pledged by Spain in March, with Kyiv’s European allies reportedly struggling to provide Ukraine with enough Patriot interceptors.
‘Needed Every Day’: Zelensky, Rutte Talk Patriots
As such, the 60 percent intercept rate likely means Kyiv has received more Patriots, acquired weapons that could do the same job as Patriots, or developed its own domestic versions that can do a nearly similar job.

Fire at Polish Starlink Hub Sparks Sabotage Investigation

articles.title: CCA Builders Start Revving Production Rates, as They Await 2027 Funding
articles.body:
General Atomics Aeronautical Systems Inc. and Anduril Industries both say they’re ready to produce Collaborative Combat Aircraft in volume as they wait for a fiscal 2027 budget to fund that work.
General Atomics announced earlier this week it has the capacity to produce its FQ-42A Vengeance drones at a rate of “six aircraft per month to meet USAF goals” and could make more if needed. Competitor Anduril, which started production of its FQ-44A Fury at its new Arsenal-1 facility in Ohio in March, aims to build 150 aircraft annually, its officials said last week at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference.
The Air Force’s 2027 budget request includes $996.5 million to acquire production CCAs in fiscal 2027, plus another $150 million in advance procurement funds for 2028. But USAF has not specified how many aircraft that might cover.
General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley declined to tell Air & Space Forces Magazine exactly how many FQ-42s are rolling off the company’s production line right now, but did confirm production is underway. “Some of those aircraft will become company aircraft,” he said, meaning that not all are for its Air Force customer.
Brinkley said the company’s potential production expansion could be used to answer international demand for its Gambit series of autonomous drones, which are closely related to the FQ-42.
General Atomics also said in its statement that it is self-funding FQ-42 production today as it awaits Congressional fiscal 2027 appropriations. The new fiscal year launches Oct. 1, but lawmakers failed to pass a budget for fiscal ’27, and instead passed a continuing resolution that would hold current year funding steady, but provides no new funding. The measure ensures funding through Dec. 11, 2026.
GA’s self-funding will help support the government’s procurement plans and prevent delivery delays, the company said, and building aircraft for its own fleet will help it invest in new technologies that reduce risk and increase capabilities.
The Air Force plans to use CCAs as a complement to crewed fighters in a bid to add combat capacity at a lower cost than convention fighter jets. CCAs are designed to be flown semi-autonomously, at times alongside piloted fighters like the F-22 and F-35 Lightning II, and could eventually carry out a variety of missions including air-to-air or air-to-ground strikes; intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance; or electronic warfare operations. The concept is still comparatively early in its development.
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Sept. 14 that USAF is aiming to field at least 500 CCAs by 2032. The Anduril and General Atomics CCAs were selected following a competition in April 2024, andboth companies won initial production contracts in June 2026.
General Atomics said a new FQ-42 was delivered to Creech Air Force Base, Nev., on Sept. 18, for test and evaluation. Creech is home to the Air Force’s Experimental Operations Unit, which has been experimenting with CCAs to develop approaches to how they might be employed in real-life operations.
Jason Levin, Anduril’s senior vice president for air dominance and strike, said Sept. 14 that his firm delivered an FQ-44 to the EOU in August. Prior to that, the YFQ-44A prototype took part in two exercises with the EOU, the first in April and the second in July.
The July exercise at Creech, Levin said, demonstrated that CCA had advanced enough for a single Air Force operator to launch and recover an aircraft on his own after just a few hours of training.
“The Air Force was operating mission autonomy by themselves, which was a first,” Levin said. “They were flying multiple times a day, operating mission autonomy without Anduril personnel—they were on-site kind of helping, but it was really the Air Force operating that.”
Levin said that during the July exercise, Fury flew in the same airspace as crewed fighters and other drones using mission autonomy, helping build Airmen’s trust that CCAs can operate in congested airspace.
The production model of the FQ-44 that will start to roll off the line next year at Arsenal-1 will be able to carry four air-to-air weapons, such as the AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, or AMRAAM, under its wings.
The FQ-42, General Atomics said, has flown in formation with piloted F-35 Lightning II and F-15E Strike Eagle jets to prepare for future test flights, when fighter pilots will actually command the drones. The FQ-42 represents fifth-generation stealth and operates with an internal weapons bay.
General Atomics previously conducted flights of its MQ-20 Avenger drone, operating as a CCA surrogate, to demonstrate how collaborative control flights might work. The company said its aircraft, including the Vengeance, Avenger, and XQ-67A Off-Board Sensing Station, have flown both semi-autonomously and autonomously using AI pilots and under the collaborative control of human pilots flying in the F-22 Raptor and F-35.
“The CCA program’s rate of progress has been incredible,” said Mike Atwood, vice president of advanced programs at General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, in a company statement. “Every week, the Air Force is pushing forward with new and more impressive accomplishments using Vengeance. It’s amazing to think of how far this program has come in such a short amount of time.”

articles.title: SBU detains ‘mole’ within AFU, preparing missile strike on unit repairing Ukrainian drones
articles.body:
Military counter-intelligence of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), with the assistance of the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, has exposed an FSB agent within the ranks of the defenders of Kharkiv region: a mobilized soldier recruited by the enemy was directing hostile fire at the positions of the motorized infantry brigade where he served.
On Thursday, the SBU reported via its Telegram channel that the man had attempted to coordinate a Russian missile attack on his own repair battalion, which restores unmanned aerial vehicle systems.
"To do this, the agent 'leaked' the coordinates of the Ukrainian repair battalion to his FSB handler and planned to leave the facility's premises ahead of the shelling under the pretext of a trip to the hospital," the message reads.
SBU officers exposed the Russian "mole" and detained him in a service vehicle as he drove out of the military base.
Concurrently, the Security Service's military counter-intelligence carried out comprehensive measures to ensure the security of locations where Ukrainian defenders are stationed.
According to the SBU, the suspect had been recruited by the FSB prior to his conscription through a female relative living in the Russian Federation.
"After being mobilized, he served as an electrician specializing in the repair of unmanned systems while simultaneously gathering data for the enemy regarding the deployment locations of his own unit and adjacent units," the message specifies.
During searches, five smartphones were seized from the detainee; he had used them interchangeably for encrypted communication with the enemy.
Security Service investigators have notified the agent of suspicion under Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (high treason committed under martial law).
The perpetrator is in custody without the right to bail. He faces life imprisonment with confiscation of property.
Comprehensive operations were conducted under the procedural supervision of the Prosecutor General's Office.

articles.title: Russia continues to receive imported components, enabling it to ramp up weapons production – Zaluzhny
articles.body:
Valeriy Zaluzhny, Ukraine's Ambassador to the United Kingdom and former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (2021–2024), has warned of the risk of Russian aggression against other countries if the world fails to halt the supply of components to the aggressor state—components that allow it to expand its weapons production.
"Russia has shifted to virtually round-the-clock attacks on Kyiv, Kharkiv, Dnipro, Odesa, and other major Ukrainian cities. They are using everything at their disposal. Both old and new Shahed drones fly straight from the assembly line toward Ukraine, while ballistic missiles are stockpiled for nights like the one we just experienced. Strikes on maternity hospitals, farms, shopping and office centers, and educational institutions constitute blatant terrorism—acts that would be impossible if the Russians lacked the resources to carry them out," Zaluzhny wrote on Facebook on Thursday.
"For years, Russia has continued to receive imported components that enable it not only to sustain but also to ramp up weapons production. The world must finally put a stop to this. Otherwise, tomorrow these weapons could be fired at targets beyond Ukraine," the diplomat emphasized.
As previously reported, in early September, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha stressed the need to systematically close sanctions loopholes following another massive Russian strike, in which foreign-made components and technologies were once again discovered within the weaponry used. "There is something fundamentally wrong with the fact that technologies developed in countries advocating for peace and security end up inside Russian missiles launched at Ukrainian homes," he stated.
Sybiha emphasized that the arrival of such components in the Russian Federation cannot be viewed merely as a side effect of global trade. According to him, Russia deliberately seeks out sanction loopholes, establishes procurement networks, and utilizes intermediaries and third countries to acquire critical components needed to sustain its war machine. He called for significantly stricter export controls, enhanced enforcement, and the imposition of real sanctions on those helping Russia circumvent restrictions. He stated that critical technologies must be kept out of Russia's reach at every stage of the supply chain.

articles.title: Russians guard Madagascar’s parliament speaker as Moscow builds Indian Ocean foothold – RFE/RL
articles.body:
Since Madagascar’s October 2025 coup, Russian military personnel have joined the parliament speaker’s security detail, and Russian instructors have begun training Malagasy soldiers, RFE/RL reported. OSINT investigators traced a flight carrying a senior Russian military intelligence officer and 40 of Russia's Africa Corps members to the island on 20 December 2025.
Madagascar’s new leadership has welcomed Russian military assistance, while Moscow has pursued media projects, energy talks, and the possible recruitment of Malagasy workers. RFE/RL says the prospective destination is Alabuga, a plant producing drones used against Ukraine. Elsewhere in Africa, Russia has sent troops, sought access to resources, and opened cultural centers.
Major General Andrei Averyanov, who oversees Russian military intelligence operations in Africa, was on the December flight. He traveled with members of Africa Corps, a Russian Defense Ministry unit that absorbed some Wagner forces. Madagascar's National Assembly speaker Siteny Randrianasoloniaiko announced the unit’s arrival that month.
Russian intelligence officer Anton Papshev attended the January launch of training for Madagascar’s 1st Airborne Battalion. The program also included a transfer of Russian weapons, though RFE/RL did not specify which ones. In February, interim President Michael Randrianirina met Vladimir Putin in Moscow and welcomed wider cooperation on defense, energy, and other areas.
Russian authorities signed a deal with Randrianasoloniaiko to open a Russia House, a Kremlin cultural center. Ukraine’s military intelligence said Moscow plans to expand the network across Africa to influence young people. Madagascar also authorized a branch of African Initiative, a Russia-linked media organization that helped National Radio launch a “Russ-Mada” program.
RFE/RL said Russian authorities appear to intend to recruit Malagasy workers for Alabuga, a drone assembly plant in Russia’s Tatarstan region.
The plant has recruited thousands of workers, mainly young women from Africa and Central and South Asia, for relatively high-paying jobs. Richard Rakotonirina, head of Madagascar’s Friends of Russia association, visited Alabuga in February. RFE/RL did not establish that any Malagasy workers had been recruited.
Moscow recruits African women to produce drones in horrific conditions — investigation exposes large-scale fraud
During a visit to Moscow, Madagascar’s prime minister discussed Russian fuel supplies, oil storage on the island, and military training.
A Russian delegation also visited an abandoned naval base that Madagascar and France had already agreed to study restoring. RFE/RL did not report any agreement giving Russia access to the base.
Russia’s wider reach in Africa
Madagascar’s emerging ties resemble security arrangements Moscow has built elsewhere in Africa. In the Central African Republic, Russian mercenaries guarded officials and trained troops in exchange for access to gold, diamonds, and timber, RFE/RL reported. Russia's Africa Corps protects the Republic of the Congo’s president, Denis Sassou-Nguesso, who has ruled since 1979, apart from a brief interruption.
In Mali, the force backs a military government and has deployed a drone of a type developed for Russia’s war against Ukraine. Residents and a rights group told RFI that Russian and Malian forces killed four civilian herders. Ukrainian drone specialists are reportedly supporting forces fighting Russian troops there.

articles.title: Kiev deliberately destabilizing global energy markets, Lavrov tells Rubio
articles.body:
Kiev deliberately destabilizing global energy markets, Lavrov tells Rubio
Ukraine’s deliberate attacks on energy and cross-border infrastructure are destabilizing global markets, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has told US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Lavrov and Rubio met on Wednesday on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly in New York, where they held an extensive discussion on Ukraine, bilateral relations, and a range of international issues.
According to the Russian Foreign Ministry, Lavrov drew Rubio’s attention to what it described as close coordination between Kiev and its European backers and raised Ukrainian strikes on civilians and “cross-border infrastructure facilities,” which Russia said are deliberately contributing to instability in global energy markets.
The issue has increasingly drawn attention in Washington as diesel prices have surged to record highs, topping $6.50 a gallon nationally in September 2026. US President Donald Trump recently urged Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky to stop striking Russian refineries, saying the attacks were creating a global shortage and “hurting the world.” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent similarly said earlier this month that Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy assets and refined products were contributing to an “energy shock.”
The US State Department’s brief readout from the Lavrov-Rubio meeting on Wednesday said only that the two diplomats had discussed the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the US-Russia relationship.
Following the meeting, Rubio said both Russia and Ukraine had expressed some interest in a limited ceasefire covering energy targets. He acknowledged, however, that such an arrangement “doesn’t solve the war,” and said reaching one would be difficult because both sides regard energy infrastructure as a strategic target.
Moscow has repeatedly rejected the idea that any limited truce can substitute for a comprehensive settlement, pointing to what it describes as Ukraine’s past violations of ceasefires and arguing that Kiev seeks talks only when the situation on the battlefield becomes critical. Zelensky said this week that Kiev was prepared to stop targeting Russian refineries if Moscow halted strikes on a wide range of Ukraine’s energy, logistics, and port infrastructure.
Lavrov reiterated on Wednesday that Russia would not halt its military operation merely to facilitate negotiations, arguing that such a pause would give Kiev and its European sponsors time to replenish depleted weapons stocks.
Zelensky has meanwhile continued to push for the “full and swift implementation” of the recently enacted sanctions package championed by the late US Senator Lindsey Graham. The law gives Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian oil and gas, potentially targeting countries such as China and India. With global supplies already strained, sharply curbing Russian exports could further disrupt energy trade and drive prices higher as major importers are forced to compete for alternative barrels.
The Russian side reiterated during the Rubio talks that it remains prepared to pursue a political and diplomatic settlement, but only one that addresses the “root causes” of the conflict. Russian officials have repeatedly identified NATO’s expansion toward Russia and Kiev’s policies toward Russian speakers among those issues.
Lavrov also called for further normalization of US-Russia relations, including resolving disputes over diplomatic missions and Russian diplomatic property in the US.
In another sign of continued engagement, Rubio announced after the talks that Washington had invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to attend the G20 summit in Miami in December. The Kremlin welcomed the invitation and said it would consider it through diplomatic channels.

articles.title: Denmark predicts an expansion of the scale of Russia’s hybrid warfare
articles.body:
Denmark predicts an expansion of the scale of Russia’s hybrid warfare
Kyiv • UNN
Danish intelligence expects more frequent and dangerous cyberattacks and acts of sabotage by Russia against the West and NATO. The risk of a limited attack is increasing.
Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service predicts that Russia will expand the scale of its hybrid warfare against Western countries. This is stated in a new threat assessment, reports UNN.
The security situation has deteriorated further. Russia has intensified its use of sabotage, destructive cyberattacks and drone attacks against targets in Europe. Hybrid warfare is gaining momentum. This concerns, for example, the thwarted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport, which, according to German authorities, had been planned in Russia for several months. Russia has become more willing to take risks. Russian drones, and in some cases even missiles, have been shot down in NATO countries bordering Ukraine
The intelligence service expects Russia to escalate its hybrid warfare even further.
Until now, Russia has primarily carried out hybrid attacks against targets in the West in order to sow fear and reduce public support for Ukraine. Russia has increasingly sought to directly disrupt the delivery of this support, for example by sabotaging defence industry facilities or railways used to transport military equipment to Ukraine. The intelligence service assesses that in the coming months Russia will intensify its hybrid warfare even further, carrying out more frequent attacks against the West and NATO that will have more serious consequences for the affected countries than before. This could, for example, include destructive cyberattacks with serious consequences for vital societal functions and sabotage attacks carrying a high risk of casualties
The intelligence service also noted that there is a low but growing risk that Russia will launch a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia. This could happen even if Russia continues its war against Ukraine and does not develop the necessary capabilities to wage a regional war.
A limited military attack would be a desperate step on Russia’s part and, like the escalation of hybrid attacks, could potentially take place in the coming months. The aim of such an attack would be to divert European resources from supporting Ukraine and divide NATO if the alliance is unable to agree on a joint response
The intelligence service predicts that a limited military attack could, for example, take the form of isolated Russian long-range strikes against infrastructure that plays an important role in providing support to Ukraine. Russia could subsequently claim that the missiles struck NATO territory exclusively because their trajectory had been altered by Ukraine. It could also involve a so-called “false flag” operation, in which Russia, for example, uses Ukrainian-made drones to attack a NATO country.
We remind you
Russia has launched a new wave of attacks on European weapons manufacturing plants under the guise of plausible deniability.

articles.title: Four "Zircon" missiles and three ballistic missiles were neutralized over Ukraine during Russia's massive attack
articles.body:
Four "Zircon" missiles and three ballistic missiles were neutralized over Ukraine during Russia's massive attack
Kyiv • UNN
At night, Russia launched 282 drones and missiles at Ukraine, including "Zircon" missiles and ballistic missiles. Air defense destroyed or suppressed 227 targets.
Russia struck Ukraine with missiles, including "Zircon" missiles and ballistic missiles, and 282 drones during the night of September 24; 4 "Zircons," 3 ballistic missiles, and 220 drones, including a "Banderol," were shot down or suppressed. UNN reports this, citing the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
What Russia attacked with and from where
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of September 24 (starting at 18:00 on September 23), the enemy attacked with Zircon anti-ship missiles from the Kursk, Rostov, and Oryol regions of the Russian Federation; Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles from the Kursk and Bryansk regions of the Russian Federation; 282 Shahed-type attack UAVs (including jet-powered ones), Gerbera UAVs, Banderol/Dan-T loitering munitions, and Parodiya-type decoy drones from the following directions: Oryol, Millerovo, Shatalovo, Kursk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk — Russian Federation; the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk; Hvardiyske, Chauda — the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea; and the waters of the Sea of Azov.
Where the enemy struck
"The main areas targeted were the Odesa and Kyiv regions," the statement said.
How air defense performed
The air assault was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense had shot down/suppressed 227 targets:
-  4 Zircon anti-ship missiles; 
-  3 Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles; 
-  1 "Banderol"/"Dan-T"; 
-  219 enemy UAVs of the Shahed and Gerbera types, as well as drones of other types.

articles.title: US Navy admits suicide attempts on carrier strike group
articles.body:
US Navy admits suicide attempts on carrier strike group
Eight US Navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during a ten-month deployment that included the country’s war against Iran, CNN reported on Thursday, citing a letter from the service’s acting secretary.
The carrier, whose tour of duty began in late November 2025, drew media attention earlier this year after reports emerged of logistical and maintenance problems, including food and basic-supply shortages, a lack of hot and potable water, and plumbing failures.
In a written response to questions from Senator Kirsten Gillibrand about the morale and mental health of the USS Abraham Lincoln’s crew, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao disclosed the figure, which hadn’t previously been made public and covers several ships that travel together, including the carrier. Cao also noted that no service members had killed themselves during the deployment that was expected to end in May but has been extended indefinitely.
In August, military outlets Navy Times and Stars and Stripes reported, citing crew members’ families, that collapsing morale, burnout, and mental health problems had driven several sailors to attempt to jump overboard.
The Pentagon has moved to dismiss senior editorial staff at Stars and Stripes, citing insubordination, after the outlet reported on US military operations in the Middle East, including problems involving weapons supplies and the extended deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln. The moves came after senior staff publicly opposed potential Pentagon interference in the outlet’s editorial independence.
Last month, multiple media outlets cited officials as saying that the aircraft carrier was finally heading home from its extended deployment. Earlier this week, Military Times reported that the ship and Carrier Strike Group 3 pulled into Guam for a short logistics stop, officially marking the tenth month of its tour of duty.
The confirmation of suicide attempts previously disclosed by the media comes ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3, amid mounting public disapproval of the Iran war.
Earlier this week, a poll conducted by SSRS for CNN suggested that Americans’ opposition to the war in the Islamic Republic had hardened, with nearly two-thirds saying the US is not winning the conflict and an even larger share saying President Donald Trump is not doing enough to end it. Last week, a Fox News national survey found that 71% of respondents believe the current administration lacks a plan to end the war, while 60% called the military action against the Islamic Republic the “wrong decision.”
Trump, along with members of his administration, has repeatedly accused media outlets of spreading “fake news” about various issues related to the Iran war, including reports that US weapons stockpiles have been depleted.

articles.title: Russian Attack Damages Medical Facility, Homes and School in Odesa
articles.body:
A Russian overnight attack on Odesa damaged a medical facility, 10 residential buildings and a school, local authorities said on Sept. 24.
The strike damaged the roof and part of the upper floor of the medical facility, while blast waves shattered windows in nearby homes and the school.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
No casualties were reported in the preliminary assessment.
Municipal workers began clearing the area overnight. The street has since been cleared, while damaged windows in residential buildings have been boarded up.
Residents are receiving assistance with applications for compensation under Ukraine’s state eVidnovlennia program and Odesa’s Unbreakable Odesa initiative.
Odesa has faced a sustained wave of Russian missile and drone attacks in recent weeks, with strikes hitting residential buildings, logistics facilities, energy infrastructure, warehouses and the city’s port.
On Sept. 23, a Russian attack hit a foreign-flagged commercial cargo ship in the Odesa region, killing its Ukrainian captain. The same attack also set fire to warehouses storing medicines, household goods and food.
Two days earlier, on Sept. 21, Russian forces struck warehouses storing food products for supermarket chains near Odesa, triggering a major fire. More than 80 rescuers were involved in extinguishing the blaze.
On Sept. 19, Russia again struck an 11-story administrative building in Odesa that had been hit the previous day, setting its upper floors on fire. A two-story educational building was also damaged, while two private homes and vehicles were damaged in Odesa district. The attack also hit energy facilities, leaving more than 178,000 households without power.
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, September 23, 2026
The previous day, Sept. 18, Russian forces struck the same 11-story administrative building in central Odesa, injuring 10 people, including two emergency responders. Russia then carried out a follow-up strike while rescuers were working at the scene.
Earlier in September, Russian strikes hit a Nova Poshta logistics facility in the Odesa region, injuring two people and damaging the building’s facade, windows and a cargo vehicle. A separate attack damaged a multi-story residential building in Odesa.
Kyiv also hit overnight
The same overnight wave also targeted Kyiv with ballistic missiles and drones.
A Russian missile attack early Thursday killed a 65-year-old man and injured two people, according to Kyiv authorities. Falling debris partially destroyed a private house in Dniprovskyi District, while a 16-story apartment building and an eight-story nonresidential building were also damaged.
In Podilskyi District, missile debris damaged windows and part of the facade of a maternity hospital. A person was killed in a nearby parking lot, where several cars caught fire. A diagnostic center was also damaged.
A warehouse caught fire in Solomianskyi District, while another warehouse building was damaged in Sviatoshynskyi District.
The missile strike followed a Russian drone barrage on Kyiv the previous day that killed two people and injured 45, according to Mayor Vitali Klitschko.
The attacks came as world leaders gathered at the United Nations to discuss efforts to end Russia’s war against Ukraine. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Wednesday that Moscow would not pause its military campaign during negotiations, while Ukraine continued to press for a ceasefire
