articles.title: Russia, Ukraine renew accusations over overnight airstrikes, killing 8
articles.body:
Burc Eruygur
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
- Operational headquarters reports fire at unspecified facility in Russia’s southern Krasnodar region due to drone debris
Russia and Ukraine on Thursday renewed their accusations concerning overnight airstrikes, with Kyiv saying that eight people were killed in the country’s capital and northeastern Kharkiv region.
Overnight, the Kyiv City Military Administration issued a missile alert in the Ukrainian capital, after which it reported that two warehouses were damaged in the city’s Sviatoshynskyi and Solomianskyi districts, while also reporting damage in other locations.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (DSNS) said on Telegram on Thursday morning that two people were killed and at least eight others were injured in the attack.
“All necessary emergency services are working at the sites,” the DSNS said, which also reported that two people were injured in the country’s southern Odesa region following overnight Russian strikes.
It said the strikes in the Odesa region caused a fire at a previously attacked shopping center, while a two-story private residential building caught fire at another location, where the injuries occurred.
It also said that the roof of a seven-story city hospital building and a 10-story non-residential building were damaged.
Separately, Kharkiv Governor Oleh Synyehubov said that six people were killed and 12 others injured following a morning strike on a farm in the village of Stara Hnylytsia.
Ukraine’s Air Force claimed that its air defenses shot down 220 out of 282 drones launched by Russia overnight, as well as seven missiles.
Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry claimed it launched a massive strike on a number of facilities involved in drone production and telecommunications centers providing services to the Ukrainian military in Kyiv.
It further claimed striking two logistics centers in Odesa “used for storing and distributing military and dual-use cargo arriving in Ukraine from European nations,” as well as a tanker “transporting fuel intended for the Armed Forces of Ukraine” to the port of Chornomorsk.
It also claimed downing 40 Ukrainian drones overnight over six regions, as well as over Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014.
The operational headquarters in Russia’s southern Krasnodar region said that a fire broke out at an unspecified facility in the region’s Dinskoy district due to falling drone debris.
“There were no casualties. Fifty personnel and 15 pieces of equipment – including units from the Russian Emergencies Ministry – have been deployed to extinguish the fire,” the statement added.
Independent verification of the claims is difficult due to the ongoing war.
Both Russia and Ukraine have ramped up strikes in recent months, targeting each other’s logistics centers, ports, and energy infrastructure.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that their strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

articles.title: Russia wants to carry out an operation similar to Ukraine’s “Spiderweb” against three European countries — media
articles.body:
Russia wants to carry out an operation similar to Ukraine’s “Spiderweb” against three European countries — media
Kyiv • UNN
U.S. intelligence warned Spain, Italy, and France about possible attacks by Russian drones launched from vessels. The likely goal is sabotage and a demonstration of capabilities.
Russia wants to repeat the Ukrainian "Spiderweb" operation against three European countries—Spain, Italy, or France. The CIA warned of possible attacks, reports El Mundo, according to UNN.
Details
Russia is preparing new attacks using drones in Europe, but this time they will target Mediterranean countries. U.S. intelligence services have gathered information about the Kremlin’s plans to escalate the conflict and shared it with the governments of several European countries
A source in Lithuania’s Ministry of Defense told the publication: ""They will use drones launched from the sea, concealed in a container on a vessel; it is not difficult at all".
It is noted that the justification for such an escalation has long been on the table. Moscow has repeatedly stressed that the supply of weapons, intelligence, and military advisers to Ukraine makes Western countries participants in the war and legitimate targets.
Until now, Russia has operated below what experts call the "war threshold," avoiding actions that could provoke a coordinated NATO response, while at the same time launching an increasingly large-scale sabotage campaign against facilities in countries supporting Ukraine, as well as isolated incidents apparently intended to test the limits and gauge the response
Most likely, Russia will use Gerbera drones against Spain, France, or Italy—the same drones with which it terrorizes Ukraine every day.
The main objective of an operation using Gerberas dropped from a merchant vessel should not be to cause large-scale destruction. With an explosive payload of approximately four to five kilograms, this device is more useful for shutting down an airport, setting something on fire, flying over a military base, or demonstrating that Russia can reach the European rear
We remind you
Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service predicts an expansion of the scale of Russia’s hybrid war against Western countries.

articles.title: How the U.K. Is Supporting Saudi Arabia In Its Fight Against the Houthis
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia will have assistance from a key Western ally in its fight against Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, as Britain is providing military support to the Kingdom in a bid to help restore stability in the region and ease pressures on the global energy supply.
“We’re working with our friends to try and deliver that de-escalation,” British Defense Minister Luke Pollard said in an interview Tuesday. The “purely defensive” deployment of an RAF Voyager to Saudi Arabia is intended to “ensure there’s no further escalation in the Red Sea, which could further risk our fuel prices,” he added.
The international assistance comes following weeks of fighting between the Saudi-backed government of Yemen and the Houthis, which shattered a four-year informal cease-fire in the country's civil war. The Houthi rebels have made significant advances along the Red Sea coastline as they seek to tighten their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb, a critical maritime chokepoint that links Asia and Europe via the Red Sea and Suez Canal. With global energy supplies already under strain due to the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz amid the Iran war, the strangling of another trade route could further impact oil and fuel prices.
“Much of our trade, both in goods and in energy, comes through that part of the world. What happens in that part of the Middle East is absolutely vital for our own national security and our own economic security,” Pollard said, explaining why Britain responded to the Kingdom’s request for help.
When talking to reporters en route to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, ahead of his sit-down with President Donald Trump on Tuesday, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham also cited the cost of living “pressures” at home as a key reason for the support and said he was “acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region.”
Burnham emphasized that it’s a “time-limited agreement in terms of the assistance that we will provide, but we will keep it under review.”
The support extended to Saudi Arabia marks Burnham’s first military deployment since he became Prime Minister in July. However, it’s far from the first time the U.K. has offered assistance to Saudi Arabia, as the two nations share a close military alliance.
How exactly will the U.K. be supporting Saudi Arabia?
The Ministry of Defense on Tuesday confirmed it had agreed to “provide an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft to support Saudi defensive activity” in the region. According to the British Royal Air Force (RAF), a Voyager provides strategic air support by allowing jets and other aircraft to refuel while in flight.
Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer in defense studies at King's College London, says the Voyager “basically allows the Saudi Air Force to stay in the air over Yemen for longer without having to fly a single sortie and then returning to base.”
“It increases the operational tempo in terms of targeting strikes and being more flexible, and more agile in responding to changing situations on the ground,” he tells TIME.
According to Pollard, the Voyager is set to operate from the British RAF base in Cyprus, which was targeted by Iran earlier this year, and will support the British-built Typhoon jets used by Saudi Arabia. “That will help them with their defensive actions against the Houthis, who have been attacking not just the capital of Saudi Arabia in Riyadh, but also the Republic of Yemen as well,” he said.
Britain has historically held the role of “guarantor for maritime freedom of navigation all around the world,” says Krieg, describing the U.K.’s latest attempt to ease tensions over the Red Sea as an example of the government “stepping up to the plate.”
“We're not just helping a partner in the region,” he adds. “We're also helping ourselves, because the Houthis having the Bab al-Mandeb is not something that the U.K. can tolerate.”
Krieg says the move signifies a small success for Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states as they seek to strengthen bilateral security relationships beyond their traditional reliance on the U.S. This is “the worst security situation the Saudis have been in [for] a very long time,” he notes.
“Gulf states are trying to supplement the existing U.S. capabilities with all kinds of [other] agreements, like the Mecca pact,” he says, referencing a trilateral defense security pact made between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey in August. “The U.K. wants to be seen as being active and being there when a friend is in need.”
The long-standing alliance between the U.K. and Saudi Arabia
The U.K. and Saudi Arabia share an alliance that dates back to almost a century ago.
“It's a very long, strategic partnership,” says Krieg. “It goes back to the early days of the current Kingdom, where Britain, at the time, was still the only superpower in the world, and was controlling the waterways and a lot of the territories in Arabia, including in South Yemen.”
Britain was among the first governments to recognize the independent territories of Saudi Arabia through the Treaty of Jeddah in 1927, which helped solidify the boundaries of the nascent kingdom ahead of the formation of modern Saudi Arabia in 1932.
Decades later, the U.K. supported the Saudi-led military coalition in its campaign against the Houthis from 2015 until the 2022 truce.
According to the Campaign Against Arms Trade (CAAT), the published value of U.K. arms export licenses to Saudi Arabia from the start of the bombing campaign in March 2015 through the April 2022 truce was £7.1 billion ($9.4 billion).
“The two main Western backers of the Saudi Kingdom are the Americans and the British,” says David Wearing, an assistant professor in international relations at the University of Sussex. “From the British and the American point of view, the Middle East is strategically important because it's a huge source of global energy suppliers, oil, and gas.”
In late 2023, the Houthis started disrupted shipping in the Red Sea, targeting cargo ships they said were linked to Israel, in what they described as a show of support for Palestinians in Gaza. Amid concerns over the impact on the world economy, the U.S. and U.K. joined forces in January 2024, striking multiple Houthi targets in Yemen. In April 2025, the U.K. government participated in another joint operation with the U.S. against a Houthi military facility in Yemen.
In March of this year, the U.K. deployed a Sky Sabre, the army’s medium range air defense missile system, to Saudi Arabia to defend the Kingdom against Iranian missile and drone attacks.
The U.K. government's Strategic Export Controls Annual Report of 2025 described the military relationship with Saudi Arabia as a “longstanding” partnership providing “Typhoon, Tornado, and Hawk aircraft, mine countermeasure vessels, and associated munitions, infrastructure, logistics and manpower support packages.”
BAE Systems—a major British defense, aerospace, and security company—said in its own 2025 report that Saudi Arabia was its largest customer by sales in its air business.
How are Saudi Arabia’s other allies responding to the Houthis' advances?
Saudi Arabia has reportedly sought assistance from allies to stave off Houthi advances. France, Pakistan, and Egypt issued strong statements condemning the Houthi attacks, but have not publicly announced new military support for the Kingdom.
Trump is understood to have received requests from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to strike the Houthi rebels. According to the New York Times, Trump reportedly considered launching strikes against the Houthis over the weekend, before ultimately deciding against it. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Asked Tuesday why Washington has held back from striking the Houthis, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said it’s “a very dangerous and complex” conflict.
“If it comes down to it, the United States will always stand with Saudi Arabia and support them because we have an agreement with them to do so,” he said, referencing the U.S. economic and defense partnership with Saudi Arabia signed last November, that deepened co-operation between the two countries.
Fears mount over global energy supply as Houthis advance
Global energy supplies have been under increasing strain since the start of the Iran war on Feb. 28, as Tehran has leveraged its chokehold over the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of global oil production flowed prior to the conflict.
In the past few weeks, the Houthis have captured Yemen’s port city of Mokha and the strategic Perim Island, which sits in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. If the Houthis were to assume control of the strait, shipping companies could be forced to travel via South Africa’s Cape of Good Hope—a longer, costlier route.
The volume of crude oil and petroleum liquids moving through the Bab el-Mandeb increased earlier this year, with the route being used as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz. The shipments surged from 5.6 million barrels per day in the first quarter of 2026 to 8.1 million per day in the second quarter, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA).
However, recent crossings have been marred by uncertainty over the potential threat posed by the Houthis. Data shared with TIME by Kpler, a commodities data and analytics firm, showed an estimated 34 vessels transited the Bab el-Mandeb on Sept. 15, a drop from the estimated 53 crossings recorded on July 15th.
A spokesperson for the Houthis on Sept. 11 insisted the waterway will remain free to roam “with the exception of Saudi ships.” Yet concerns among global leaders and shipping companies remain.
Burnham and other U.K. officials have framed Britain’s defensive support partly around the potential economic consequences at home. The average price of petrol rose by 9.1 pence per litre between July and August 2026, compared with a rise of 0.3 pence per litre between July and August 2025, according to data from the Office of National Statistics.
Wearing says that because oil is traded on a global market, supply disruptions in one region can push up benchmark prices worldwide, with those costs cascading through the broader economy.
“What Americans call gas and what we call petrol, if that goes up, think how many goods to market are taken by heavy lorries on petrol. It can push up the price of everything: shipping, road transit, energy, all kinds of industrial production and many consumer products,” he says. “Oil is the lifeblood of the world economy, the longer you restrict the supply, the higher the price goes, the more inflationary pressure there is on everything, and that affects Britain, but it affects the whole system. It's like a heart attack in a human body, suddenly it's not being pumped round."

articles.title: Poland says Starlink fire was sabotage
articles.body:
The fire at a Starlink ground station near Warsaw on Wednesday night was an act of sabotage and part of hybrid warfare against Poland, Digital Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said Thursday morning.
“[This was] sabotage and an attempt to disrupt the operation of a vital station that is crucial for the security and continuity of internet services in Ukraine,” Gawkowski told state broadcaster TVP Info, stopping short of blaming Russia for the incident directly.
“It’s about actions aimed at shutting down the internet and disrupting the functioning of basic services. These may concern the supply of water, gas or electricity, as well as the financial system,” Gawkowski added.
Advertisement
The fire broke out in the village of Wola Krobowska, 50 kilometers south of Warsaw. It didn’t cause significant damage and there were no injuries. Poland’s counterintelligence agency, ABW, and the police are investigating the incident.
Operated by the state-owned telecoms company Exatel, the station links Starlink satellites to terrestrial internet networks. Together with a station in Kaunas, Lithuania, it serves Central European users as well as Ukraine, Polish media reported.
The minister has previously warned that Poland faces some 2,000–3,000 cyberattacks on its infrastructure daily.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned last week that NATO, Ukrainian and Polish intelligence assessments point to Russian plans to step up hybrid attacks on countries supporting Kyiv, including Poland, in the coming months.
Tusk also said Moscow would mask such strikes as accidents to undermine NATO’s willingness to respond collectively.
Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski urged Moscow to end the war at the U.N. Security Council Wednesday, citing the West’s economic superiority over Russia.
“You can still kill a lot of people, but you cannot win. You can stop this imperial war of choice at any time,” Sikorski said.

articles.title: Russians attack Kyiv with ballistic missiles while Zelenskyy discusses Graham Act with congressmen

articles.title: Russian attacks kill at least 16, injure 59 across Ukraine as Kyiv hit by waves of drones, ballistic missiles
articles.body:
Russian attacks kill at least 16, injure 59 across Ukraine as Kyiv hit by waves of drones, ballistic missiles
At least 16 people were killed and 59 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, as Russia launched several waves of ballistic missiles at Kyiv overnight, local authorities said on Sept. 24.
Two people were killed and eight others injured in Kyiv, where Russian ballistic missiles struck the capital in three waves overnight. Residential buildings, a maternity hospital, energy, and logistics infrastructure were among the sites damaged, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky.
"Every such attack happens because pressure on the aggressor has still not become total, and Russia believes it can continue relying on ballistic terror," Zelensky said. "We need ballistic missile interceptors to protect lives."
Russia launched 282 attack drones of various types overnight, including jet-powered drones, as well as Zircon anti-ship missiles and Iskander-M, S-400, and KN-23 ballistic missiles, the Air Force said. Ukrainian air defenses shot down 227 aerial targets, including 219 drones, four Zircon missiles, three ballistic missiles, and one Banderol munition. Strikes were recorded at 13 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at 10 locations.
In Donetsk Oblast, eight people were killed and 19 others injured in Russian attacks over the past day, regional Governor Vadym Filashkin said. Five people were killed in Oleksandrivka, two in Kramatorsk, and one in Sloviansk.
In Kharkiv Oblast, Russian attacks killed six people and injured 12 others over the past day, regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Among the attacks, Russia struck an agricultural enterprise in Stara Hnylytsia, where 12 people were injured, according to the Governor.
In Sumy Oblast, nine people were injured in Russian attacks over the past day, local authorities said. Russian forces carried out nearly 60 attacks against 22 settlements.
In Odesa Oblast, two people were injured in a mass combined Russian attack that damaged a hospital, a school, residential buildings, a shopping center, warehouses, and other civilian infrastructure, regional Governor Oleh Kiper said.
In Kherson Oblast, two people were injured as Russian forces attacked critical infrastructure as well as residential areas, local authorities said. Two apartment buildings, a house and gas pipelines were damaged.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, six people were injured in Russian attacks on the Zaporizhzhia district, Governor Ivan Fedorov said. Russian forces carried out 690 strikes against 55 settlements across the region over the past day.
Russian attacks on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast injured one person over the past day, regional authorities said. Russian forces attacked three districts more than 10 times with drones and artillery.

articles.title: Ukraine transfers two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, Zelensky says
articles.body:
Ukraine has transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday in an address to the United Nations General Assembly.
"Recently, we sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea," said Zelensky in his speech.
"These guys are not easy to capture alive. One of them, when he realized he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself. And he was shocked that fate did not let him die."
Zelensky did not provide more details about the return. Ukraine captured the two North Koreans in Russia's Kursk region in January last year.
They were the first North Korean soldiers to be apprehended alive since the country entered the Russia-Ukraine war in 2024.
Zelensky said at the time that he would hand them over to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un if he could facilitate their exchange for Ukrainians held captive in Russia.
Human rights groups, however, urged him to repatriate them to South Korea citing the risks of punishments the soldiers faced.
South Korean media reported that the two captured soldiers had expressed their desire to defect to South Korea.
South Korea's unification and foreign ministries did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Zelensky criticizes North Korea's military support for Russia
Zelensky in his speech also criticized North Korea for sending its troops to fight for Russia.
"This is madness too. Why should Koreans give their lives in a war against Ukraine? Kim Jong Un uses them like currency. And he gets something in return," he said.
North Korea has sent around 14,000 to 15,000 soldiers since 2024 to support Russia's war against Ukraine, according to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates.
Most of them have been deployed in the Russian region of Kursk, where they helped Moscow's forces repel a Ukrainian incursion.
The country has also supplied Russia with millions of artillery and mortar rounds, ballistic missiles, long-range artillery and multiple-launch rocket systems, according to Ukrainian and independent assessments.

articles.title: Surveys Show More Americans Warming to China
articles.body:
Americans are warming to China, new surveys show.
A Pew Research Center survey published Wednesday found that the share of Americans with a cold view of China has fallen to 54% from 68% in 2021. Over the same period, the share of Americans with a warm view of China grew from 11% to 19%, while those with a neutral view grew from 20% to 27%. The findings are based on responses from 1,168 U.S. adults who were asked to rate China as part of a broader survey conducted Sept. 14-20.
Another survey published this week by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs found that American sentiment towards China has warmed since a record low in 2024. The survey, conducted July 10-21, showed that fewer Americans see China as a threat, with 41% considering China’s territorial ambitions a critical threat to the U.S. as compared to 52% in 2022. Americans also increasingly favor cooperation with China over containment: 57% said the U.S. should engage with China, while 40% think the U.S. should actively limit the growth of China’s power.
“There is appetite for engagement. Part of this may be recognition that better understanding is a positive,” says Ja-Ian Chong, associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore.
Chong says the results reflect a “rebound” from pandemic-era lows of U.S. views of China. A Pew survey published in July 2020 found that 73% of Americans viewed China unfavorably—then the highest share since Pew began tracking the measure in 2005. By 2023, a separate Pew survey found that figure had risen to 83%, amid widespread concern about Beijing’s relationship with Russia and tensions over Taiwan.
Mixed politics
President Donald Trump has also signaled greater openness to Beijing, at least in its economic relationship. The “positive language coming from the White House” may have fuelled some of the shift, Chong tells TIME.
Early into his second term, Trump raised tariffs on many Chinese imports to a staggering 145% in an effort to bring manufacturing back to the U.S. His Administration also increased scrutiny of Chinese visa applicants and revoked the visas of some Chinese students, raising alarms about a “China Initiative 2.0.” The Administration also restricted sales of Nvidia’s H20 artificial intelligence chip to China and added dozens of Chinese entities to an export blacklist over national security concerns.
The Trump Administration has also continued its crackdown on “birth tourism,” a practice Trump has singled out Chinese nationals over. On Wednesday, the State Department announced that it would restrict visas for foreigners who knowingly participate in or facilitate commercial arrangements to give birth in the U.S. in order to secure their children American citizenship, a policy widely seen as an effort to restrict birthright citizenship.
But Trump has since eased some technology restrictions, pursued a trade truce, and renewed dialogue with Beijing. Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington on Wednesday to much fanfare, marking the leaders’ third in-person meeting since Trump returned to office. Economic negotiations have been central to that diplomatic thaw, which the Chicago Council report said suggests that the Trump Administration views China primarily through an economic lens, rather than strategic competition.
“The top leadership on both U.S. and Chinese sides have made significant steps to try and arrest the downward trend in their relationship,” says Dylan Loh, associate professor of public policy and global affairs at Nanyang Technology University in Singapore. “The warming trend isn’t admiration but a moderation of threat perception, driven by a shift toward viewing China as a competitor rather than an immediate adversary as other crises take precedence.”
Still, Chong cautions: “There remains a deep reservoir of apprehension” among Americans towards China.
Trump’s MAGA Republican base remains hawkish. According to the Chicago Council survey, 63% of MAGA Republicans favor containing China rather than cooperating with it, whereas 57% of non-MAGA Republicans favor cooperation. A March 2026 poll by the Chicago Council, alongside NPR and Ipsos, found that MAGA Republicans were more likely than non-MAGA Republicans to prefer higher tariffs on Chinese imports and more restrictions on U.S.-China trade, even if it resulted in higher costs for American consumers, as well as limits on Chinese international students studying in the U.S.
Skepticism towards China is also pronounced on Capitol Hill. In a Sept. 18 letter, Rep. John Moolenaar (R, Mich.), chair of the House Select Committee on China, urged the Trump Administration to restrict Beijing’s access to U.S. AI and semiconductor technology. In December, Sen. Pete Ricketts (R, Neb.) and Sen. Chris Coons (D, Del.) also introduced legislation to block exports of advanced AI chips to China.
Lawmakers have also pressed Trump to stand firm on Taiwan as the President described a pending U.S. arms package to the island as a “negotiating chip” in talks with Beijing. Moolenaar warned against concessions on U.S. arms sales to Taiwan, while Ricketts urged that the U.S. cannot allow China to take the island by force.
By contrast, public support for direct military intervention over Taiwan has declined. The Chicago Council study this week found that just 38% of Americans support using U.S. troops to defend Taiwan in case of a Chinese invasion, down from 52% in 2021.
Shifting global attitudes
The shift in U.S. attitudes comes as China’s global image has improved and America’s has deteriorated. A Pew survey published in July found that people in most of 36 countries surveyed viewed China more favorably than the U.S., a reversal from last year when the U.S. generally retained an advantage despite declining ratings.
Internationally, “perceptions of Washington’s unfriendly and unhelpful trade and security policies abroad and how it is causing problems to various countries' own domestic economies” has driven a shift in sentiment away from the U.S., says Loh.
The Trump Administration imposed sweeping tariffs on much of the world in April 2025, and has pursued new ones after the Supreme Court struck down the bulk of “reciprocal tariffs.” The Administration has also pulled back from international institutions and foreign aid. World leaders have also expressed concern with Trump’s expansionist rhetoric towards Canada, Greenland, Venezuela, and Cuba, as well as the U.S. and Israel’s war against Iran, which has driven up energy prices around the world.
The U.S.-China geopolitical rivalry invites comparisons that can work in China’s favor, says Benjamin Ho, assistant professor and coordinator at the Singapore-based S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies’s China Program. Disillusionment with Washington may make Beijing look more appealing by contrast, even to Americans, he adds. Domestically, Trump’s job approval rating was at a record low of 32% in September, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling.
“It’s easy when you’re unhappy with things at home to instead look at your peer rival,” Ho says.
Kishore Mahbubani, a Singaporean diplomat and former President of the United Nations Security Council, tells TIME that, against the backdrop of the U.S. withdrawing from the global stage, China has come across as a more dependable partner for much of the Global South.
Meanwhile, Chinese consumer brands and cultural exports have found new audiences abroad, like Pop Mart’s Labubu dolls. On TikTok, which is owned by Chinese company ByteDance outside the U.S., users have embraced Chinese customs, like drinking warm water and practicing tai chi as part of the “Chinamaxxing” trend.
Ho points to social media exposure as a significant factor in driving youth opinion. He notes that China has toned down its assertive “wolf warrior” diplomacy in favor of a more flexible approach. Many positive depictions of China online appear to be organic, although media watchdogs previously reported that Beijing has used international broadcasting and advertising campaigns to spread propaganda.
China has taken deliberate steps to project an open, positive global image, analysts say. Beijing has expanded visa-free access for foreign tourists and sought to bring in more international students. China’s foreign ministry announced in May that more than 50,000 young Americans had visited for exchanges since November 2023. Mahbubani says that as more people visit China, they “see that Chinese cities represent the future.”
China has also invested heavily in overseas infrastructure through its Belt and Road Initiative.
Young Americans were more likely to view China warmly, the Pew survey found. Americans under 50 gave China a more positive rating than those 50 and older, although younger Americans were still more likely to view China coldly.
Earlier polling also found that younger Americans are less concerned about China’s growing global power. In a 2025 survey by the Chicago Council, just 34% of Gen Z Americans view China’s power as a critical threat to the U.S., as compared to 43% of Millenials, 56% of Gen Xers, and 62% of Boomers.

articles.title: Eight months of 2026 brought more Ukrainian civilian casualties than all of last year, UN says
articles.body:
Russian strikes have killed or wounded more Ukrainian civilians in the first eight months of 2026 than in all of last year, a senior United Nations official told the Security Council, Censor.net reported. The official warned that the toll keeps climbing as missiles and drones increasingly reach cities far from the front line. She also cautioned that mounting attacks on Ukraine's battered energy grid could push millions into a dark, cold winter.
In the war's fifth year, Russia's long-range strikes on Ukrainian cities have shifted the danger from the front to the streets where people live, and the rising civilian toll now tracks how far those weapons reach.
Casualties outpace all of 2025
Rosemary DiCarlo, the UN Under-Secretary-General for Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, gave the toll as the Council met on Ukraine, Ukrinform reported.
"In just the first eight months, more civilians were killed or injured in Ukraine than in all of 2025," she said.
The heavy toll already recorded in September shows the trend continuing, she added, as strikes hit populated areas away from the front.
The UN human rights office has confirmed at least 17,257 civilians killed since February 2022, including 835 children. Another 53,693 people have been wounded, among them 3,247 children, and DiCarlo said the real numbers are likely far higher. Kyiv and other cities have faced near-daily attacks in recent weeks, she said, with strikes hitting railways, shopping centers, gas stations, warehouses, and food and logistics firms.
A warning over the coming winter
DiCarlo said the mounting strikes on Ukraine's already-damaged energy infrastructure are especially worrying with another war winter near.
"The cumulative impact of these strikes could plunge millions of people into darkness and cold in the coming months," she said.
She urged an immediate moratorium on strikes on populated areas and urgent action to protect the power grid. Targeting civilians and civilian sites is prohibited under international law, she noted.
The warning follows the deadliest stretch of the war for civilians, when UN monitors counted 437 people killed in July, the worst monthly toll since May 2022. Russia has also renewed strikes on gas production and power plants ahead of the heating season.

articles.title: Israel ready to resume strikes on Iran as regime aims to rebuild nuclear program - report
articles.body:
Israeli officials believe that it's only a matter of time until the resumption of strikes against Iran, according to a report by Saudi state-owned news outlet Al Hadath on Thursday.
The official told the outlet that the Israeli intelligence has detected an attempt by Iran to revive and activate its nuclear program in anticipation of a strike, following reports in Israel about the regime transferring its remaining nuclear project to Jabal al-Fas, near the Natanz nuclear facility.
The report also cited the official saying that Israel is "defensively and offensively prepared for the possibility of renewed war on Iran and on other fronts as well, at any time."
"We will move to strike nuclear facilities and any site belonging to them again if Tehran crosses any of the red lines, whether with or without the participation of the US," the official added.
The official also warned that the current economic sanctions taken against Iranian-linked entities are generating pressure in Tehran, causing internal division and domestic pressure. "These factors could push it [the Iranian regime] toward military responses in the region, including against Israel."
He then insisted that the only way to have a non-nuclear Iran is through a regime change in the country.
Elections don't constitute a decisive variable against Iran
The official also revealed that the elections in Israel, which will be held on October 27, aren't a factor that could influence the decision-making about striking Iran.
He also said that the current sanctions by the Trump administration are having better effects than expected, with current estimates suggesting that a regime collapse could happen sooner than anticipated.
Finally, the official warned Al Hadath that Israel doesn't see much value in the current negotiations between Americans and Iranians, despite the continuation of contacts and mediations, due to Tehran’s procrastination and its bets on political developments in the United States and Israel that could stop an attack from happening.
Iran, US meet on sidelines of UNGA
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner communicated through mediators on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, the first such contacts since an interim ceasefire agreement collapsed in July.
"Steve and Jared had a very productive meeting today with mediators of Iran, merely mediators. Let's see what happens with that," US President Donald Trump said. "They've been mediated for a while, but I think there's a lot of momentum for them to make a deal. It's what we're hearing from everybody."
The Al Hadath report mentioned that no agreement was reached during this meeting, as disagreements continued over several issues, most notably the Strait of Hormuz, in addition to the lack of trust between them.

US steps up military activity near Iran – media
The US has stepped up military activity around the Strait of Hormuz, with reconnaissance aircraft spotted near Iranian territory and additional fighter jets reportedly deployed to the region, RIA Novosti reported on Thursday, citing sources.
US reconnaissance aircraft were observed overnight near the Iranian islands of Qeshm and Hengam, while aircraft and small drones were also seen over Kermanshah Province in western Iran, according to people familiar with the matter.
Washington has also reportedly transferred 12 F-16 fighter jets from Spangdahlem Air Base in Germany to the region, the source said, adding that the increased activity could signal a possible escalation.
The reported activity comes as oil tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has risen sharply. TankerTrackers, a vessel-tracking service, said this week that crude flows across the US Navy blockade line have doubled in less than a month to around 13 million barrels per day (bpd). It estimated actual Hormuz transits at about 10.35 million bpd after excluding exports from Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates and Mina al-Fahal in Oman.
The numbers have doubled in less than a month.
The total crude oil egress via the USN-BL is now 13 Mbpd, with estimated SoH transits at 10.35 Mbpd given that Fujairah and Mina al-Fahal together account for around 2.65 Mbpd on average.

The Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy routes, has been a major flashpoint since the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran in February. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) moved to restrict shipping through the waterway following the initial strikes, while Washington later imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports. Oil flows through the strait fell from 21.6 million bpd in the final quarter of 2025 to 4.9 million in the second quarter of this year, according to US government data.
The tracking service attributed the increase partly to Saudi Arabia redirecting exports through the Persian Gulf following disruption to its East-West pipeline, as well as to daytime Hormuz crossings under additional US Central Command protection.
The East-West pipeline carries Saudi crude to the Red Sea, allowing exports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. It had been transporting around 4 million bpd after the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupted shipping through the strait, but was shut earlier this month following drone attacks that Riyadh said originated in Iraq, where Iranian-backed armed groups allegedly operate.
Saudi Arabia restarted the pipeline at a reduced rate this week, although a return to normal flows could reportedly take several weeks.
The developments follow renewed threats from US President Donald Trump against Tehran. Addressing the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump said he faced a “big decision” between reaching an agreement with Iran and “annihilat[ing] the Islamic Republic.” He also called on other countries to join Washington in economically isolating Iran.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian responded by saying Tehran remained open to talks but would not negotiate under pressure.
US and Iranian officials also resumed contact on the sidelines of the General Assembly, with Tehran conveying its conditions for peace through Qatari mediators. They include an end to hostilities and the US naval blockade, the release of frozen Iranian assets, and arrangements for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei reportedly told Iranian state television that Tehran would not resume negotiations with Washington until its conditions are met.

AP compares Trump's meetings with Xi Jinping and Putin
Associated Press has compared the ceremonial welcomes US President Donald Trump gave Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian ruler Vladimir Putin.
Source: АР
Details: Xi Jinping arrived in Washington on the night of 23-24 September (Kyiv time). Trump personally met him at the foot of the aircraft steps, a gesture that is unusual, after senior officials from both countries agreed to extend their trade truce until January.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the extension of the truce – under which the two sides agreed to reduce tariffs and refrain from introducing new trade restrictions – in an interview with Fox News at the very moment Trump was meeting Xi at Joint Base Andrews near Washington.
AP noted that trade has become one of the main sources of tension in relations between the two superpowers, alongside issues involving artificial intelligence, Trump's conflict with Iran and China's claims over Taiwan. However, Xi Jinping's three-day visit is expected to be largely ceremonial, as evidenced by Trump's decision to meet the Chinese leader immediately after his landing rather than wait for him to arrive at the White House.
The welcoming ceremony also included a flyover by two B-1 bombers, a guard of honour with different branches of the military represented and the display of the flags and the playing of the national anthems of both countries.
During the meeting, Trump sought to replicate the pomp with which he was welcomed in China earlier this year. Xi was not at the airport to greet Trump. However, a red carpet was rolled out for Trump's Air Force One in Beijing.
The AP report noted that the long red carpet laid out for Xi Jinping's arrival was reminiscent of a similarly exceptionally long carpet that the US rolled out for Putin when he landed at a US Air Force base in Alaska last summer to attend a meeting aimed at finding ways to end Russia's war against Ukraine.
The two leaders are expected to discuss substantive issues in greater detail on 24 September, after a welcoming ceremony at the White House and a military parade. They will later exchange toasts at a formal dinner attended by technology industry leaders, including Jensen Huang of Nvidia and Elon Musk of SpaceX.
On 25 September, Xi and his wife will return to the White House for a private tea with the Trumps and then visit the National Archives in Washington together. The White House said they will view historical documents highlighting the relationship between the two countries.

articles.title: Saudi oil exports hit new hurdle as insurance costs soar
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saudi oil export strategy hits new hurdle as Red Sea insurance costs soar
The cost of insuring an oil tanker loaded from Saudi Arabia's main Red Sea port has tripled in recent weeks, industry sources told Reuters, adding to the major crude producer's struggles to find a viable channel for its exports.
Saudi Arabia used its East-West pipeline to divert around 4 million barrels per day - 4% of global supply - to the Red Sea after Iran constrained Gulf exports via the Strait of Hormuz from March in response to US and Israeli air strikes.
The kingdom shut the pipeline on September 11 after drone attacks that it said came from Iraq, where Iran backs some militia groups. It is now building volumes back but loadings at the major port of Yanbu have yet to resume, according to industry sources, satellite images and shipping data.
Quoted war risk premiums for Saudi-linked tankers calling at Yanbu have risen to around 3% of a vessel's value, four industry sources told Reuters. They were less than 1% in early July, before London's marine insurance market designated that stretch of water as high-risk in response to Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis attacking shipping near the Bab el-Mandeb strait.
For ports south of Yanbu, including Jizan, around 50 miles (80 km) from the border with Yemen, quoted premiums - around 1% in early July - can rise as high as 7%, almost as much as transits through Hormuz, which range between 6% and 9%, the sources said, declining to be named due to data sensitivity.
"It's easier to do the Strait of Hormuz right now ... because at least in the Strait of Hormuz, the US is providing some cover. In the Red Sea, there's nothing," Pankaj Khanna, CEO of shipping group Heidmar Maritime Holdings Corp, told Reuters.
"If you have a Saudi connection, then you have a problem."
The Iran-aligned militants who seized swathes of the Yemeni coast and captured Perim Island in the middle of the Bab el-Mandeb strait this month have vowed to target only vessels linked to Saudi Arabia due to its backing of Yemen's government.
Tankers transiting the Red Sea without any Saudi connection typically pay between 0.2% and 0.3%, with additional discounts often available, the four industry sources said.
Khanna said any tanker docking at Yanbu will have a Saudi connection and hence be at risk of being hit. Heidmar is avoiding Saudi ports while remaining active in both Hormuz and the Red Sea, he said.
The Houthis have also targeted Saudi Arabia itself. The kingdom intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on Thursday, including towards the Yanbu area, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said.
Earlier this week, two trading sources said traders were getting ready for Saudi oil loadings in the Red Sea by moving tankers to Egypt's Mediterranean Port Said for ship-to-ship transfers.
That could allow them to sail south out of the Red Sea via Bab el-Mandeb instead of heading north through the Suez Canal and then - for Asia-bound cargoes - via southern Africa, a much longer and more costly route.
There is no public data for agreed rates in the marine insurance market, which could vary from those quoted by brokers and underwriters.
But the jump in quoted premiums shows that despite Saudi Arabia's investment of billions of dollars in infrastructure to provide an alternative export corridor, it now faces similar constraints as other Gulf oil producers relying on Hormuz.
"We have seen rates certainly north of 7% for all calls south of Yanbu," said David Smith, head of marine at insurance broker McGill and Partners.
Saudi Arabia's government media office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The US-Iran war has prompted some Gulf oil producers to rush to buy their own tankers to protect their oil exports, shipping sources say.
As a result, the average price of old tankers has soared to above $100 million, five sources said. Saudi Arabia this week denied allegations by Iraq that it had bought 25 oil tankers worth an estimated $4.5 billion, saying that the rise in oil transport costs was due to other factors linked to the war.
War risk premiums typically cover 7-day voyage periods and are reviewed every 24 hours, meaning a journey from Yanbu could cost $3 million, or some $7 million from other Saudi ports further south or via Hormuz, up from at least $100,000 before the war.
Oil producers also need to pay at least $500,000 a day for chartering a tanker, according to industry estimates, and bunker fuel costs during the voyage could add another $100,000 or more.
The US military has been providing some aerial support to ships sailing via Hormuz in recent months, sources have told Reuters. No such protection exists in the Red Sea, where the European Union provides security but says it needs more ships.
A US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the United States did not automatically provide protection when asked by private companies.
Saudi Arabia's crown prince sought US military help this month to counter the Houthis, sources told Reuters, and the Saudi cabinet has appointed the Saudi Reinsurance Company to lead the country's marine war risk insurance pool.
Corey Ranslem, CEO of maritime security group Dryad Global, said Bab el-Mandeb transits remained challenging, with tanker-only figures totaling "only a handful of vessels per day".
"What continues to move consists primarily of dry bulk cargo, certain products, and a limited number of tankers without Saudi affiliations."

articles.title: Le Pen says she won’t leave NATO until Russia’s war in Ukraine ends
articles.body:
PARIS — Far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen still wants to take France out of NATO’s integrated command — but won’t do so while Russia's war in Ukraine still rages on.
"As long as there is a war on Europe's doorstep, this is not the time to take action in that regard, but of course my will to do so remains," the National Rally leader told POLITICO on Thursday at the Playbook Paris Live summit.
Le Pen is the front-runner in next spring’s high-stakes presidential election to replace Emmanuel Macron, according to polls.
Advertisement
She and far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon both want Paris to leave the military alliance, raising alarm bells at NATO headquarters about France's future defense policy.
The National Rally has long advocated withdrawing from NATO's integrated command, but Le Pen's comments indicate a slight shift in her position. Back in May, she said France would pull out during her first term, without referring to the war in Ukraine, while the party's president Jordan Bardella wanted to wait for a peace agreement between Kyiv and Moscow.
Le Pen and Bardella are campaigning as a ticket that would see the 31-year-old become prime minister.
Le Pen also said that France should not enter into a war with Russia, a nuclear-armed power, and rejected the notion that it is currently in a conflict with Moscow despite the Kremlin's hybrid attacks against European nations.
By publishing a statement condemning Russia last week, Le Pen and Bardella sought to fend off attacks from center-right and center-left opponents who have frequently portrayed the party as an ally to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
However, Le Pen repeated her pledge Thursday to stop financial help to Ukraine if she wins next year's presidential election.
Advertisement
“We can train their soldiers and their military leadership, and provide them with military aid. We can no longer provide financial assistance to Ukraine, and we regret that,” she said.
However, she did not push back against the Coalition of the Willing, a group led by France and the U.K. that aims to provide a military presence in Ukraine once the war ends.
"A potential peacekeeping force that’s actually quite similar to UN peacekeepers seems entirely feasible to me. And if the Coalition of the Willing is one of the conditions for negotiating a ceasefire, then I would obviously be in favor of moving forward with this proposal," she told POLITICO.

President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly during a meeting with Prime Minister of the Netherlands Rob Jetten, has stated Ukraine's readiness not to strike Russian energy and export targets provided Moscow shows a reciprocal willingness.
"Met with Prime Minister of the Netherlands Rob Jetten at the UN. I briefed him on the latest negotiations with the American side and the proposals for de-escalation currently on the table," the President's Telegram channel states.
According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine desires peace like no other, and "we are ready to act symmetrically and not respond against the aggressor's energy and export sectors if there is a corresponding readiness in Moscow."
He noted that instead of readiness, there are currently Russian strikes with ballistic missiles and jet drones, which is why Ukraine is doing everything to protect its people.
"And the Netherlands' assistance – military, energy, financial – truly helps strengthen our positions. I thank the Netherlands and Rob personally for always standing with Ukraine," the President added.

articles.title: Why is Kosovo joining Gaza's International Stabilisation Force?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Why is Kosovo joining Gaza's International Stabilisation Force?
On 30 March, Kosovo’s government approved the deployment of Kosovo Security Forces personnel to Gaza as part of the proposed International Stabilisation Force (ISF) backed by the United States and envisioned under President Donald J. Trump’s peace plan.
Then on 7 September, Pristina formally signed an agreement to join the United Nations-mandated force, according to a statement posted on social media by the Board of Peace.
The decision places Kosovo at the centre of a wider international effort to establish security and support reconstruction in Gaza, while also raising questions about the mission’s role, its legal and political implications, and Kosovo’s ties with the United States and Israel.
Kosovo's strategic calculation
Kosovo’s decision to join the Board of Peace and the ISF underscores Pristina’s commitment to the United States. The small Muslim-majority Balkan state has long regarded Washington as its most important international partner.
This is particularly because of the US role in supporting Kosovo during and after the Kosovo War (1998–99) and in backing its independence, which the US under the George W. Bush administration formally recognised in February 2008 as one of the first countries in the world to do so.
But Dr Ramadan Ilazi, head of research at the Kosovar Centre for Security Studies (KCSS), said Kosovo’s decision should not be understood solely as an attempt to please Washington.
He described the motivation as a combination of principle, pragmatism, and strategic interest, arguing that Kosovo also wants to demonstrate that it can contribute to international security after more than two decades as a recipient of international assistance.
“There is now a strong desire to demonstrate that it can also be a contributor. Kosovo remains grateful for the international engagement that helped end the war in 1999, supported post-war reconstruction, and continues to provide security through KFOR. Participating in the ISF is therefore also a way of expressing solidarity and giving something back,” Dr Ilazi told The New Arab.
Lily Lynch, editor-in-chief of the Balkanist Magazine, holds that participating in Trump’s initiative sends a message that Kosovo’s relationship with the United States is intended to remain strong regardless of which political party controls the White House.
This is quite significant given concerns in Kosovo that a Trump administration could potentially be more accommodating toward Serbia.
“Kosovo decided to join the Board of Peace and [ISF] as a demonstration of its fidelity to the United States. The decision indicates that regardless of who is in the White House, Kosovo's commitment to its relationship with the United States is ironclad,” she told The New Arab.
“Some foreign policy commentators see Kosovo's existence as an independent state as a product of Clintonite foreign policy and liberal internationalism; there was concern among some in Kosovo that a Trump presidency would give Serbia an advantage,” added Lynch.
“But participation in the Board of Peace and ISF suggests that Kosovo wants to make clear that its commitment to a strong relationship with America transcends party politics.”
The Kosovo-Gaza comparison and its limits
Prime Minister Albin Kurti has framed the decision through Kosovo’s own experience with international peacekeeping. In announcing the government’s support for the deployment, Kurti pointed to the fact that Kosovo itself has benefited from international forces since 1999.
The analogy is also linked to the continued presence of NATO’s KFOR mission, which has provided security in Kosovo for more than two-and-a-half decades.
Lynch sees this as a deliberate attempt by Kurti to explain why Kosovo should now contribute to an international mission elsewhere, based on the argument that international forces helped provide security in Kosovo, and therefore Kosovo can now use its own experience and capabilities to assist another population.
Kosovo’s Security Forces have developed expertise in areas including search-and-rescue operations and demining, which policymakers in Pristina say could be relevant to the Gaza mission.
But the comparison between Kosovo and Gaza is also one of the most contested aspects of the decision because the circumstances surrounding NATO’s intervention in Kosovo and the proposed Gaza mission differ in fundamental ways.
In Kosovo, international intervention followed a war between Serbian forces and the Kosovo Albanian population and ultimately preceded Kosovo’s declaration of independence in 2008. Questions remain over whether Kosovo’s experience can straightforwardly serve as a model for the Gaza initiative. This distinction is important because Kurti’s comparison is not simply historical. It is also political.
Jelena Novakov, a Belgrade-based geopolitical analyst who writes for Kosovo Online, said the comparison is understandable given Kosovo’s own experience of conflict and international protection, but argued that it also contains a significant contradiction.
“For a young country that is still struggling with international recognition and, in a way, remains a recipient of international assistance through KFOR, this represents a significant demonstration of improved stability, even if largely symbolic,” she told The New Arab.
“What is debatable is the decision to participate in an initiative launched by the country that is largely responsible for the devastation in Gaza, after Kosovo itself experienced aggression,” Novakov added.
Dr Ilazi noted that Kosovo’s experience could provide a point of reference but cautioned against treating it as a model for Gaza.
“Kosovo and Gaza have different histories and political circumstances. Our experience cannot tell Palestinians what their future should look like. It can, however, remind us that people need both physical security and a say over how they are governed,” he said.
He also pointed to Kosovo’s own experience with international administration, arguing that this provided another lesson that could be relevant to the Gaza mission.
“We also know the frustrations of international administration, as we had our own share of that with [the United Nations Interim Administration Mission in Kosovo (UNMIK)], and these include decisions made far from the people affected, unclear accountability, and arrangements described as temporary that become very difficult to change. That experience is worth sharing too,” Dr Ilazi said.
Kurti appears to be carefully framing his message to reassure Kosovar Albanians who may be uneasy about Kosovo’s involvement in Trump’s Gaza initiative. With 4,600 KFOR troops stationed in Kosovo, at least as of earlier this year, the southeastern European country continues to depend on international peacekeeping troops.
“Kurti is trying to say, ‘international peacekeeping troops have helped keep us safe, so now we can use our own unique expertise to help others.’ Kurti is also undoubtedly trying to communicate Kosovo’s unique value to Trump’s putative peace effort. Of course, all of this would be far more meaningful if Trump’s plan for Gaza actually benefited the people of Gaza the way NATO helped Kosovar Albanians,” Lynch explained to The New Arab.
"I would say this is the main problem with Kurti's framing: He’s right that international forces helped the [Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA)] force Serbian troops out of Kosovo in 1999. This was a prerequisite for Kosovo’s eventual declaration of independence in 2008. That’s the difference here,” she noted.
“By Kurti’s own analogy, what’s happening with Trump's Gaza peace plan is much more akin to what would have happened in 1999 if NATO troops had helped Serbia retain control of Kosovo and had helped Serbian forces keep Albanians in submission.”
By invoking Kosovo’s experience with international protection, the country’s prime minister is presenting participation in the ISF as an extension of a principle that Kosovars know personally, which is the idea that international forces can provide security to a population emerging from conflict.
Whether that principle applies to Gaza, however, remains a matter of significant disagreement.
Between Palestinian sympathy and strategic necessity
The decision is also likely to be viewed through the lens of Kosovo’s domestic politics. With many citizens of Kosovo sympathetic to Palestinians, there is tension between public sentiment and Pristina’s strategic interests.
Kosovars who oppose Trump’s Gaza plan or support the Palestinian cause may nevertheless view participation as a necessary cost of maintaining the United States as Kosovo’s closest ally, which can be understood as a limitation faced by a small state.
Novakov said, however, that the issue has so far generated little sustained public debate in Kosovo. She attributed this partly to the country’s wider political and economic problems, including prolonged political instability, inflation, stalled negotiations with Belgrade and the EU, deteriorating relations with Washington, and the legal proceedings involving former KLA leaders.
“There is currently no large-scale public conversation about this issue in Kosovo,” Novakov told The New Arab. “There is support for Palestine among Kosovars, but the government’s alignment with the US is rarely raised as one of the main issues during demonstrations.”
Dr Ilazi cautioned against assuming that political support for the deployment necessarily translates into broad public support for every aspect of the mission. Although he stated that the parliament’s 89-0 vote on 17 April to approve the government’s earlier decision to deploy Kosovo’s forces to the ISF “shows broad political support for participation,” Dr Ilazi stressed that it does “not tell us how the public will respond to every task the mission might undertake, and I would avoid claiming a public majority without reliable polling.”
As he explained, much will depend on what people see unfolding in Gaza.
“Clearing unexploded ordnance, helping aid reach families and making neighbourhoods safer are contributions the government can explain clearly. Public confidence would be harder to sustain if Kosovo’s soldiers became associated with restricting Palestinian movement or protecting arrangements that leave people displaced,” Dr Ilazi told The New Arab.
Kosovo has relatively little ability to influence major international conflicts and may therefore prioritise maintaining relationships with powerful allies, chiefly Washington. The result is a complicated political position in which criticism of the Gaza policy can coexist with acceptance of Kosovo’s participation, according to Lynch.
“The majority of Albanians are sympathetic to Palestinians, though there are some very vocal Zionist Albanians as well. But even those who support Palestine and deplore Trump’s Gaza plan are likely to accept the Kosovo government's decision to participate as a necessary cost of keeping America as their closest ally. The prevailing thought in Kosovo is ‘we’re a small country, there’s not much we can do to shape major world events and distant conflicts, so we will accept this arrangement because this is what our closest ally wants,’” she told The New Arab.
For Novakov, the calculation is ultimately rooted in Kosovo’s continuing reliance on international support. Around 100 countries have yet to recognise Kosovo’s independence, including five European Union members (Cyprus, Greece, Romania, Slovakia, and Spain), while Russia and China remain opposed to its statehood.
With Brussels’ focus increasingly shifting towards Ukraine, she argues, maintaining a close relationship with Washington remains particularly important for Pristina.
Questions over responsibility and accountability
Beyond public opinion, the deployment raises questions about legal and reputational responsibility. There are valid concerns to raise about the possibility that Kosovo’s involvement could expose its personnel or government to scrutiny if the wider operation were associated with forced displacement, the consolidation of Israeli control over Gaza, or other conduct that violates international law.
Lynch argues that these concerns deserve particular attention because of Kosovo’s own experience with international justice and accountability. The recent conviction and 25-year sentence of former Kosovo political and military leader Hashim Thaçi on war crimes charges has already placed questions of wartime responsibility at the centre of public debate.
Against that background, participation in a controversial international operation could create additional scrutiny if Kosovar personnel became associated with actions later determined to be unlawful.
Dr Ilazi distinguished between the legal and reputational risks Kosovo could face.
“I would also separate legal responsibility from reputational damage. Establishing legal responsibility requires evidence about particular actions and circumstances. Public trust can be lost much earlier if a mission is seen as facilitating abuse or denying Palestinians control over their future,” he told The New Arab.
He also argued that Kosovo should establish clear limits on what its personnel can be asked to do.
“Those restrictions need to shape operational planning, with legal review, reporting to the Assembly and a credible option to suspend or withdraw the contingent. We should not leave individual soldiers to resolve political ambiguities that their government failed to address,” commented Dr Ilazi, who also argued that the perspectives of Palestinians themselves should receive greater attention in discussions about the force.
“One issue that deserves more attention is how Palestinians themselves view the force. Most discussions focus on Washington’s intentions and the calculations of contributing countries. Yet the people expected to live alongside this mission need meaningful influence over the arrangements it supports. From Kosovo’s experience, we should understand how much that matters,” he argued.
A new test for Kosovo's foreign policy
Ultimately, Kosovo’s decision to participate in the Gaza stabilisation effort highlights the difficult choices facing a small state whose security and international standing have been closely connected to the United States for many years.
For Kurti’s government, participation offers an opportunity to demonstrate continued commitment to Washington and to portray Kosovo as a country capable of contributing to international security rather than simply receiving international assistance.
At the same time, the decision places Kosovo between competing pressures, including domestic sympathy for Palestinians, its strategic partnership with the United States, questions about the nature of the Gaza mission, and concerns about legal and reputational consequences.
As the deployment moves forward, the central question will be whether Kosovo can maintain its strong relationship with Washington while avoiding becoming entangled in the contentious political and legal disputes surrounding Gaza.
Giorgio Cafiero is the CEO of Gulf State Analytics.
Follow him on Twitter: @GiorgioCafiero

The foreign ministers of Poland and Belarus have met for the first time in a decade, as both sides indicated that they are open to thawing their long-frosty relations.
The two countries have regularly clashed in recent years, in particular over Minsk’s alliance with Moscow, the migration crisis Belarus has engineered on the Polish border, and the persecution of Belarus’s ethnic Polish minority. Warsaw, meanwhile, has supported the Belarusian democratic opposition.
However, on Tuesday this week, Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski confirmed to reporters that he had met with his Belarusian counterpart, Maxim Ryzhenkov, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Sikorski said that the initiative had come from the Belarusian side.
Przełom w relacjach z Białorusią? Sikorski potwierdza "spotkanie zapoznawcze" https://t.co/uDUPM9CiHo #swiat #radoslawsikorski #bialorus #aleksanderlukaszenko #msz #andrzejpoczobut
— Onet Wiadomości (@OnetWiadomosci) September 23, 2026
“When a neighbour wants to unfreeze and improve relations, Poland is the first to reach an agreement,” said Sikorski, quoted by broadcaster RMF.
“This is a first, introductory meeting, but meetings with other ministries and at other levels are also taking place,” he added, noting that Poland will also “soon be opening a new embassy building in Minsk”.
When asked what topics had been discussed, Sikorski said that they had included the border situation and regional security. Asked if he had requested that Belarus not allow Russia to fly drones and missiles through its territory, he said that this was discussed “among other things”.
The last known time that the Polish and Belarusian foreign ministers met was in October 2016, when Belarus’s Vladimir Makei visited Witold Waszczykowski in Warsaw.
Sikorski said that this week’s meeting with Ryzhenkov had been possible because the situation on their shared border – where Belarus has since 2021 encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants, mainly from Asia and Africa, to cross into Poland – is now “more normalised”.
Poland has installed physical and electronic barriers along the border, sent thousands of armed officers to guard it, and has banned asylum claims by migrants who cross irregularly. Following those measures, the number of attempted crossings has fallen dramatically this year.
Sikorski also noted that relations have been improved by Belarus’s recent decisions to release political prisoners, including Polish ones. Most prominent among them is Andrzej Poczobut, a leader of the Polish community in Belarus, who had been imprisoned on trumped-up charges for five years.
The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98%
Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026
Minsk’s recent actions have provided “more freedom and greater reasons to try to stabilise relations”, said Sikorski. “A snowdrop can bloom if the weather is favorable.”
Belarus’s foreign ministry continued that metaphor in a post on social media on Wednesday, sharing a photo of Sikorski meeting with Ryzhenkov and writing that “snowdrop diplomacy is a nice restart”.
“But we’re in it for the harvest,” added the ministry. “Let’s plant an orchard – it needs nurturing every year, not once a decade. Minsk is ready to host.”
Last year, Belarus called for “dialogue” with Poland in order to “reduce the risk of armed clashes” amid a military build-up around the border. However, it also issued a formal protest to Poland over a demonstration in Warsaw organised by exiled opponents of Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko.
.@sikorskiradek, snowdrop diplomacy is a nice restart. But we’re in it for the harvest. Let’s plant an orchard 🍎 – it needs nurturing every year, not once a decade. Minsk is ready to host 🇧🇾🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/WSN5n4uOtE

News of Tuesday’s meeting was criticised by Stanisław Żaryn, who served as spokesman for the Polish security services under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government and later as an advisor to President Andrzej Duda.
In a social media post, he said that Sikorski and media outlets are “forcibly pushing us into another reset with Belarus (and perhaps even with Russia)”. However, “Belarus chose its strategic path long ago and won’t turn away from Russia”, he added.
He asked if Poles are meant to forget about the death of Mateusz Sitek, a Polish soldier killed by a migrant from a group trying to force its way over the border from Belarus. His suspected killer, a Moroccan national, is believed by Polish prosecutors to still be in Belarus, which has refused to extradite him.
Should “we just move on as if nothing happened regarding Belarus’s involvement in the war against Ukraine and the intelligence war against Poland?” continued Żaryn.

— Stanisław Żaryn (@StZaryn) September 23, 2026
Francišak Viačorka, a leading figure in the exiled Belarusian democratic opposition, also expressed scepticism in an interview with Polish newspaper Fakt.
“We believe that the authorities in Minsk cannot be trusted,” he said. “Of course, when the authorities communicate with Western partners, they promise that everything will be fine, that they want dialogue, but then their words fail to match their actions.”
“I understand that Minister Sikorski is doing everything to protect Polish interests and the sovereignty and security of his country, but I think that in Minsk they see it differently.”
