articles.title: Poland scrambles military aviation for 2nd time due to fresh Russian strikes on Ukraine – Armed Forces
articles.body:
The Polish military has deployed aviation in its airspace for the second time due to Russia's fresh strikes on the territory of Ukraine, the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces has reported.
During the first deployment of aviation, the Polish military reported that in connection with the strikes of the Russian Federation on the territory of Ukraine, military aviation was operating in Polish airspace. Ground-based air defense and radar reconnaissance systems were put on alert.
"These measures are of a preventive nature and are aimed at ensuring the safety of the airspace and protecting it, especially in areas adjacent to threatened zones," the command's message on the social network X says.
Subsequently, the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces reported the completion of military aviation operations conducted to ensure security during Russian strikes on targets in Ukraine.
"We report that no violations of the airspace of the Republic of Poland were recorded," the command noted.
Approximately an hour after this report, the Polish military announced the repeated deployment of aviation due to fresh Russia strikes on Ukraine.
"Attention. In connection with the fresh strikes of Russia on the territory of Ukraine, carried out using air attack weapons, military aviation is operating in Polish airspace again," the report says.
The Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces noted that in accordance with applicable procedures through the Air Operations Center – Air Component Command – the necessary forces and assets were deployed. Ground-based air defense and radar reconnaissance systems went on alert again.

articles.title: Arab Centre in Washington examines shifting US Palestine policy
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Arab Centre in Washington examines shifts in US policy toward Palestine and its future
US support for Israel is fuelling wars in the Middle East and obstructing prospects for peace, political scientist Ian Lustick warned at the Arab Centre Washington DC's third annual conference on Palestine, arguing that the region’s crises are increasingly rooted in US domestic politics.
Lustick, a professor of political science at the University of Pennsylvania, said at the conference on Wednesday that the influence of pro-Israel lobbying groups over Washington had helped ensure continued US backing for Israel even as its policies became increasingly extreme.
"Support for Israel hinders peace, fuels wars and drags America into them, diverting our attention from the threats posed by China and Russia elsewhere," Lustick said.
"Quite simply, the biggest problem in the Middle East today, or one of the biggest, is an internal American political problem."
Speaking during a session moderated by Yousef Munir, head of the Palestine and Israel Program at the Arab Centre, Lustick argued that lobbying groups supporting Israel wield significant influence over US politicians and foreign policy.
The conference, titled Shifting Tides: Palestine, US Elections, and Pathways Forward, was organised by the Arab Center Washington DC as its Third Annual Palestine Conference and held at the National Press Club in Washington, DC, on Wednesday.
It brought together academics, analysts and advocates to examine developments in Palestine, shifts in US policy towards Palestine and Israel, and whether changing American public opinion could ultimately translate into changes in Washington's policy.
Lustick is the co-author with Eli Clifton of The Israel Lobby, America in the Grip of a Foreign Power. Speaking separately to The New Arab, he described the situation facing Palestinians as one of "frustration and horror", while criticising the disregard of political leaders for events on the ground.
"What is infuriating is the disregard of those in power for what is happening, despite the situation on the ground and what we hear about Israeli objectives aimed at emptying the land of as many Palestinians as possible through killing, repression and impoverishment," he said.
Lustick argued that fundamental change for Palestinians living under Israeli control would be impossible without challenging the influence of the Israel lobby over US policy.
"We treat Israel as if it were a crazy state, and the Israel lobby's remarkable success in ensuring there is no divergence between the positions of the United States and Israel, regardless of how extreme Israeli policies become, has strongly contributed to turning Tel Aviv into a rogue regime and an internationally isolated state," he said.
He argued that unconditional US backing had also shaped Israeli domestic politics by convincing voters that Washington would continue to protect Israel from accountability regardless of the policies pursued by its leaders.
Lustick also rejected the viability of the two-state solution, describing it as a "safe political option" for Democrats and Republicans that allowed politicians to avoid confronting the question of Palestinian democratic rights.
"We should not abandon the struggle to end the occupation. The occupation must end, but it will not end through regional agreements or military withdrawals. It will end through democratic transformation," he said.
He instead advocated a one-state framework centred on equality and democratic rights.
Can shifting US opinion change policy?
Lustick's intervention came as speakers at the conference examined whether growing support for Palestinian rights in the United States could translate into changes in Washington's longstanding policies towards Israel.
Opening the conference, Arab Centre Washington DC executive director Tamara Kharroub pointed to recent opinion polling showing declining support for Israel and growing opposition to US military aid.
She said at least 55% of Americans now believe military assistance to Israel should either be reduced or stopped, while Israel's net approval rating had fallen sharply over the past eight years.
"The support for Palestine that was once considered an electoral liability has now become part of a successful coalition," Kharroub said.
She argued that the significance of the 2026 US midterm elections would extend beyond how many pro-Palestinian candidates enter Congress.
"The importance of the 2026 elections should not be measured only by the number of candidates who reach Congress but also by the emergence of political constituencies and voters for whom the Palestinian issue is a decisive factor in choosing their candidate," she said.
Kharroub said Palestine had increasingly become connected in the US political debate to civil liberties, freedom of expression, lobbying, the use of taxpayers' money and international law.
"The balance has changed today, and the question now is, can this shift in public opinion and political activism become a fundamental change in US foreign policy?" she said.
Gaza suffering becoming 'permanent reality'
Other sessions focused on conditions facing Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
Jihad Abu Salem, executive director of the Gaza Genocide Centre, said Palestinian suffering was being transformed from an emergency into a "permanent and painful reality" nearly a year after the ceasefire.
"The killing has not stopped. More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire began," he said.
He said nearly 11,000 buildings had been destroyed during the same period, bringing the proportion of damaged buildings in Gaza to more than 82 percent, while much of the population continued to live in tents, damaged buildings or temporary shelters.
Yara Asi, an assistant professor at the University of Central Florida's College of Global Health and Management, meanwhile highlighted escalating settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
She said more than 1,600 settler attacks against Palestinians had been recorded between January and mid-September this year, citing figures from the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.
Omar Rahman, a researcher at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, criticised the political framework created by the Oslo agreements, arguing that it had left the Palestinian leadership dependent on Western funding while weakening links between the Palestine Liberation Organisation and Palestinian communities abroad.
Calls to turn public opinion into political pressure
The conference concluded with discussions about how changing attitudes towards Israel could be converted into concrete US policy.
Participants called for Palestinian rights to remain a political priority and for campaigners to connect the issue with human rights, freedom of expression, domestic spending and the economic costs of US involvement in foreign wars.
They also called for continued efforts in Congress to halt weapons shipments to Israel, even where legislation has little immediate prospect of passing, as a way of building a congressional bloc capable of influencing future administrations.
Daniel Levy, president of the US/Middle East Project, argued that greater pressure could also be applied over Israeli settlements, including by examining the banks and financial institutions involved in financing them.
Participants also called for normalising proposals for sanctions on Israel and an end to US arms sales, while looking towards the 2028 presidential election as another opportunity to turn changing public opinion into political pressure.
The central question running through the conference was whether the increasingly visible shift in American attitudes towards Israel and Palestine can ultimately break through in Washington and produce a corresponding change in US policy.

articles.title: Inside the bunker: How a Zelensky aide struggled to explain away corruption
articles.body:
Inside the bunker: How a Zelensky aide struggled to explain away corruption
A senior official in Vladimir Zelensky’s office frantically tried to reconcile her official annual salary of $12,500 with what surveillance records suggest was $30,000 per month in cash payments received from her new boss, a former head of Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR), according to a new investigation.
In records published by veteran investigative journalist Vladimir Boyko, Irina Mudraya, a former deputy justice minister serving as deputy head of Zelensky’s office, allegedly confided in her property magnate accomplice: “Who will ever believe me that I live on 50,000 hryvnia [$1,100] a month? Who?”
Mudraya was fired in August after being accused of laundering millions through Ukraine’s banking system to bail out one of Zelensky’s energy ministers, who himself had been arrested in a separate case involving the Ukrainian leader’s long-time associate Timur Mindich.
Boyko has been publishing pages of what he says are transcripts of surveillance recordings produced by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) between January and June as detectives followed Mudraya and her partner, former MP Maksim Mikitas.
Who is tasked with countering corruption in Kiev?
NABU and its sister agency, the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO), established after the armed coup of 2014, have repeatedly clashed with Zelensky’s cabal. Last year, the Ukrainian leader attempted to place them under his control, but reversed course after Western donors threatened to suspend all aid.
Most recently the agencies exposed a massive scam-call center protection racket that was run through the office of Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, who then fled abroad under the false pretense of attending a conference in Paris.
Earlier this month, HUR agents engaged in a gunfight in Kiev with agents from the rival Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), which some news outlets linked to the fight for protection money from the scam-call criminal businesses.
Aside from NABU and SAPO, the National Agency on Corruption Prevention (NAPK) obliges hundreds of thousands of civil servants to submit annual finance and property declarations.
What did Mudraya have to worry about, according to the transcripts?
According to the transcripts, Mudraya received some $30,000 a month in cash payments from a man she called “Kirill Alekseyevich.”
Zelensky appointed Kirill Budanov, whose patronymic is Alekseyevich, as head of his office in January, replacing Andrey Yermak. Yermak resigned last year as initial news broke of Zelensky insiders syphoning some $100 million through energy contracts.
Mudraya appeared to seek advice from her partner Mitkas on hiding her ill-gotten riches from NAPK.
“You can declare the Bvlgaris and at least the Van Cleef. But no way can you declare the earrings,” the man said. “I’ll put you in touch with a man who will handle the income issue.”
Buying a Van Cleef piece during the war with Russia was “f**ked up,” Mudraya admitted.
The exchanges, which Boyko has staked his reputation on, suggest senior officials were flying under NAPK’s radar.
Mudraya and Mikitas discussed securing a highly paid sinecure that could cover for her enormous under-the-table income. She mentioned her envy of Zelensky’s adviser on sanctions policy, Vladislav Vlasyuk, who she said officially earned $335,000 a year as a member of the oversight committee of state-owned Sense Bank.
Sense Bank is the former Ukrainian branch of Alfa Bank, nationalized in 2023 under Kiev’s anti-Russian sanctions and through which Mudraya allegedly laundered cash by having the bank’s anti-fraud team suspend their digital monitoring platform.
While Mudraya said netting a job like Vlasyuk’s would not be legally possible, Mikitas suggested that a teaching position at a private institution could serve the same purpose. He offered to speak to a friend who headed a construction university, but Mudraya said she would look ridiculous teaching anything other than law.
Does the corruption link reach upwards?
According to the recording, Mudraya’s new boss personally delivered her first “salary,” unlike his predecessor who had a “specially trained girl” to carry cash. The payout turned out to be larger than expected:
“It was 30 [thousand dollars]. I went to him and said: ‘Kirill, it’s too much.’ Brought the hat with me. He says: ‘You said 30.’ I say: ‘No, I said I used to get 30. But we agreed to 20, not 30.’ He said: ‘Well, I won’t take it back.’”
Subsequent transcripts suggest the higher monthly payments continued and that Mudraya received an additional $20,000 bonus in May.
“He values you a lot,” Mikitas concluded. “Mark my word, in two months you’ll become first deputy prime minister,” he added, saying he expected “Kirill” to become the new cabinet chair.
What could the leaks mean for Budanov?
Some Ukrainian media have argued that NABU is targeting Zelensky’s inner circle to leverage reforms demanded by the EU.
Bloomberg reported that European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen had a “tense meeting” with Zelensky this week, conditioning further financial support on implementing the changes Kiev had promised to Brussels.
Reform would give more power to NABU and SAPO and introduce oversight by EU-aligned experts for appointments of senior officials, curbing Zelensky’s extensive influence and the corrupt network he runs through his inner circle.
NABU and SAPO accused Yermak of involvement in a major money-laundering scheme in May and leaks to pro-EU media implicated Zelensky himself.
No formal charges can be filed against Zelensky as long as he holds presidential powers, which he has attempted to retain under martial law since his term expired in 2024.
Replacing Zelensky’s personal friend Yermak with Budanov, who has extensive contacts among Western special services, seems to be consistent with the EU’s goals.

articles.title: Trump gives Xi rare airport welcome as Chinese leader begins US state visit
articles.body:
Trump gives Xi rare airport welcome as Chinese leader begins US state visit
US President Donald Trump personally welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping at a military airfield outside Washington on Wednesday, kicking off a lavish state visit focused on trade, artificial intelligence and Iran, as the two powers seek to preserve a fragile diplomatic and economic truce.

US President Donald Trump treated Chinese President Xi Jinping to a rare personal airport welcome Wednesday, kicking off a pomp-filled state visit aimed at smoothing superpower tensions on everything from AI and trade to Iran.
The summit is expected to be more about spectacle than substance – but there was an early breakthrough when Washington announced a two-month extension of a trade truce with Beijing that was due to expire in November.
After officials literally rolled out the red carpet, Trump and First Lady Melania shook hands with Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan once the Chinese president descended from his plane at Joint Base Andrews, a US military airfield outside Washington.
Trump, wearing a long coat and gloves, and Xi then stood side by side on the tarmac as a military band played national anthems.
A noisy flyover by two B-1 bombers clearly jolted the 80-year-old Trump, who grimaced at the roar of jets, while his Chinese guest stood by impassively.
Trump brushed off the fact that Xi had not given him a similar airport welcome when he visited Beijing in May.
"I thought it was a great little meeting, a great greeting, and I think they appreciate it," Trump told reporters at the White House after welcoming Xi.
Iran, AI, trade
The lavish visit – the third between Xi and Trump since the US leader returned to power – will include a formal welcome and another flyover, talks in the Oval Office and a state banquet at the White House on Thursday.
It will wrap up on Friday morning when the two presidential couples have tea at the White House and then visit the National Archives, home to the US Declaration of Independence.
Expectations of any breakthroughs are low. Analysts say the main aim of the pageantry is to maintain a fragile calm between the superpower rivals.
The Iran war will be on the agenda, Trump confirmed Wednesday, despite having earlier played down reports that Beijing was supplying Tehran with intelligence as the conflict drags on.
"I'll be talking about that and many other subjects – but it's all coming along well, including that," Trump said when an AFP reporter asked if he would bring up Iran.
On the simmering trade war sparked by Trump's sweeping tariffs last year, US Treasury Scott Bessent announced Wednesday after intensive pre-summit talks that there had been an extension of a truce.
The "economic detente" will now extend beyond its November 10 deadline to January 10, Bessent said.
But hopes of business deals have been dimmed by the fact that there are no Chinese CEOs in Xi's delegation, two sources told AFP.
In contrast, top US tech bosses including the leaders of major AI companies are set to attend Thursday's banquet.
'Oppressive dictator'
AI is set to dominate the summit amid growing fears – boosted by warnings from AI CEOs – that the technology risks wiping out humanity.
China and the United States are racing for supremacy in the field, viewing it as crucial for the rest of the century.
Preliminary talks on Sunday between Bessent and his Chinese counterpart He Lifeng included discussion of creating a communication channel for AI concerns.
But overall the idea is to extend the "gentleman's agreement" to reduce tensions between Beijing and Washington despite their rivalry, Jonathan Czin of the Brookings Institution told AFP.
Trump's five-star welcome for Xi has drawn criticism from China hawks within his own party, especially amid reports that Beijing supplied Iran with intelligence for attacks on US troops.
"Our commander-in-chief should keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator," said Republican Senator Roger Wicker, chairman of the powerful Senate Armed Services Committee.
But for Trump, Xi's visit is also a chance to focus on pageantry instead of problems at home, where the Iran war's effect on fuel prices has sent his approval rating plummeting to historic lows ahead of midterm elections in November.
The last American president to welcome a foreign leader at Andrews – except for papal visits – was John F. Kennedy in 1962, although Trump welcomed Russian President Vladimir Putin off his plane in Alaska last year.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Yemeni Houthis Set Up Missile and Drone Production Using Chinese Components – Bloomberg
articles.body:
Yemeni Houthis have established missile and drone production using equipment and components of Chinese origin that are entering Yemen as commercial goods and dual-use items.
This is reported by Bloomberg, which analyzed intercepted cargo, customs documents, and UN reports, and spoke with Yemeni officials and experts.
The publication describes these shipments as part of a network supporting the Houthis’ military-industrial capabilities.
During a detailed inspection in July 2026, phenolic resin—a heat-resistant material that can be used in missile production—was found in one of the containers, along with tail fins and other parts resembling ballistic missile components.
Subsequently, three more containers linked to the same supply network were inspected at the port of Aden. They were found to contain what appeared to be missile body components, guidance systems, launch equipment, CNC machine tools, and twin-cylinder engines suitable for use in unmanned aerial vehicles.
The head of the port department of the counterterrorism unit stated that the components had been deliberately distributed among four containers, making them difficult to detect. In his assessment, the seized parts collectively constituted the components of a nearly complete missile assembly.
The cargo also included earthmoving and ventilation equipment, which, according to Yemeni security officials, could be used in the construction of underground infrastructure.
At the same time, a significant portion of the discovered products is dual-use and can be legally used in the civilian industry. Bloomberg notes that there is no evidence that the Chinese manufacturers were aware of the products’ end user.
Experts interviewed by the publication note that the availability of Chinese engines, electronics, flight controllers, GPS modules, servo drives, and composite materials makes it possible to procure a significant portion of the components needed for the production of attack drones through regular commercial channels.
Previously, the Houthis relied heavily on shipments of finished weapons from Iran. In July 2025, Yemeni forces intercepted a large shipment of weapons bound for the group, which included missiles and other systems of Iranian origin.
However, the supply model subsequently began to change: instead of exclusively receiving ready-made weapons, the Houthis began to receive components, equipment, and materials that allow them to assemble missiles and drones directly in Yemen. It is precisely this trend that is confirmed by the shipments of Chinese components and industrial equipment described by Bloomberg.
The results of their development of in-house drone systems are already becoming apparent on the battlefield. In August 2026, Militarnyi reported that the Houthis had struck a Saudi M1A2S Abrams tank with munitions dropped from a UAV.
At the same time, the group is expanding its control over strategic areas of the country. In September, the Houthis captured the port of Mocha near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, so the growth of their ability to independently produce missiles and drones is becoming increasingly important for the safety of shipping in the Red Sea.

articles.title: Russian oil helping India weather Iran energy shock – Russian deputy FM
articles.body:
Russian oil helping India weather Iran energy shock – Russian deputy FM
Russian crude supplies helped cushion India from an oil-supply shock after the conflict in the Middle East disrupted energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, showing Moscow’s reliability as an energy partner, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko has said. 
Rudenko’s statement comes amid renewed scrutiny on India’s Russian oil purchases, and after Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky called for choking off Russia’s oil trade under a new US sanctions law. 
Indian refiners turned heavily to Russian crude after the US-Israeli attacks on Iran disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which used to handle roughly one-fifth of global oil supplies. 
The scale of the shift was most visible in March, when India’s Russian crude imports nearly doubled from the previous month to 2.25 million barrels per day (bpd) and accounted for half of its oil purchases. 
Gulf shipments to India simultaneously plunged 61% to 1.18 million bpd. Existing arrangements between Moscow and New Delhi helped “significantly mitigate” the consequences of disruptions to global energy trade, Rudenko told Russian news outlet NEWS.ru on Wednesday.
It showed Moscow could meet demand from its partners even in difficult geopolitical conditions, he added.
Good to meet @SecRubio of the US #UNHighLevelWeek
Reiterated India’s interests and concerns with regard to SRIA. Also discussed the Gulf and Ukraine situations.
🇮🇳 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/163YRVlMZG
Meanwhile, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar, who is in New York to attend the United Nations General Assembly meeting, raised New Delhi’s concerns about the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday. 
The law gives US President Donald Trump the authority to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top buyers of Russian oil and gas. India’s Russian oil purchases have eased from record summer levels as other supplies recovered, but Moscow remains India’s largest crude supplier.
Russian shipments stood at about 2.1 million bpd in August, and are tracking at around 1.9 million bpd in September, according to preliminary data from commodity analytics firm Kpler. India has maintained that securing affordable and dependable energy for its 1.4 billion people requires multiple suppliers, and warned against restrictions that could distort or constrict global energy markets.
Russia’s energy cooperation with India extends beyond oil. Rudenko pointed to the Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant in southern India built in collaboration with Russia and said another site will soon be allocated for a Russian-designed nuclear facility.

articles.title: Russia Tests Molniya Strike Drones as “Flying Couriers” for Carrying Weapons and Food to Frontline

Russia Tests Molniya Strike Drones as “Flying Couriers” for Carrying Weapons and Food to Frontline
Russian forces have begun experimenting with Molniya drones as a means of transporting weapons and supplies to frontline positions, according to footage released by the Sunstrike unmanned systems unit of Ukraine’s 82nd Separate Air Assault Brigade.
The footage published by the Ukrainian unit shows several configurations of the Russian drone carrying different types of cargo. In one instance, a rifle is attached to the aircraft, while another drone is shown carrying a package of supplies.

According to Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi, the modifications suggest Russian forces are testing ways to expand the Molniya’s role beyond its primary use as a strike drone, potentially turning the platform into a lightweight logistics system capable of delivering supplies to troops on the battlefield.
Such a configuration could allow Russian troops to transport small loads to frontline positions without relying on personnel or conventional vehicles for the final stage of delivery.
However, there is currently no evidence that the use of Molniya drones for logistics has become a standard practice or is being employed on a large scale by Russian forces, Militarnyi noted.
The Molniya is a relatively basic Russian fixed-wing attack drone primarily used to deliver explosive payloads. It has a range of around 30 to 40 kilometers and can carry a warhead weighing up to seven kilograms. Modified versions of the drone have also been employed for reconnaissance and artillery fire correction.
The apparent experimentation with the Molniya comes as Russia continues to develop drones for operations against Ukrainian logistics. Trident Group CEO Yurii Humenchuk told RBC-Ukraine in an interview published on July 13 that Russia was working on a new category of medium-range strike drones intended to target Ukrainian supply routes.
According to Humenchuk, Russia is seeking a platform that would bridge the gap between relatively inexpensive Molniya drones and the larger, heavier Shahed-type attack UAVs.

Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev is set to meet US officials in New York on Thursday, Sept. 24, as Washington makes a new attempt to revive negotiations over Russia’s war against Ukraine.

The visit was approved by Russian President Vladimir Putin and will take place on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, according to Reuters.
US pushes three-step de-escalation plan
Washington is currently promoting three immediate measures: a reciprocal ceasefire covering energy infrastructure, the reopening of the Black Sea grain corridor, and a trilateral US-Ukraine-Russia meeting, potentially in Abu Dhabi, Axios reported.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine was prepared to accept a mutual halt on energy strikes.
“On the table now there is a proposition: energy ceasefire. We are ready,” Zelensky told Axios.
He stressed, however, that Kyiv would stop attacking Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities only if Moscow halted strikes against Ukraine’s power grid, heating systems, and other critical infrastructure.
Previously, Zelensky also expressed readiness for direct trilateral talks involving himself, Trump, and Putin.

The US has floated Abu Dhabi as a possible location for an initial meeting between technical delegations. Zelensky has also suggested that the G20 summit in Miami in December could provide an opportunity for talks at the leaders’ level.
On Wednesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that both Kyiv and Moscow had shown interest in a limited arrangement covering grain shipments and energy infrastructure. He also expressed hope that Putin would accept Trump’s invitation to attend the G20 summit.
Moscow sends mixed signals
Despite the renewed diplomatic activity, the Kremlin has publicly downplayed the prospect of an imminent breakthrough.
On Wednesday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the conditions for resuming negotiations with Ukraine were not yet in place and that there was currently no prospect of a high-level meeting.
Dmitriev’s visit nevertheless provides Moscow with another direct channel to the Trump administration.
The Russian official, who heads the Russian Direct Investment Fund, participated in Putin’s Sept. 5 meeting with Witkoff and Kushner in Moscow. He also held a separate three-hour discussion with the US envoys before their meeting with Putin.
The Kremlin described those talks as useful, but announced no concrete progress. The US delegation later traveled to Kyiv for discussions with Zelensky.
Dmitriev has emerged as one of Moscow’s principal intermediaries with Washington, participating in negotiations concerning energy sanctions, prisoner exchanges, and possible postwar economic cooperation.
His New York meetings come after Trump and Zelensky held talks during the UN General Assembly.
Zelensky said the US envoys appeared optimistic about Putin’s readiness to negotiate but cautioned that he remained skeptical of the Russian leader’s intentions.
“They said, ‘We think that Putin is ready.’ I said, ‘Look, I’m not sure,’” Zelensky recalled.

articles.title: Putin’s Sochi residence was demolished and rebuilt from scratch. A contractor linked to his friend Arkady Rotenberg is behind the project, BBC’s Russian Service reports.
articles.body:
Putin’s Sochi residence was demolished and rebuilt from scratch. A contractor linked to his friend Arkady Rotenberg is behind the project, BBC’s Russian Service reports.
Construction of a new Bocharov Ruchey residence for Vladimir Putin is nearing completion in Sochi: the old buildings there were demolished in 2024, and by the fall of 2026 new ones had already gone up in their place. The general contractor for the construction is the Crimea-based Transstroyinvest Group of Companies, which is tied to Putin’s friend Arkady Rotenberg, BBC Russia reports.
A classified state defense contract for the FSO covers the reconstruction of the Bocharov Ruchey residence, but journalists found the contract’s 25-digit identifier in court records. The digits show the contract covers 2023–2027, that it was awarded without competitive bidding or an auction, and that its price was fixed.
The general contractor is the Transstroyinvest Group of Companies, whose beneficiary is believed to be developer Alexei Fomenko. Russian media have linked Fomenko to Arkady Rotenberg. The company also built dachas in occupied Crimea for Vladimir Putin and Alexander Bortnikov, director of Russia’s Federal Security Service, and carried out the reconstruction of the Artek children’s camp.
BBC could not determine the total cost of the contract to reconstruct Bocharov Ruchey, but the scale can be gauged from publicly available job postings for individual construction subcontracts. Those postings listed work budgets of 90, 150, 250, 400, and 500 million rubles.
Workers for the construction site were recruited through social media and job-listing websites. The postings described the site as a “strategic facility” and warned candidates that they would face strict background checks. Builders were promised piece-rate pay in cash, three meals a day, and accommodation in a “hostel with a pool.”
BBC says construction at Bocharov Ruchey has continued even though Putin has visited Sochi far less often since Russia’s full-scale war in Ukraine began. According to calculations by the Financial Times, he visited there 24 times before the full-scale war, 13 times in 2022, and only twice a year in both 2024 and 2025, as Ukrainian drones increasingly reached the Black Sea coast.

articles.title: America, China and the Evolving New World Order
articles.body:
On Thursday, President Xi Jinping of China is meeting President Donald Trump at the White House. The United States and China are in significantly different places and the world increasingly fragmented and multi-polar since he last visited the White House to meet President Barack Obama in 2015. As the American and Chinese leaders meet, the most consequential question is: who is shaping the international order, and according to whose principles and rules?
The answer may be more nuanced than many expected: while the U.S. remains the world’s most powerful country, China is emerging as an architect of that order.
Beijing is creating institutions, proposing diplomatic initiatives, establishing technological standards and offering infrastructure to countries across the world. But its influence extends beyond diplomacy. China offers developing countries alternative paths to prosperity, mobilizing its technological champions as sources of power. Rather than replicating the American system of military alliance and security guarantees, Beijing is building networks of trade and alternative financial institutions. China is also promoting a new vocabulary of international affairs—one that is deliberately distinct from the American language of power.
China does not have a miraculous, surefire plan to succeed the U.S. as the world’s new hegemon. Nor is there evidence that other countries are prepared to embrace a Chinese-led system entirely. China’s ambition appears more complicated: it seeks greater influence over the ideas and institutions that determine how the international system works. Beijing wants not merely a decisive vote in the game, but a hand in writing its rules.
Beijing is pursuing this ambition at a moment when Washington, despite its power, appears less willing to shoulder the traditional burdens of global leadership. Its domestic political divisions, the Trump Administration’s apparent disregard for international law, and its erratic approach to foreign policy and global conflicts have raised questions about the future of American stewardship.
Yet China is not inheriting a vacuum. Thanks to its power, Washington remains deeply entrenched in the institutions, alliances, and technologies that underpin its supremacy. China is gaining room to shape the international order, but it is not yet replacing the power that built much of it. Instead, Beijing is creating alternatives that allow other countries to become less dependent on the existing American-led system.
China’s new new world vision
Perhaps the most powerful element of China’s vision for a different international order is not its defense of national sovereignty or multipolarity, but its proposition about development. Beijing is asking a pointed question: what if countries need not follow the Western path to modernity?
For much of the past eight decades, the prevailing vision of development was associated with a broadly Western model: foreign aid, privatization, and political liberalization. China offers something different, defying the hopes of Western intellectuals and policymakers who believed that Beijing’s entry into the World Trade Organization in 2001 would eventually lead to its political liberalization.
China’s own experience suggests that economic success can be built, at least partly, through investments in infrastructure, financed by public finance and state loans. The old Chinese expression about “getting richer by building roads” has also shaped its approach abroad: Beijing has committed itself to financing and promoting across the Global South the type of infrastructure that helped power its own economic miracle.
The developing world has been receptive. China’s Global Development Initiative places development at the center of its international engagement. Although the Belt and Road Initiative has been heavily criticized since its inception, it has provided Beijing with a practical platform for financing and building infrastructure overseas. Beijing is making its case not through elegantly written standards of governance but through tangible things: roads, railways, and ports.
Over the past decade, the Chinese government and its state-owned enterprises invested approximately $634 billion into building physical infrastructure around the world, along with $419 billion in direct investments outside the financial sector in the developing world. For many governments in Latin America—a region Washington has long regarded as its strategic backyard—access to Chinese development finance and Chinese markets has led to significant economic gains.
China’s development strategy creates economic relationships that should endure for decades, especially when its financing carries conditions that serve Beijing’s interests, including privileged access to critical minerals and resources. But the era of immense Chinese overseas spending is becoming harder to sustain as Beijing grapples with its own economic woes.
The ultimate test of Beijing’s economic statecraft, then, is whether it can build lasting relationships across the globe that rest on more than financial largesse and accumulated diplomatic capital. China must demonstrate that it understands what developing countries actually need and that those needs will evolve over time.
A new age of Chinese tech
Influence is no longer exerted through explicit military might but built quietly into the infrastructure of everyday economic life. As development becomes increasingly intertwined with technology, a country that adopts Chinese cloud computing may also embed itself in a Chinese-led ecosystem that endures for decades.
Artificial intelligence offers the clearest example of technology as a source of geopolitical power. China is rapidly promoting its AI capabilities globally, including open-weight models that can be deployed at a fraction of the cost of their Western competitors. For much of the developing world, the appeal is obvious: those countries can gain access to cutting-edge technology without having to rely exclusively on American tech giants.
The technological race is also becoming a competition over the development choices countries make. If most economies build their digital infrastructure and AI systems primarily around American technologies, Washington will retain an enormous structural advantage. As countries invest in those systems, they will become increasingly dependent on them, while American tech giants gain access to vast stores of user data. If more countries come to rely on Chinese technologies and the standards and supply chains associated with them, China will acquire greater influence: less visible than military power, but potentially just as consequential and enduring.
This is why China’s enormous industrial capacity has become a central instrument of its effort to shape the global order. Beijing is not merely exporting products: it is helping determine which technologies countries use to modernize themselves, and by extension, the systems their economies will rely on.
A central ambiguity lies at the heart of China’s development strategy. Chinese technology can expand a country’s economic opportunities but is bound to increase its dependence on China. That tension is likely to persist longer than many anticipated. Many governments are choosing Chinese technology for its affordability and not because they have been persuaded by Beijing’s governing philosophy. A country may adopt Chinese systems while remaining aligned with the U.S. on security.
China therefore does not depend on others becoming “pro-China”. It may be enough for them to become less dependent on the West. This is a vital distinction. Beijing need not convince the world that its model is superior. It only needs to show that alternatives to Western technologies exist. The cumulative effect of those alternatives could gradually alter the balance of the global order.
China’s statecraft is a way of redistributing economic and technological power. Unlike the U.S., China’s most significant export may not be a political model but the infrastructure and technology through which other countries seek to build prosperity. In adopting those systems, they become part of a world less dominated by the U.S. and its European allies.
Networks, not alliances
Before arriving in Washington, President Xi undertook a flurry of overseas travel, visiting places that American presidents have largely neglected: Bishkek, Cairo, New Delhi. His itinerary illuminated an interesting pattern. Each of his September stops connected China to the expanding international networks Beijing has championed and some Western governments regard with suspicion, notably the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) and BRICS.
Consider BRICS. What began as an informal gathering of emerging economies has become a much larger political forum, with countries from the Middle East, Africa, and elsewhere seeking membership or closer connections. It would be a mistake to consider BRICS as a Beijing-led anti-American bloc. Its members have sharply different interests, and countries such as India have no intention of joining an anti-Western alliance. But the group’s expansion reflects a critical shift: a growing number of countries want access to institutions in which the Group of 7 does not set the terms.
The Group of 7 is an exclusive club whose members broadly share political values and standards of governance. China does not demand that other countries abandon institutions led by Washington; instead, it builds alternatives that exist alongside them. That distinction matters.
This is why I expect that the emerging world order will not be divided neatly between a Chinese camp and an American one. Most countries will continue to use the dollar, trade with the U.S., and participate in Western institutions while simultaneously joining BRICS, borrowing from Chinese-backed institutions, and engaging with the SCO. For many governments, the fundamental attraction is the freedom to choose among competing sources of finance, technology, and diplomatic support.
Beijing’s advocacy of multipolarity is neither merely about building a fairer world, nor is it about replacing one hegemon with another. It is an attempt to widen the range of choices available to other states. By establishing new institutions and initiatives, Beijing is accelerating the movement of power away from the traditional centers of the West. For China, being an architect of the international order does not necessarily mean replacing America, but building a world where the U.S. can no longer design all the rules or define legitimate international behavior by itself.
Yet the China dilemma remains. Beijing opposes an international order dominated by a single power, but fragmenting that system would inevitably increase China’s global influence. And the more influence China acquires, the more other countries may begin to question whether Beijing’s vision is truly intended to produce greater equality, or merely a new distribution of power that benefits China most.
An order shaper in the making
President Xi’s meeting with President Trump will be scrutinized for the usual signs of rivalry: tariffs, technology restrictions, and strategic tensions. But beneath those headlines lies the great contest over how the international order itself should work.
China is not seeking to inherit the world America built. It is trying to change how that world works by giving other countries choices beyond the American-led system. For decades, the U.S. was identified with policing the rules-based international order, while China was portrayed primarily as its challenger. But during President Trump's second term, questions of sovereignty and international law have themselves become more contested, blurring what once seemed a clear distinction between the American and Chinese approaches.
Whether China’s ascent produces a fairer international order, a more genuinely multipolar one, or simply a new system in which Chinese power carries greater weight remains uncertain. The answer will depend not only on what Beijing wants, but also on what other countries are willing to accept. For now, China’s ambition may not be to write all the rules, but to ensure that Washington is no longer the only power capable of writing them.

articles.title: Netanyahu expected to attack Mamdani in UN general assembly speech – latest updates
articles.body:
Palestinian delegation was unlawfully denied entry visas, Abbas tells UN
Mahmoud Abbas, the longtime president of the Palestinian Authority, is now addressing the gathering. He is delivering his speech via a pre-recorded video for the second year in a row, after the Trump administration refused to grant him a visa.
He said:
For the second consecutive year, the Palestinian delegation was denied the entry visas required to reach New York and participate in the meetings of the United Nations General Assembly in person. We reject these unlawful punitive measures, and we reject the accusations and justifications on which they were based.”
The state department said in a statement that the Palestinian Authority and the Palestine Liberation Organisation had “failed to live up to their commitments”, accusing the groups of “taking actions to internationalise the Israeli-Palestinian conflict including through the international criminal court and international court of justice” and of “glorifying terrorism” among other allegations.
Abbas denied the accusations, saying:
We affirm that we have fulfilled our obligations, carried out a comprehensive national reform programme, and upheld our commitment to international law, to shunning violence and terrorism, and to the two state solution and to peace on the basis of resolutions of international legitimacy.”
Netanyahu claims Mamdani is antisemetic while defending Israel’s efforts to spare Palestinian lives
We’ve taken innumerable steps to protect the civilian population,” Netanyahu claims. “Is this genocide? Of course not. It’s the opposite of genocide.
“To all those spreading lies about my country and its brave soldiers, whether they sit in this hall, or in the antisemitic office of the mayor of New York, I say this: Shame on you. Shame on you for distorting the facts. Shame on you for inverting victim and aggressor. Shame on you for spitting in the face of truth.”
He adds: “Mr Mamdani, since you were elected mayor of this city, many jews no longer feel safe in New York.”
Earlier this month, The Guardian reported that Israeli attacks in Gaza since 2023 have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, and injured more than 174,000 others, together representing more than 10% of Gaza’s prewar population.
Netanyahu hails the IDF as “the most moral army in the world”.
“For three years, our brave soldiers have been valiantly fighting a seven-front war. But there’s an eighth front to this war. It’s the war for truth. It is waged in the world’s media, and most perniciously, in social media. Several foreign countries have spent untold billions to spread lies about my country.”
He salutes the Israeli people for their “unrelenting resolve”.
“This is Israel. One nation fighting for one future,” he adds.
Netanyahu lashes out at the international media for what he says is distorted coverage of settler violence, which he puts down to a small number of teenage “delinquents”.
He says he has no time for vigilantism. “I won’t stand for it. We’re a country of law,” he says, and goes on to describe “peaceful settlers – honest people – law-abiding people”.
Netanyahu outlines the horror Israel faced on 7 October 2023 – “the worst slaughter of Jews since the holocaust”.
“They went house to house, shooting Israeli civilians point blank. They did so with fiendish glee, with sadistic joy. They live-streamed as they murdered.
“And who did they murder – their neighbours – the very Israelis who gave them jobs. Who picked up Palestinian children at the Gaza border and drove them to Israeli hospitals for cancer treatment, and then brought them back.”
“These Hamas monsters killed holocaust survivors,” he says. “They burnt babies alive in front of their parents.
“Altogether they slaughtered 1,200 Israelis that day. I want to give you an idea of what this means for a country of 10 million. Proportionately, this is equal to 40,000 innocent Americans slaughtered in less than 24 hours. That’s 16 times 9/11.”
Speaking about Israel’s strikes on Iran, Netanyahu says that “in defending itself, Israel is also defending many of the countries whose delegates have just left this hall.”
He claims that in private, many representing these countries have thanked Israel for “taking out Iran’s nukes”.
“It’s hard to imagine more mind-blowing hypocrisy. But that is what it is,” he says.
Israel’s prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu now takes to the stage to deliver his highly anticipated address.
His appearance at the UN General Assembly in New York comes after the city’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, called him a war criminal.
Earlier this week Netanyahu addressed Mamdani directly and said he was going to New York “to tell the truth about our heroic soldiers” and “to tell the truth about you.”
He falsely accused Mamdani of supporting Hamas militants.
Ahead of his speech, Netanyahu’s government paid to place 500 pro-Israel and anti-Iran billboards and dozens of trucks carrying messages in support of Israel across Manhattan, Netanyahu’s office said in a statement.
“Freedom doesn’t defend itself. America and Israel stand together against terror,” one of the billboards states. Under it appears the subtext: “Paid for by the State of Israel“.
Meanwhile, anti-Israel protesters have taken to New York’s streets. Several hundred anti-Israel protesters gathered near the UN’s HQ in Manhattan on Thursday with dozens blocking traffic and chanting: “Stop arming Israel, let Gaza live” and “Stop arming Israel, let Iran live.”
The vice president of Colombia José Manuel Restrepo is on the podium. Reading the words of Colombian president, Abelardo de la Espriella, he begins by speaking about the major earthquake which hit Colombia in August – the strongest to hit the country this century, and which left over 300 dead and thousands without homes.
He says the disaster highlighted Colombia’s resilience and the power of the international community. He goes on to outline the problems posed by organised crime, affecting Colombia, but related to international demand for illicit drugs.
“Drug trafficking is a transnational criminal enterprise,” he says. “Its networks operate across numerous countries. I will do everything necessary to combat that scourge.” But he says it also requires an international response to stamp out this issue, one which provides a solid base for economic growth, and calls for greater investment in the country.
International community must do their ‘utmost’ to end Russian aggression
Costa says Russia’s escalation of war has been “unacceptable”.
Human rights and international law apply everywhere – in the Middle East, in Ukraine and in Africa, he says.
“This was a war chosen by Russia, the consequences of which are worldwide in scope.”.
“It is unacceptable that over the last 12 months that Russia has on several occasions threatened the security of several European Union member states. Russia must bring an end to this escalation,” he adds.
He goes on to say the international community “must do their utmost to bring an end to this war”.
“This war must end. The same goes for the Middle East.”
“The two state solution is the only one that can ensure lasting peace in the Middle East,” he says.
The president of the European Council of the European Union, António Costa, is now speaking about the role the UN can play in the future.
Multilateralism is the only way to deal with the numerous problems the world faces, he says, including tackling the climate crisis, global health concerns and the risks posed by AI.
The UN “must remain at the centre of the multilateral system,” he says, adding that he recognises that the UN is under pressure from “geopolitical polarisation, financial constraints and institutional shortcomings, and calls for reform and re-investment.
On the international challenge posed by AI he adds: “We need an AI that serves humanity, not controls it.” And it should not be controlled by a handful of large companies. The UN should play a major role in setting “global standards” on AI governance, he suggests.
President of Hungary András Baka uses his address to warn about Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
“A lasting peace must respect Ukraine’s sovereignty,” he tells delegates. “If taking territory by force becomes an accepted way of settling disputes, every smaller country will have reasons to worry about its own future.”
Speaking about the Middle East, he outlines Hungary’s support for international law.
“We call for full respect for humanitarian law and for aid to reach those who need it safely and without interruption,” he says. “Israelis and Palestinians must be able to live in security and dignity. A lasting peace must give their families reasons to believe that their children can grow up without the fear that has marked so many lives. For people forced from their homes by war or persecution, protection may mean first finding safety in another country. Hungary’s own history gives us reason to understand that need.”
Zelenskyy tells Russian journalist he will visit Moscow 'on a rocket'
A video showing an exchange between the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy and a Russian journalist is making the rounds on social media.
In the clip, the journalist repeatedly asked Zelenskyy in Russian when he will visit Moscow as the Ukrainian president walked with security guards along a street in New York, where he attended the UN general assembly.
According to a report by the independent Russian news outlet Meduza, Zelenskyy replied over his shoulder “on a rocket”, before apparently adding an obscenity which cannot be heard clearly in the recording.
Meduza reported that the journalist was Valentin Bogdanov, a correspondent for the Russian state broadcasting company VGTRK.
It caught the attention of Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, who responded to the incident during a briefing today. “Zelenskyy didn’t refuse to come to Moscow; at least, I haven’t heard that,” Peskov said, according to the Russian Tass news agency.
Plans to set up a global UN body on inequality modelled on the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) are likely to be proposed to a meeting of the UN general assembly in the coming months.
Speaking at an event on the sidelines of the general assembly in New York, left-leaning leaders from Brazil, Norway and Spain claimed momentum was building behind calls for a standing international panel on inequality that would recognise the issue as a global challenge threatening world security. Two G7 countries – Germany and Japan – have given public backing.
Joseph Stiglitz, the Nobel prize-winning economist, recommended the establishment of the new body in a report commissioned by South Africa for its G20 chairing last November. The dislocation caused by inequality was also the focus of the 2024 G20 meeting, chaired by Brazil.
But the proposal is likely to make little political headway during this year’s G20, to be led by Donald Trump, and some countries are wary of talk about new globally imposed taxes, or assertions that economic analysis can be compared to climate science.

articles.title: NATO chief wants Europeans to fight American wars
articles.body:
NATO chief wants Europeans to fight American wars
European NATO nations should take greater responsibility for security in the Middle East, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has said. He also defended the US-Israeli war on Iran and argued that European members should spend less on social programs and more on the military.
Rutte made the remarks at a Chicago Council on Global Affairs event in Iowa on Tuesday after being asked to “make the case” for NATO to Americans by explaining “what’s in it” for them.
He described the Middle East as “Europe’s backyard” and “not the United States’ backyard,” arguing that Washington’s war against Tehran was “necessary” but that the US had to launch it because “somehow the Europeans did not have enough capabilities to do it themselves.”
“In the future, what you get from a stronger NATO is that Europeans can take care of their own backyard,” Rutte said.
The US-Israeli war on Iran, launched in late February, caused major friction within NATO as several European members resisted supporting Washington’s belligerence. Spain refused to allow American warplanes to use its bases for the campaign, drawing US President Donald Trump’s ire. Germany and the UK described the conflict as “not our war,” while stopping short of condemning the US and Israel.
Trump has since repeatedly accused European allies of failing to meet their NATO commitments and claimed the bloc “was not there when we needed them.” In April, US War Secretary Pete Hegseth said NATO’s future was uncertain and Washington could not currently reaffirm its commitment to collective defense.
Rutte also argued on Tuesday that the burden within NATO was unfair because European members spend heavily “on pensions and welfare,” while Washington has to devote more resources to weapons but “would also like to spend more on all these other lofty, beautiful items, but they can’t because they have to spend so much on defense.”
He described raising NATO’s defense spending target from 2% to 5% of GDP as “the fairness element” and part of an “equalizing” process. The remarks come as Washington pushes for a reorganization dubbed NATO 3.0, under which European members would sharply increase military spending and production while assuming “primary responsibility for the conventional defense of Europe.”
Rutte also offered to help “protect the United States from threats of Russia” and China and prevent the Arctic “from becoming militarized by the Russians and the Chinese.”
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said last month that Moscow was primarily interested in “preserving the Arctic as an area of peace and cooperation” and accused NATO of “driving the region towards militarization.” His comments followed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s proposal earlier this year to use increased EU military spending on “Arctic-ready equipment.”

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Putin is patient zero and has to be stopped
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: Putin is patient zero and has to be stopped
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has called Russian leader Vladimir Putin "patient zero" who is spreading the idea of war around the world.
Source: Zelenskyy's address to the UN General Assembly in New York, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Zelenskyy stressed that Putin "is always looking for someone who can help him kill more people for every kilometre of land, take more territory and attack another country" rather than stopping and running his own country.
"After all of this, can you even imagine him without war? He is 'patient zero' – the one from whom this idea of war keeps spreading further. And wherever it spreads, it brings only pain, instability, new risks and, of course, new crises," the president emphasised.
Zelenskyy said that the more freedom Putin has to act, the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else.
He explained that Ukraine is targeting Russia's oil industry in an effort to stop Moscow and undermine its ability to finance the war.
"Oil itself is not Ukraine's target. It is not our target. Not gasoline or diesel, not factories or ports as such. Our target is Russia's ability to finance this war, to drag it out, to make it more brutal and more destructive. Russia's finances and Russia's production are what must be stopped if Putin is to be stopped," he stressed.
In this context, Zelenskyy pointed out that when anyone lifts or eases sanctions against Russia, they "give this war more time".
"And when someone in the world weakens sanctions, weakens sanctions against Russian oligarchs, it may make life more comfortable for rich Russians, but it also gives the war more time – more time for Putin to send poor people into the kill zone," he added.
Zelenskyy noted that Russia threatens lives in Ukraine every hour by attacking the country with drones and missiles.
"Would your country survive if, God forbid, you had to face something like this? Ukraine has," the president asked those present, urging them to join efforts to strengthen Ukraine's air defence.
Background:
- Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha stressed during a UN Security Council meeting that Russia's war against Ukraine poses a threat to the entire world.
- It was also reported that 50 countries and the European Union issued a joint statement in support of Ukraine at the UN, calling on Russia to agree to a ceasefire. The United States did not join the statement.
- The previous day, US President Donald Trump called on Putin to "settle the war" against Ukraine.

articles.title: ADF neutralizes four Zircon missiles, three ballistic missiles and 219 Russian UAVs used to attack Ukraine overnight
articles.body:
ADF neutralizes four Zircon missiles, three ballistic missiles and 219 Russian UAVs used to attack Ukraine overnight
According to Ukrinform, Ukraine's Air Force reported this on Telegram.
Beginning at 18:00 on Wednesday, September 23, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with Zircon anti-ship missiles launched from the Kursk, Rostov and Oryol regions; Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles launched from the Kursk and Bryansk regions; and 282 attack UAVs, including jet-powered drones, of the Shahed type, Gerbera drones, Banderol/Dan-T loitering munitions, and Parodiya-type decoy drones.
The drones were launched from areas including Oryol, Millerovo, Shatalovo, Kursk and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia; temporarily occupied Donetsk; as well as Hvardiiske and Chauda in temporarily occupied Crimea and the waters of the Sea of Azov.
The Odesa and Kyiv regions were the main targets of the attack.
The air assault was repelled by Ukrainian combat aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned-systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00 on Thursday, September 24, air defense forces had shot down or suppressed 227 targets:
- four Zircon missiles;
- three Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles;
- one Banderol/Dan-T munition;
- 219 drones.
Hits were recorded at 13 locations, while falling debris from downed targets was reported at another 10 locations.
The attack is ongoing, with dozens of enemy UAVs still in Ukrainian airspace.
As Ukrinform reported, during the night of September 24, Russian forces attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles and drones.
A 57-year-old woman was killed in the Podilskyi district and a 65-year-old man was killed in the Solomianskyi district.
Another eight people, aged between 25 and 77, were injured. A police officer was among those wounded.
Photo: Defense Forces

articles.title: Kremlin slams EU over transfer of Russian profits to Ukraine
articles.body:
Kremlin slams EU over transfer of Russian profits to Ukraine
The EU is committing “theft” by handing over profits from frozen Russian assets to Ukraine, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said.
Some $300 billion in Moscow’s funds were blocked by the US and EU after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022. Around $240 billion of the sum is still being held at the Belgium-based clearing house Euroclear.
On Wednesday, high-ranking Russian Foreign Ministry official Vladislav Maslennikov told RIA Novosti that Brussels has already transferred €8 billion ($9.1 billion) in income generated by the frozen Russian assets to the government in Kiev. Some €3.5 billion from the sum has been used to purchase arms for Ukrainian forces that are fighting the Russian military, he added.
When asked to comment on the development by journalists on Thursday, Peskov replied by saying that Moscow considers such actions as illegal.
“We truly believe this is theft. And we treat it accordingly, nothing has changed in our position here,” the spokesman noted.
Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) said on Tuesday that the EU is working on a new scheme to confiscate the $240 billion in Moscow’s frozen sovereign assets altogether.
The bloc’s leaders have “a vital interest in stealing Russian assets” because they fear they will not be able to indefinitely finance Ukraine on their own, it said.
EU bureaucrats in Brussels are now discussing the creation of a new supranational structure that could take control of Russian central bank funds after they are moved outside Belgium’s jurisdiction, the SVR said.
The Belgian government has repeatedly blocked proposals to seize the assets, with Prime Minister Bart De Wever warning that such a step would expose his country to legal and financial liability. Euroclear has also said it could sue the EU if the funds are confiscated.
The bloc is “in a hurry” to pull off the seizure before elections in several EU states in 2027, the SVR stated, arguing that future governments in the bloc could be less willing to back further financial support for Ukraine.
The agency also warned that the move would undermine trust in European financial institutions among major foreign investors, including China, India, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Singapore.
Moscow has long said that any attempt to appropriate its sovereign funds would be against the law, warning that it would trigger legal action and retaliation, potentially including measures against Western assets held in Russia.

articles.title: Former prosecutor general Kravchenko appears to have violated Vienna residency registration rules – UP
articles.body:
Former prosecutor general Kravchenko appears to have violated Vienna residency registration rules – UP
Former Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko appears to have violated the rules concerning his registered place of residence after moving to Vienna.
Source: an article by Ukrainska Pravda journalist Mykhailo Tkach
Details: The address listed in a document from the Austrian register is not Kravchenko's place of residence, as required by law.
Apartment No. 12 in the building at 7 Jordangasse is not a residential property but the office of CS Corporate Services GmbH. On its website, the company offers four services: domiciliation, meaning a registered legal address for Austrian limited liability companies; secretarial services; management services; and the sale of shelf companies that are already registered and ready to be transferred to a new owner.
The description of its domiciliation service says that an address in Vienna's first district, a few minutes' walk from the central square Stephansplatz, is registered with the Commercial Court, tax authorities and municipal authorities, while staff receive clients' post and, on their instructions, forward it unopened, scan it or reply to it themselves.
At least two dozen other legal entities are registered at the same address. They include subsidiaries of genuine international companies such as Duracell Austria GmbH and KPLER GmbH, but most are little-known companies, including Numitor, Febania, Nobeka, Furninet, Code Panda IT Solutions and others.
Kravchenko and his wife may have taken this step to conceal their actual place of residence in Vienna.
Registration in Vienna may also indicate that Kravchenko plans to establish legal residence in the Austrian capital, as it is well known that Austria does not extradite people wanted by Ukraine.
Tkach noted that when speaking to an influential official about the fate of Ukrainian officials in Austria, he had heard a wry comment: "At this rate, Vienna will soon have an entire Ukrainian government-in-exile."
Apart from the prosecutor general, who appears to have registered in Vienna only recently, the city is already home to former constitutional court chairman Oleksandr Tupytskyi, former National Bank governor Kyrylo Shevchenko, former MP Andrii Kholodov and many other "former" officials who have largely become stranded in one of Europe's best cities for years, either because of the war or to avoid punishment.
"In a city where there are no air-raid warnings, ballistic missiles, notices of suspicion issued by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) or the need to pay bail. In a city that does not extradite people wanted by Ukraine. For now," Tkach added.
Previously: It was reported that Kravchenko had left Ukraine on the night of 13-14 September, travelling abroad in a luxury taxi rather than an official vehicle and crossing the border at the Shehyni-Medyka checkpoint.
It is also known that Kravchenko submitted a letter of resignation from the prosecution service. It was accepted, and Kravchenko was dismissed from the prosecution service on 21 September.
Background:
- On 7 September, Kravchenko resigned as prosecutor general amid an investigation by NABU and SAPO into the alleged "protection" of scam call centres.
- On 14 September, Kravchenko said he had signed a notice of suspicion against NABU director Semen Kryvonos and accused NABU and SAPO of seizing materials from criminal proceedings against employees of the anti-corruption agencies in the course of searches conducted as part of Operation Carthage.
- According to Ukrainska Pravda sources in law enforcement, Kravchenko left Ukraine in an official car on the night of 13-14 September.
- He said in a statement that he had left to go on an official trip. According to an order by the prosecutor general dated 13 September, a copy of which was seen by Ukrainska Pravda, Kravchenko left for Paris for five days "to take part in PACE hearings on Ukrainian children". However, he was not listed among the speakers on the event agenda.
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged the Verkhovna Rada (Ukrainian parliament) to back Kravchenko's dismissal as prosecutor general.
- On 14 September, Zelenskyy signed a decree suspending Kravchenko as prosecutor general. The Verkhovna Rada later voted in favour of his dismissal.
- As of 21 September, Kravchenko, whose official trip abroad ended on 18 September, had not returned to work.

articles.title: Russians hit Kyiv with ballistic missiles: two killed, eight injured – photos
articles.body:
Russians hit Kyiv with ballistic missiles: two killed, eight injured – photos
Two people are known to have been killed and eight injured in a Russian ballistic missile strike on Kyiv on the night of 23-24 September.
Source: Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko; Kyiv City Military Administration; State Emergency Service of Ukraine
Quote from Klitschko: "One person has been killed and two others injured in the capital. Medics have taken both the injured people to hospital."
Details: Since the beginning of the night there had been reports of several waves of ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv, numerous explosions in the capital, damage caused, and calls for medical assistance.
Klitschko also said a house in Kyiv's Dniprovskyi district had been partially destroyed after debris fell in the courtyard of a private property. There may be people trapped under the rubble.
In the Podilskyi district, debris fell on a car park near a medical facility, causing vehicles to catch fire.
Update: Klitschko later reported that windows and part of the facade of a maternity hospital in the Podilskyi district had been damaged after missile debris fell nearby.
Early reports indicate that there are no casualties at the medical facility.
However, Klitschko said that one person had been killed in a car park near the facility.
A nearby medical diagnostic centre was also damaged.
"As of now, two people have been killed and three injured in the capital. All those injured have been taken to hospital," he stated.
He also reported that debris had fallen at two more locations in the Dniprovskyi district, both on the grounds of private properties. One of the houses was damaged.
Missile debris fell onto a road in the Darnytskyi district.
Quote from Klitschko at 03:00: "Two people have been killed and five injured in the capital. Three of those injured have been taken to hospital. Two are in a critical condition."
Details: It later became known that the number of people injured had risen to six.
Update: In the morning, emergency services reported that the number of people injured in the ballistic missile strike on Kyiv overnight had risen to eight.
According to the State Emergency Service, warehouse buildings in the Solomianskyi district were partially destroyed and subsequently caught fire, with the flames spreading to basement areas. The fire has been extinguished. Three people were taken to hospital.
In the Podilskyi district, a fire broke out involving four cars in a car park following the strike near the maternity hospital. The fire was extinguished and a body was found.
At another location, a single-storey non-residential building caught fire. This fire was also extinguished.
In the Dniprovskyi district, another person was injured, while a fire in an office building was also extinguished.
At another location, a house was destroyed and two neighbouring houses were damaged. A fire was extinguished and one person was rescued.
